uni-cse-graphics.description: A complete computer-graphics course: output primitives, 2-D and 3-D transformations, viewing and clipping, projections, curves and surfaces, hidden-surface removal, illumination, shading and ray tracing, with code labs and a practical/viva revision unit.

lessons.title: Graphics systems, pixels and frame buffer

scenes.text: Asha designs a banner at 640x480 and projects it on a 1920x1080 screen. It looks blocky.
Her teacher explains that the picture is a grid of pixels and the screen simply has more of them than the file.

steps.title: Pixels and resolution
steps.body: A **raster** image is a 2-D grid of **pixels** (picture elements). Resolution = columns x rows (e.g. 1920 x 1080). **Colour depth** (bits per pixel, bpp) decides how many colours: 2^bpp. 8 bpp = 256 colours, 24 bpp = 16.7 million (true colour).

steps.title: Frame buffer
steps.body:
The **frame buffer** is video memory holding one value per pixel. The **video controller** reads it repeatedly (the **refresh rate**, in Hz) and sends it to the display.

**Size in bytes = (width x height x bpp) / 8.**

steps.title: Solved: how many colours from 12 KiB of memory for 128 x 96 pixels?
Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting to divide by 8 (bits vs bytes).
- Mixing 1 KB = 1000 and 1 KiB = 1024; state your convention.
- Confusing resolution (pixel count) with size (inches) and with dpi.

activity.prompt: A display is 1280 x 1024 pixels at 8 bits per pixel. How many bytes must the frame buffer hold?

lessons.title: Display devices: raster scan, random scan and flat panels

story.title: Why old arcade games looked sharp

scenes.text: Vector arcade machines drew glowing lines directly, so diagonals were smooth but they could not fill large areas.
Home TVs used raster scanning: every pixel row was swept, so filled colour was easy but diagonals showed jaggies.

steps.title: Random-scan (vector) vs raster-scan
steps.body:
**Random scan**: the beam is steered only along the lines to draw; a **display file** stores line-drawing commands; picture is redrawn 30-60 times/s. Good for line drawings, smooth lines, no aliasing; poor at filled areas and shading.

**Raster scan**: the beam sweeps row by row (**scan lines**), intensity set per pixel from the frame buffer. Good for realistic, filled, shaded images; suffers aliasing.

steps.title: Refresh details
steps.body:
- **Interlaced** scanning draws odd lines then even lines to reduce flicker; **progressive** draws all lines each pass.
- **Horizontal retrace** = beam returns to the next line start; **vertical retrace** = return to top. Both are blanked.
- Flicker disappears above about 60 Hz.

steps.title: Modern flat panels
steps.body: **LCD**: liquid-crystal cells twist polarised backlight; **LED-LCD** uses LED backlight; **OLED** pixels emit their own light (true blacks, no backlight); **plasma** used gas discharge (obsolete). All are raster devices addressed by a matrix.

steps.title: Solved: refresh bandwidth
steps.body:
1920 x 1080 pixels, 24 bpp, 60 Hz.
1. Pixels/frame = 2,073,600.
2. Bytes/frame = 2,073,600 x 3 = 6,220,800.
3. Per second = 6,220,800 x 60 = **373,248,000 B/s ~ 373 MB/s** (ignoring blanking).

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: Saying raster scan is 'better' always. Vector displays still win for crisp line plots; raster wins for filled, shaded scenes.

story.title: Drawing a slanted line on a grid

scenes.text: Ravi must light pixels from (2,3) to (8,7) on a pixel grid.
He cannot light fractions of a pixel, so he steps along the longer axis and rounds.

steps.title: The idea
steps.body: The **Digital Differential Analyser** uses the line equation y = mx + c incrementally. Let dx = x2-x1, dy = y2-y1. **steps = max(|dx|,|dy|)**; x-increment = dx/steps; y-increment = dy/steps. Starting at (x1,y1) add the increments each step and plot **round(x), round(y)**.

steps.title: Weaknesses
steps.body:
- Floating-point addition accumulates round-off drift on long lines.
- Rounding is a slow operation. Bresenham fixes both using integers only.
- Mistake: using steps = dx always; for steep lines this skips rows.

lessons.title: Lab: Bresenham line and its decision parameter

scenes.text: An embedded display chip has no floating-point unit.
The engineer uses Bresenham's algorithm, which chooses the next pixel using only integer additions.

steps.title: Derivation sketch (0 < m < 1)
steps.body: At each x-step the line is closer to either pixel (x+1, y) or (x+1, y+1). Define the decision parameter p = 2dy - dx at the start. If **p < 0** choose (x+1, y) and p += 2dy; else choose (x+1, y+1) and p += 2dy - 2dx. Derived by comparing the distances d1 and d2 from the true line and scaling by dx to remove the division.

steps.title: Other slopes
steps.body: For m > 1 swap the roles of x and y. For negative slopes decrement y. Always reduce to the 0 < m < 1 case by symmetry, then map back.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using p0 = 2dy + dx.
- Updating p *before* choosing the pixel with the old p.
- Forgetting the last point (x2,y2).

activity.prompt: Implement Bresenham for (20,10)-(30,18) and print the last three plotted points as a list.
activity.starter:

x,y=x1,y1
out=[(x,y)]
while x<x2:
    x+=1
    # update y and p
    out.append((x,y))
print(out[-3:])
activity.solution:
x1,y1,x2,y2=20,10,30,18
dx,dy=x2-x1,y2-y1
p=2*dy-dx
x,y=x1,y1
out=[(x,y)]

    else:
        y+=1
        p+=2*dy-2*dx

lessons.title: Lab: Capstone - Midpoint circle algorithm and 8-way symmetry

scenes.text: A game needs a pixel circle of radius 10 centred at the origin.
Instead of computing the whole circle, we compute one 45-degree arc and mirror it eight ways.

steps.title: Symmetry
steps.body: A circle x^2+y^2 = r^2 is symmetric about both axes and the line y = x, so each computed point (x,y) gives eight: (+-x,+-y) and (+-y,+-x). We compute only the octant from (0,r) until x >= y.

steps.title: Decision parameter
steps.body: Use f(x,y) = x^2 + y^2 - r^2 evaluated at the midpoint between two candidate pixels. Start p0 = 1 - r. At each step x -> x+1: if **p < 0**, y stays, p += 2x + 1 (with the new x); else y -> y-1 and p += 2x + 1 - 2y (with new x and y).

steps.title: Solved: r = 10
steps.body: p0 = 1 - 10 = -9. Points: (0,10) p-9; (1,10) p-6; (2,10) p-1; (3,10) p6; (4,9) p-3; (5,9) p8; (6,8) p5; (7,7) p6. Stop at x = y. First octant has 8 points; mirror each to get the full ring.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using p0 = 5/4 - r without rounding (fine for integer r: 1 - r).
- Not stopping at x >= y (duplicates points).
- Plotting the centre offset wrongly: add (xc, yc) to every mirrored point.

activity.prompt: Generate the first-octant points of the midpoint circle for r = 10 and print the list.
activity.starter:
r=10
x,y=0,r
p=1-r
pts=[(x,y)]
while x<y:
    x+=1
    # update y and p
    pts.append((x,y))
print(pts)
activity.solution:
r=10
x,y=0,r
p=1-r
pts=[(x,y)]
while x<y:
    x+=1
    if p<0:
        p+=2*x+1
    else:
        y-=1
        p+=2*x+1-2*y
    pts.append((x,y))
print(pts)
activity.hint: After x+=1: if p<0 then p+=2*x+1 else y-=1 and p+=2*x+1-2*y

courses.title: Unit 2 · Two-dimensional transformations
courses.summary: Translation, scaling, rotation, reflection and shear in 2-D; homogeneous coordinates; composite transformations such as rotation about a pivot; why order matters. Solved matrix problems and code labs.
outcomes: Write 2-D transformation matrices in homogeneous form
Compose transformations and apply them in the right order
Rotate or scale about an arbitrary point
Apply reflection and shear to polygons

scenes.text: In a 2-D game, a sprite must move right, grow when a power-up is taken, and spin.
Each action is a transformation of every vertex of the sprite.

steps.title: Translation
steps.body: Shift by (tx, ty): x' = x + tx, y' = y + ty. It preserves shape, size and orientation (a rigid motion).

steps.title: Scaling
steps.body: About the origin: x' = sx.x, y' = sy.y. If sx = sy it is **uniform**; otherwise differential. sx,sy > 1 enlarges and moves the object away from the origin; < 1 shrinks it toward the origin.

steps.title: Rotation (anticlockwise by theta about the origin)
steps.body:
x' = x cos(theta) - y sin(theta)
y' = x sin(theta) + y cos(theta)

Derivation: write the point as (r cos a, r sin a) and expand cos(a+theta), sin(a+theta).

steps.title: Solved: rotate (10,0) by 60 degrees
steps.body: x' = 10 cos60 = 5; y' = 10 sin60 = 8.66. New point (5, 8.66). Check length: sqrt(25+75) = 10, so distance from origin is preserved.

steps.title: Solved: scale triangle (1,1),(3,1),(2,4) by sx=2, sy=3
steps.body: (2,3), (6,3), (4,12). Area before = 0.5 x 2 x 3 = 3; after = 3 x (2x3) = 18 = area x sx.sy.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using degrees in a calculator set to radians.
- Forgetting that scaling is about the origin, so the object also moves.
- Mixing clockwise and anticlockwise (negative theta = clockwise).

lessons.title: Homogeneous coordinates and rotation about a pivot

scenes.text: A door must swing about its hinge, not about the screen origin.
We move the hinge to the origin, rotate, and move it back. Homogeneous matrices let us glue all three into one.

steps.title: Why homogeneous coordinates?
steps.body:
Translation is an addition, while rotation and scaling are multiplications. Adding a third coordinate (x, y, 1) lets all three be 3x3 matrices so they can be multiplied into a **single composite matrix**.

T(tx,ty) = [[1,0,tx],[0,1,ty],[0,0,1]]
S(sx,sy) = [[sx,0,0],[0,sy,0],[0,0,1]]
R(theta) = [[cos,-sin,0],[sin,cos,0],[0,0,1]]

steps.title: Composite rule
steps.body: For column vectors, apply the **rightmost** matrix first: P' = M3 . M2 . M1 . P means M1 happens first. Matrix multiplication is not commutative (except special cases such as two rotations or two translations).

steps.title: Pivot rotation
steps.body: Rotation about (xp,yp): **T(xp,yp) . R(theta) . T(-xp,-yp)**. Scaling about a fixed point is the same pattern with S in the middle.

steps.title: Solved: rotate (3,2) by 90 degrees about (1,1)
steps.body:
1. Translate pivot to origin: (3,2) -> (2,1).
2. Rotate 90: (x',y') = (-y, x) = (-1, 2).
3. Translate back: (-1+1, 2+1) = **(0,3)**.

steps.title: Solved: scale square (2,2),(4,2),(4,4),(2,4) by 2 about its centre (3,3)
Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Reversing the order of the three matrices.
- Forgetting that the last row of a homogeneous matrix for affine transforms is (0,0,1).

scenes.text: A drawing app has 'flip horizontal' and 'make italic' buttons.
Both are matrix transformations: reflection and shear.

steps.title: Reflection
steps.body:
- About x-axis: (x,y) -> (x,-y): matrix [[1,0],[0,-1]].
- About y-axis: (x,y) -> (-x,y).
- About origin: (x,y) -> (-x,-y) (same as rotation by 180).
- About line y = x: (x,y) -> (y,x).
- About line y = -x: (x,y) -> (-y,-x).
The determinant is -1 (orientation flips).

steps.title: Shear
steps.body: x-direction shear: x' = x + shx.y, y' = y. y-direction shear: y' = y + shy.x, x' = x. Rectangles become parallelograms; areas are preserved (determinant 1).

lessons.title: Lab: Capstone - Does order matter? Numerical investigation

scenes.text: One engineer translates a part and then scales; the other scales and then translates.
Their final positions differ. Who is right? Both - for different instructions.

steps.title: Statement
steps.body: Take the point P(1,1), translation T(2,3) and uniform scaling S(2) about the origin.

steps.title: Scale then translate
steps.body: S: (1,1) -> (2,2). T: (2,2) -> **(4,5)**. Different, so T and S do not commute.

steps.title: Which pairs commute?
steps.body: Two translations commute; two rotations about the same point commute; two scalings about the same point commute; uniform scaling commutes with rotation about the origin. Translation with rotation or with scaling generally does not.

steps.body: If a question gives a sequence in words ('first ... then ...'), write the matrices right-to-left.

courses.title: Unit 3 · Viewing, clipping and area filling
courses.summary: The 2-D viewing pipeline and window-to-viewport mapping, Cohen-Sutherland and Liang-Barsky line clipping, Sutherland-Hodgman polygon clipping, and scan-line / flood fill. Fully worked numericals and code labs.
outcomes: Map window coordinates to viewport coordinates
Compute outcodes and clip lines with Cohen-Sutherland
Use the parametric Liang-Barsky method
Clip polygons with Sutherland-Hodgman
Distinguish scan-line, boundary-fill and flood-fill and 4- vs 8-connectivity

scenes.text: A map app shows a small window of a huge city map on a phone screen.
Pinching to zoom changes the window; the phone's rectangle is the viewport.

steps.title: Definitions
steps.body: **World coordinates** describe the scene. A **window** is the rectangle of the world to be shown; a **viewport** is the rectangle of the screen where it appears (in normalised or device coordinates). The **viewing transformation** maps window to viewport.

steps.title: Formula
steps.body:
sx = (xvmax - xvmin)/(xwmax - xwmin), sy = (yvmax - yvmin)/(ywmax - ywmin)
xv = xvmin + (xw - xwmin).sx
yv = yvmin + (yw - ywmin).sy

It is a composite: translate window corner to origin, scale by (sx,sy), translate to the viewport corner. If sx != sy, shapes are distorted.

steps.title: Solved: window (20,10)-(80,70) to viewport (0,0)-(400,300)
steps.body: sx = 400/60 = 6.667; sy = 300/60 = 5. Point (50,40): xv = 30 x 6.667 = 200; yv = 30 x 5 = 150. The window's centre maps to the viewport's centre (200,150).

steps.title: Solved: zoom
steps.body: Shrink the window to (35,25)-(65,55) and keep the same viewport: sx = 400/30 = 13.33, sy = 300/30 = 10. Objects look twice as big: that is zoom-in.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting to subtract the window minimum.
- Using the viewport's width where the window's width is needed (sx inverted).
- Ignoring aspect ratio, which stretches circles into ellipses.

story.title: Don't draw what you can't see

scenes.text: A CAD drawing has a million lines but the window shows a small part.
Cheap bit tests reject most lines before any arithmetic.

steps.title: Region codes
steps.body: Divide the plane by the window edges into 9 regions. Each end point gets a 4-bit outcode **TBRL**: bit1 (T=8) above ymax, bit2 (B=4) below ymin, bit3 (R=2) right of xmax, bit4 (L=1) left of xmin. Inside = 0000.

steps.title: Algorithm
steps.body:
1. If both outcodes are 0000: **trivially accept**.
2. If (code1 AND code2) != 0: **trivially reject** (both on the outer side of one edge).
3. Else pick an end point outside, intersect with a violated edge, replace that end point, recompute its outcode, repeat.

steps.title: Solved: window (0,0)-(10,10), line P(-2,5) to Q(12,12)
Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Rejecting when OR != 0 (should be AND).
- Using the wrong edge when the end point violates two edges: any order works, but recompute the outcode each time.
- Dividing by dx = 0 for vertical lines: use x = const handling.

activity.prompt: Write an outcode function for window x 0..10, y 0..10 (bits T=8,B=4,R=2,L=1) and print the codes for 4 points as 4-bit strings.
activity.solution:
def code(x,y):
    c=0
    if x<0: c|=1
    if x>10: c|=2
    if y<0: c|=4
    if y>10: c|=8
    return format(c,'04b')
print(code(-2,5),code(12,12),code(5,5),code(5,-3))

scenes.text: Liang and Barsky noticed that clipping is just finding the parameter range of the line that lies inside the window.

steps.title: Parametric form
steps.body:
x = x1 + u.dx, y = y1 + u.dy, 0 <= u <= 1. A point is inside when xmin <= x <= xmax, ymin <= y <= ymax. This gives four inequalities u.p_k <= q_k with
p1 = -dx, q1 = x1 - xmin; p2 = dx, q2 = xmax - x1; p3 = -dy, q3 = y1 - ymin; p4 = dy, q4 = ymax - y1.

steps.title: Rules
steps.body:
- p_k = 0 and q_k < 0: line parallel and outside: reject.
- p_k < 0: line enters at u = q_k/p_k -> u1 = max(0, those).
- p_k > 0: line leaves at u = q_k/p_k -> u2 = min(1, those).
- If u1 > u2 reject; else visible from u1 to u2.

steps.title: Solved: same line (-2,5)-(12,12), window 0..10
steps.body:
dx = 14, dy = 7. p = (-14, 14, -7, 7), q = (-2, 12, 5, 5).
Entering: 1/7 = 0.143 and -0.714 -> u1 = 0.143. Leaving: 12/14 = 0.857 and 5/7 = 0.714 -> u2 = 0.714.
End points: u1 -> (0, 6); u2 -> (8, 10). Same as Cohen-Sutherland, but fewer operations.

steps.title: Why it is faster
steps.body: Only u1 and u2 updated with comparisons; the intersection coordinates are computed once at the end.

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: Mixing the signs of q (q1 = x1 - xmin, not xmin - x1).

steps.title: Scan-line polygon fill
steps.body: For each scan line y: find intersections with polygon edges, sort by x, fill between pairs (odd-even rule). Use incremental x += 1/m per scan line. A vertex shared by two edges is counted once if the edges are on opposite sides (monotonic), twice if it is a local extremum.

steps.title: Seed fills
steps.body: **Boundary fill**: grow from a seed until the boundary colour. **Flood fill**: replace an old interior colour. **4-connected** uses N,S,E,W neighbours; **8-connected** adds diagonals and can leak through one-pixel diagonal gaps. Use 4-connected to fill regions bounded by 8-connected boundaries and vice versa.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Naive recursion overflows the stack on big regions (use an explicit stack or span fill).
- Using 8-connected fill with a boundary that is only 4-connected? Safe. The reverse leaks.

steps.title: Right-handed system
steps.body: Curl the fingers of the right hand from +x to +y; the thumb points along +z. Positive rotation about an axis is **anticlockwise when looking from the positive end of the axis towards the origin**.

steps.title: 4x4 homogeneous matrices
steps.body:
Translation: identity with (tx,ty,tz) in the last column. Scaling: diag(sx,sy,sz,1).

Rz(t): x' = x cos t - y sin t; y' = x sin t + y cos t; z' = z.
Rx(t): y' = y cos t - z sin t; z' = y sin t + z cos t; x' = x.
Ry(t): **x' = x cos t + z sin t, z' = -x sin t + z cos t**; y' = y.

Common mistakes
steps.body:
- The sign pattern of the sin terms in Ry differs from Rx and Rz.
- 3-D rotations do **not** commute: Rx then Ry is not Ry then Rx.
- Rotation about an arbitrary axis needs translate-to-origin, align with a coordinate axis, rotate, undo.

steps.title: Parallel projection
steps.body: Projectors are parallel, so **parallel lines stay parallel** and sizes along axes are preserved; there is no foreshortening with distance. **Orthographic**: projectors perpendicular to the plane (front, top, side views; **axonometric** variants isometric, dimetric, trimetric). **Oblique**: projectors are slanted.

steps.title: Oblique formulas
steps.body: Projecting onto the z = 0 plane: x_p = x + L.z.cos(phi), y_p = y + L.z.sin(phi). **Cavalier**: L = 1 (true length for depth, looks long). **Cabinet**: L = 1/2 (depth halved, looks natural). phi is usually 30 or 45 degrees.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using L = 1 for cabinet.
- Believing orthographic views show depth: they do not; you need two views.
- Isometric: all three axes foreshortened equally (angles 120 degrees apart).

scenes.text: Standing between rails, the parallel tracks seem to meet at a point far away.

steps.title: The model
steps.body: Centre of projection at the origin, view plane z = d. By similar triangles a point (x,y,z) maps to **x_p = x.d/z, y_p = y.d/z**. Objects twice as far appear half as large. As a 4x4 matrix: bottom row (0,0,1/d,0); after multiplying, divide by w = z/d (**perspective divide**).

steps.title: Vanishing points
steps.body: Sets of parallel lines not parallel to the view plane converge at a **vanishing point**. 1-point (view plane parallel to one face), 2-point, and 3-point perspective: the number of principal axes that are not parallel to the view plane.

steps.title: Solved: lines z-direction
steps.body: Line (1,0,z): x_p = d/z -> 0 as z -> infinity: the line converges to the centre (0,0), the vanishing point for the z-axis direction.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Dividing by d instead of z.
- Points with z <= 0 are behind the centre of projection and must be clipped first.
- Perspective does not preserve parallelism, lengths or angles.

scenes.text: A 3-D film model passes through stages before a pixel lights: model, world, camera, clip, screen.

steps.title: Pipeline stages
steps.body:
1. **Modelling transform**: object -> world.
2. **Viewing transform**: world -> camera (eye at origin looking down -z).
3. **Projection**: view volume (a box for parallel, a **frustum** for perspective) -> canonical cube.
4. **Clipping** against the six planes in homogeneous space (before the divide).
5. **Perspective divide** by w.
6. **Viewport transform** to pixels, with depth kept for hidden-surface tests.

steps.title: Why 4-D?
steps.body: Adding w makes translation and projection linear. The same maths lets us project a 4-D hypercube (tesseract) to 3-D: a 3-D picture of a 4-D object, just as a cube's shadow is a 2-D picture. Below, rotate the projected tesseract and notice that the inner cube appears to turn inside out - that is the effect of rotating in a plane that involves the 4th axis.

steps.title: Frustum
steps.body: Near plane n = 1, far f = 100, field of view 90 degrees, aspect 1: the half-width at distance z is z. At z = 50 the visible width is 100 units.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Clipping after the perspective divide (loses points behind the eye).
- Mixing camera looking down +z with -z conventions between APIs.

courses.summary: Bezier curves and the de Casteljau algorithm, B-splines and continuity, polygon meshes, Euler's formula and fractals, back-face culling, the z-buffer and other visible-surface methods. Includes worked numericals and code labs.
outcomes: Evaluate a cubic Bezier curve by formula and by de Casteljau

scenes.text: Every letter in a vector font is a few Bezier curves, so it scales without pixel jaggies.

steps.title: Definition
steps.body: A Bezier curve of degree n has n+1 control points P0..Pn: **B(t) = sum_{i=0..n} C(n,i) (1-t)^(n-i) t^i P_i**, 0 <= t <= 1. For the **cubic**: B(t) = (1-t)^3 P0 + 3(1-t)^2 t P1 + 3(1-t) t^2 P2 + t^3 P3.

steps.title: Properties
steps.body:
- Passes through the first and last control points only.
- Tangent at the ends is along P0P1 and P2P3 (B'(0) = 3(P1-P0)).
- Lies inside the **convex hull** of control points (basis weights are non-negative and sum to 1).
- **Variation diminishing**; invariant under affine transformations; global control (moving one point changes the whole curve).

steps.title: Solved: tangent
steps.body: B'(0) = 3(P1-P0) = (3,6): the curve leaves P0 heading steeply up-right.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Believing the curve passes through P1 and P2.
- Forgetting the binomial coefficients (1,3,3,1).
- Joining two Beziers smoothly requires P2, P3 = P0', P1' collinear (G1) and equal vectors (C1).

scenes.text: Instead of the formula, de Casteljau just keeps taking midpoints (or t-points) between neighbouring control points.
The last single point is the curve point, and numerically it is more stable.

steps.title: Algorithm
steps.body: Given control points and a parameter t, repeat: replace the list by the linear interpolations (1-t).Pi + t.P(i+1). After n rounds, one point remains: B(t). The intermediate points also split the curve into two Beziers (used in subdivision and flatness tests when rendering).

steps.title: By hand, t = 0.5
steps.body: Round 1: (0.5,1), (2,2), (3.5,1). Round 2: (1.25,1.5), (2.75,1.5). Round 3: **(2,1.5)** - agrees with the Bernstein formula.

steps.title: Why graphics libraries use it
steps.body: It needs only additions and multiplies by t, is numerically robust, and gives subdivision for free.

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: Using t as a distance instead of a parameter: t = 0.5 is not necessarily the midpoint by arc length.

steps.title: B-spline
steps.body: A degree-p B-spline with n+1 control points uses a **knot vector** of **n+p+2 knots** (= control points + p + 1). It consists of n-p+1 polynomial segments (e.g. 6 points, p=3: 3 segments). Each point influences only p+1 segments: **local control**. Higher degree = smoother but wider influence.

steps.title: Continuity
steps.body:
- **C0**: positions meet. **C1**: tangent vectors equal. **C2**: curvature vectors equal.
- **G1** (geometric): tangents parallel, magnitudes may differ.
Uniform cubic B-splines are C2 everywhere. Bezier pieces are C0 by default.

steps.title: NURBS
steps.body: Non-Uniform Rational B-Splines add a **weight** per control point and non-uniform knots. They represent circles and conics exactly, and are the standard in CAD (IGES, STEP).

steps.title: Solved: counting knots
steps.body: 10 control points, cubic: knots = 10 + 3 + 1 = 14; segments = 10 - 3 = 7.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Mixing degree with order (order = degree + 1).
- Assuming B-spline passes through the control points (it generally does not unless endpoint knots have multiplicity p+1).

steps.title: Polygon meshes
steps.body: Stored as a vertex list plus face lists (indexed face set) or a half-edge structure. **Euler's formula** for a simple closed polyhedron: **V - E + F = 2**.

steps.title: Solved: cube and icosahedron
steps.body: Cube: 8 - 12 + 6 = 2. Icosahedron: V = 12, F = 20, so E = V + F - 2 = 30; check by faces: 20 triangles x 3 / 2 = 30.

steps.title: Fractals
steps.body: Self-similar shapes with non-integer dimension: **D = log N / log(1/s)** where the shape is N copies scaled by s. **Koch curve**: N = 4, s = 1/3: D = log4/log3 = 1.262; its length after n steps is (4/3)^n times the original: infinite in the limit. Others: Sierpinski triangle D = log3/log2 = 1.585. Midpoint displacement generates terrain.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Applying Euler's formula to a torus (V-E+F = 0 for a torus).
- Using s = 3 instead of s = 1/3: D = log N / log(scale-up factor).

steps.title: Back-face detection
steps.body: Polygon normal N = (B-A) x (C-A) for vertices in anticlockwise order seen from outside. With V the vector from the eye toward the polygon, **the face is a back face if V . N > 0**. About half of the faces of a closed object are culled cheaply.

steps.title: Visible-surface methods
steps.body:
- **Z-buffer (depth buffer)**: per pixel keep depth; if new z < stored z (nearer), update colour and depth. Simple, handles any order, memory = pixels x depth bits, aliasing and transparency are weak.
- **Painter's algorithm**: sort polygons far to near and paint; fails for cyclic overlap.
- **Scan-line**, **area subdivision (Warnock)**, **BSP trees**, **ray casting**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Applying culling to open or transparent objects.
- Using the wrong sign convention for V (from eye vs towards eye): state it.
- Z-fighting when two surfaces have nearly equal depth.

scenes.text: Isha's poster looks bright on screen but dull on paper.
The screen adds light (RGB); the printer subtracts light with inks (CMY/CMYK), and the range (gamut) is smaller.

steps.title: Additive and subtractive
steps.body:
**RGB** (additive): red, green, blue light add to white. Used for screens. A 24-bit pixel has 8 bits per channel (0-255).
**CMY(K)** (subtractive): inks absorb light. Normalised **C = 1-R, M = 1-G, Y = 1-B**. Printers add **K** (black) for true black and ink economy.

steps.title: HSV and YIQ
steps.body: **HSV**: hue (angle 0-360), saturation, value; intuitive for colour pickers. **YIQ**: luminance Y plus chroma I,Q; used in NTSC TV so black-and-white sets could use Y: **Y = 0.299R + 0.587G + 0.114B** (the eye is most sensitive to green).

steps.title: Solved: RGB to CMY
steps.body: (0.2, 0.5, 0.8) -> (0.8, 0.5, 0.2). Pure red (1,0,0) -> (0,1,1): cyan absent, magenta and yellow full.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Mixing 0-255 with 0-1 ranges.
- Treating RGB values as linear light: displays use gamma (about 2.2), so average colours in linear space for correct blends.

story.title: Why a shiny ball has a highlight

scenes.text: A red billiard ball shows a white glint where the light bounces towards your eye.
Phong's model adds ambient, diffuse and specular parts to imitate it.

steps.title: The equation
steps.body:
**I = Ia.ka + Id.kd.(N.L) + Is.ks.(R.V)^n**
- Ambient: constant background light, ka = ambient reflectivity.
- Diffuse (Lambert's cosine law): depends on angle between surface normal N and light direction L; independent of viewer. Use max(0, N.L).
- Specular: R = 2(N.L)N - L is the mirror direction; V points to the viewer; n (shininess) is large for tight highlights (10-1000).
All vectors are unit vectors. Multiple lights add. Colour: apply per R, G, B channel. Add distance attenuation 1/(a + b d + c d^2) for point lights.

steps.title: Blinn-Phong
steps.body: Replace R.V by N.H with the half-vector H = (L+V)/|L+V|. Cheaper, used in fixed-function OpenGL.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Not normalising N, L, V.
- Letting N.L go negative (light behind the surface): clamp to 0.
- Believing Phong is physically exact: it is an empirical model.

scenes.text: A low-polygon sphere looks faceted with flat shading, smooth with Gouraud, and has crisp highlights with Phong shading.
Early consoles chose Gouraud as the best price/performance.

steps.title: Three methods
steps.body:
- **Flat shading**: one intensity per polygon (from its normal). Fast; shows facets and Mach bands.
- **Gouraud shading**: compute intensity at the vertices (using averaged vertex normals), then **bilinearly interpolate intensity** along edges and scan lines. Smooth; can miss specular highlights inside a polygon.
- **Phong shading** (per-pixel normal interpolation): interpolate the **normal vectors** and evaluate the illumination at every pixel. Best highlights, most expensive (modern GPUs do it in fragment shaders).

steps.title: Solved: Gouraud scan line
steps.body: Edge intensities: I_a = 0.4 at x = 2 and I_b = 0.8 at x = 6. At x = 3: I = I_a + (x - xa)/(xb - xa) x (I_b - I_a) = 0.4 + (1/4)(0.4) = **0.5**.

steps.title: Vertex normal
steps.body: A vertex shared by 3 faces with normals (0,0,1), (1,0,0), (0,1,0): average (1,1,1)/3, normalised to (0.577, 0.577, 0.577).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Interpolating intensity (Gouraud) and calling it Phong.
- Not renormalising the interpolated normals in Phong shading.

scenes.text: A ray tracer shoots a ray from the eye through every pixel and asks: what does it hit first?
If the surface is a mirror, it shoots another ray from the hit point, recursively.

steps.title: Recursive ray tracing
steps.body: For each pixel: cast a **primary ray**; find the nearest intersection; compute local shading (Phong) after a **shadow ray** to each light; then spawn a **reflection ray** (and a **refraction ray** by Snell's law n1 sin a = n2 sin b) up to a maximum depth. Handles shadows, mirrors and glass naturally; slow; later extended by path tracing for global illumination.

steps.title: Ray-sphere
steps.body: Ray P(t) = O + tD, sphere centre C, radius r. Substituting into |P - C|^2 = r^2 gives a quadratic **a t^2 + b t + c = 0** with a = D.D, b = 2 D.(O-C), c = |O-C|^2 - r^2. Discriminant b^2 - 4ac: <0 miss, 0 tangent, >0 two hits; the nearest positive root is the visible surface.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Picking t < 0 (behind the origin).
- Forgetting shadow-ray offset (epsilon), which causes 'shadow acne'.
- Not normalising D when the formula assumes a = 1.

activity.prompt: Compute the nearest intersection parameter t for the ray and sphere above and print it.

a=sum(d*d for d in D)
b=2*sum(D[i]*oc[i] for i in range(3))
c=sum(v*v for v in oc)-r*r
disc=b*b-4*a*c
# nearest root
t=0
print(t)
activity.solution:

O=(0,0,0); D=(0,0,1); C=(0,0,5); r=2
oc=[O[i]-C[i] for i in range(3)]
a=sum(d*d for d in D)
b=2*sum(D[i]*oc[i] for i in range(3))
c=sum(v*v for v in oc)-r*r
disc=b*b-4*a*c
t=(-b-math.sqrt(disc))/(2*a)
print(t)

lessons.title: Lab: Capstone - Animation, texture mapping and the GPU pipeline

story.title: From code to 60 frames per second

scenes.text: A phone game must produce a new picture every 16.7 ms.
The GPU runs thousands of tiny programs (shaders) in parallel to meet that deadline.

steps.title: Animation basics
steps.body: **Keyframing** stores poses at key times and interpolates (linear, spline). **Frame rate** 24 fps (film), 60 fps (smooth UI), 144 Hz gaming displays. **Double buffering** draws to a back buffer then swaps to avoid tearing; vsync aligns the swap to the display refresh. Techniques: skeletal animation, morph targets, physics simulation, motion capture. Frame time = 1000/fps ms.

steps.title: Texture mapping
steps.body: A 2-D image is mapped onto a surface using (u,v) coordinates stored at the vertices. Per pixel: interpolate (u,v) perspective-correctly, sample the texture (nearest or bilinear filter), use **mipmaps** to avoid shimmering at distance. Variants: bump/normal maps, environment maps, shadow maps.

steps.title: Real-time pipeline
steps.body: Application -> **vertex shader** (transform, per-vertex lighting) -> primitive assembly and clipping -> **rasterisation** (triangles to fragments) -> **fragment shader** (texturing, per-pixel lighting) -> depth/stencil test and blending -> frame buffer. APIs: OpenGL, Vulkan, DirectX, Metal, WebGL.

steps.title: Solved: frame budget
steps.body: At 144 Hz, frame time = 1000/144 = 6.94 ms; at 60 fps = 16.67 ms; at 30 fps = 33.3 ms.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Linear (not perspective-correct) interpolation of texture coordinates on slanted triangles warps textures.
- Drawing without double buffering causes flicker.

steps.title: Output primitives
steps.body:
- Frame buffer bytes = W x H x bpp / 8.
- DDA: steps = max(|dx|,|dy|). Bresenham: p0 = 2dy - dx; p<0: p += 2dy else y++, p += 2dy - 2dx.
- Midpoint circle: p0 = 1 - r; p<0: p += 2x+1 else y--, p += 2x+1-2y; octant until x >= y.

steps.title: 2-D and 3-D transforms
steps.body:
- Rotation: x' = x cos t - y sin t, y' = x sin t + y cos t.
- Composite: rightmost matrix first; pivot: T(p).R.T(-p).
- Reflection about y = x swaps (x,y); shear keeps area; scaling multiplies area by sx.sy.
- 3-D matrices are 4x4; Ry has x' = x cos + z sin.

steps.title: Viewing and clipping
steps.body:
- sx = (xvmax-xvmin)/(xwmax-xwmin).
- Outcode TBRL; accept if both 0000; reject if AND != 0.
- Liang-Barsky: p = (-dx, dx, -dy, dy), q = (x1-xmin, xmax-x1, y1-ymin, ymax-y1); u1 = max entering, u2 = min leaving.
- Sutherland-Hodgman: 4 cases per edge.

steps.title: Projection, curves, shading
steps.body:
- Perspective: x_p = x d / z. Cavalier L = 1, cabinet L = 0.5.
- Cubic Bezier weights (1-t)^3, 3(1-t)^2 t, 3(1-t)t^2, t^3. B-spline knots = n + p + 2 (n+1 points).
- Euler: V - E + F = 2.
- Phong: I = Ia ka + Id kd (N.L) + Is ks (R.V)^n. Gouraud interpolates intensity, Phong interpolates normals.

lessons.title: What is information retrieval? The inverted index

scenes.text: Kavya must find the email in which a vendor mentioned 'July invoice' among 40,000 messages.
Scanning every email takes minutes; her mail client answers in milliseconds because it built an index in advance.

steps.title: Definition and scope
steps.body:
**Information retrieval (IR)** is finding material (usually documents) of an unstructured nature (usually text) that satisfies an **information need** from within large collections.

- *Information need* = what the user wants to know; *query* = the words typed. They differ: the need 'is red wine healthier than white?' becomes the query 'red wine white wine health'.
- A document is **relevant** if it addresses the need, not merely if it contains the query words.
- IR vs database: databases return exact matches on structured fields (SQL), IR returns a **ranked** list of approximately matching unstructured items.
- Ad hoc retrieval = arbitrary queries over a fixed collection; filtering/routing = fixed queries over a stream of documents.

steps.title: Term-document incidence and why it fails
steps.body:
The simplest model is a **term-document incidence matrix**: rows = terms, columns = documents, entry 1 if the document contains the term. For 1 million documents and 500,000 distinct terms the matrix has 5×10¹¹ cells, i.e. about 62.5 GB even at 1 bit per cell, yet it is *extremely sparse* (at most about 1 billion 1s if each document has 1,000 tokens).

The **inverted index** stores only the 1s: a **dictionary** of terms, and for each term a **postings list** of document IDs (docIDs) sorted in increasing order. Each entry (docID, optionally tf/positions) is a **posting**. Dictionary entries also store **document frequency (df)**, the length of the postings list.

steps.title: Solved example 1 · Build the index
steps.body:
Collection:
- D1: new home sales top forecasts
- D2: home sales rise in july
- D3: increase in home sales in july
- D4: july new home sales rise

Steps: (1) tokenise and lower-case; (2) emit (term, docID) pairs; (3) sort by term then docID; (4) merge duplicates and record df.

Result (term → postings, df):
- forecasts → 1 (1)
- home → 1,2,3,4 (4)
- in → 2,3 (2)
- increase → 3 (1)
- july → 2,3,4 (3)
- new → 1,4 (2)
- rise → 2,4 (2)
- sales → 1,2,3,4 (4)
- top → 1 (1)

Note 'in' occurs twice in D3 but D3 appears once in its postings list (tf = 2 would be stored separately).

steps.title: Solved example 2 · Answer queries from the index
steps.body:
Query *new OR rise*: new = {1,4}, rise = {2,4}. Union = {1,2,4} so **3 documents**.

Query *july AND rise*: july = {2,3,4}, rise = {2,4}. Intersection = {2,4}.

Query *home AND NOT sales*: home = {1,2,3,4}, sales = {1,2,3,4}; difference is empty.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Treating *query words* as the *information need*; evaluation is always against the need.
- Forgetting that postings must be **sorted by docID**; the merge algorithm depends on it.
- Counting df as the total number of occurrences. df = number of documents containing the term; collection frequency (cf) = total occurrences.

lessons.title: Skip pointers, biwords and positional indexes

scenes.text: Imran searches "to be or not to be" with quotes and expects only exact phrase matches, not pages that merely contain all the words.
The engine needs to know not just which documents contain a word, but where.

steps.title: Skip pointers
steps.body: To speed up AND on long lists, add **skip pointers**: from some postings jump ahead to a later docID. During the merge, if the skip target is still ≤ the other pointer's docID, take the skip. A common heuristic for a list of length P is **√P evenly spaced skips**. Skips help most when lists are static and in memory; too many skips mean many comparisons that rarely pay off.

steps.title: Phrase queries
steps.body:
**Biword index:** index every consecutive pair ('stanford university' as a term). Cheap but longer phrases need AND of biwords which can give false positives, and the dictionary explodes.

**Positional index:** postings store, for each doc, the term positions: *term → doc: <pos1, pos2, …>*. A phrase 'to be' matches doc d if some position p of 'to' has p+1 in the positions of 'be'. A proximity query 'A /k B' requires |posA − posB| ≤ k. Positional indexes are typically 2–4 times larger than non-positional ones but support phrases and proximity exactly; real engines combine both (e.g. biwords for frequent phrases).

steps.title: Solved example 1 · Phrase match
steps.body:
Document: *to be or not to be to be* → positions: to = 1,5,7; be = 2,6,8; or = 3; not = 4.

lessons.title: Tokenisation, normalisation, stop words and stemming

scenes.text: A student searches 'colour' and 'color' and expects the same results.
Before indexing, every document passes through a text-processing pipeline that decides what a 'term' is.

steps.title: The pipeline
steps.body:
Raw document → character decoding → **tokenisation** (split into tokens) → **normalisation** (map tokens to equivalence classes: case folding, removing accents/hyphens, expanding abbreviations) → optional **stop-word removal** → **stemming/lemmatisation** → index terms.

Terminology: a **token** is an instance of a character sequence; a **type** is the class of all tokens with the same characters; a **term** is a type that is included in the dictionary after normalisation. Example: in 'to be or not to be' there are 6 tokens, 4 types.

steps.title: Hard cases and choices
steps.body:
- Apostrophes (*O'Neill*, *aren't*), hyphens (*state-of-the-art*), numbers and dates, e-mail addresses and URLs have no single right answer; use the same rules for documents and queries.
- Languages without spaces (Chinese, Japanese) need segmentation; German needs compound splitting (*Lebensversicherungsgesellschaftsangestellter*); Hindi needs Unicode normalisation (e.g. nukta forms, chandrabindu/anusvara variants).
- **Stop words** (the, of, a) are very frequent and add little to ranking; modern engines keep them (they matter for phrases like 'to be or not to be') and rely on compression and ranking instead.
- **Stemming** chops suffixes heuristically; **lemmatisation** uses a dictionary and morphology to return the lemma (*better → good*). Stemming raises recall, may lower precision.

steps.title: Solved example 1 · Porter step 1a
steps.body:
Rules (apply the longest matching suffix): SSES→SS, IES→I, SS→SS, S→(nothing).
- caresses → caress (SSES→SS)
- ponies → poni (IES→I)
- caress → caress (SS→SS)
- cats → cat (S→∅)

Note stemming can over-stem (*university* and *universe* may collapse) and under-stem (*data* and *datum* do not).

steps.title: Solved example 2 · Types versus tokens
steps.body: Text: 'the cat saw the dog and the cat ran'. Tokens = 9. Types: the, cat, saw, dog, and, ran = **6**. After removing stop words {the, and}: tokens 5 (cat, saw, dog, cat, ran), types 4.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using different tokenisers for indexing and querying: the query term then never matches.
- Treating stemming and lemmatisation as identical; lemmatisation needs part-of-speech and a lexicon.
- Removing stop words unconditionally and then failing on phrase or name queries ('The Who', 'IT').

story.title: How big will the dictionary get?

scenes.text: An engineer must size memory for the dictionary of a news archive that will keep growing.
Two empirical laws let her estimate vocabulary size and word frequencies before indexing.

steps.title: Heaps' law (vocabulary growth)
steps.body:
**M = k · Tᵇ**, where M = vocabulary size (types), T = number of tokens in the collection, with typically 30 ≤ k ≤ 100 and b ≈ 0.5. For a newswire corpus of the RCV1 type, k ≈ 44 and b ≈ 0.49.

On a log–log plot vocabulary vs tokens is a straight line of slope b. Consequences: the dictionary keeps growing with no ceiling; and collections of the same language but different size have very different vocabularies, so you cannot 'finish' the dictionary.

steps.title: Zipf's law (frequency distribution)
steps.body:
If terms are ranked by collection frequency, then **cfᵢ ∝ 1/i**: the i-th most common term has frequency about cf₁/i. Equivalently cf = c·i⁻¹ (log–log slope −1).

Consequences: a handful of terms (stop words) account for a large part of all tokens, while about half the dictionary consists of terms occurring only once (**hapax legomena**). So long postings lists are few and short ones very many: compression and stop-word handling matter.

steps.title: Solved example 2 · Zipf's law
steps.body:
Suppose the most frequent term 'the' has cf₁ = 1,000,000. Then the predicted cf of rank 10 = 1,000,000/10 = **100,000**, rank 100 = 10,000 and rank 1,000 = 1,000.

Sum of cf for the top 3 terms = 1,000,000(1 + 1/2 + 1/3) = 1,833,333.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Assuming vocabulary grows linearly with collection size (it grows as T^b with b ≈ 0.5).
- Applying Zipf's law exactly; it is an empirical approximation, especially off at the extremes of rank.
- Confusing cf (total occurrences) with df (documents containing the term).

lessons.title: Index construction: BSBI, SPIMI and distributed indexing

story.title: The index that doesn't fit in RAM

scenes.text: An archive project has 100 million postings but only 100 MB of free RAM for sorting.
The team must build the index in blocks and merge them on disk.

steps.title: Blocked sort-based indexing (BSBI)
steps.body:
1. Map each term to a **termID** (needs a dictionary kept in memory).
2. Read documents and collect (termID, docID) pairs until a block of memory is full.
3. Sort the block (O(n log n)), write the inverted file for the block to disk.
4. After all blocks, **multiway merge** the block files into the final index.

Cost is dominated by the initial sort: O(T log T) overall for T pairs.

steps.title: SPIMI and MapReduce
steps.body:
**Single-pass in-memory indexing (SPIMI)** avoids the global termID dictionary and the sort of pairs: each block has its own dictionary; when a term is first seen it gets a postings list, and docIDs are appended directly. When memory is full, sort the *dictionary terms* only (not the postings) and write the block; merge as in BSBI. Complexity is **O(T)** apart from sorting terms.

For huge collections, **distributed indexing** uses **MapReduce**: map tasks parse document splits and emit (term, docID); a partitioner groups by term ranges (a–f, g–p, q–z); reduce tasks sort and write postings. **Dynamic indexing** keeps a large main index plus a small auxiliary in-memory index, merging periodically (logarithmic merging reduces cost).

steps.title: Solved example 1 · Number of blocks
steps.body:
100 million (termID, docID) pairs, each 8 bytes (two 4-byte integers) = 800 MB. If only 100 MB can be sorted at once → pairs per block = 100 MB / 8 B = 12.5 million.

Blocks = 100 M / 12.5 M = **8 blocks**. Final merge reads 8 files simultaneously with a small read buffer for each.

steps.title: Solved example 2 · Why SPIMI is faster
steps.body: BSBI sorts all T pairs: with T = 10⁸, log₂T ≈ 26.6, so ≈ 2.7×10⁹ comparisons. SPIMI appends each posting in O(1) and sorts only the distinct terms of each block (say 10⁶ per block): 10⁶ × 20 ≈ 2×10⁷ comparisons per block, a far smaller sorting cost.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting that BSBI needs the termID dictionary in memory; SPIMI removes this requirement.
- Sorting the postings of SPIMI: they are already in docID order because documents are processed in order.
- Thinking MapReduce changes the index; it only parallelises the construction.

lessons.title: Lab: Compress postings — gaps, variable-byte and gamma codes

scenes.text: Ananya's index of 50 GB must fit on one SSD node and be read faster than raw docIDs.
She stores differences between docIDs and encodes them with as few bytes as possible.

steps.title: Gap encoding and codes
steps.body:
Postings are increasing docIDs, so store **gaps**: 824, 829, 215406 → 824, 5, 214577. Frequent terms have small gaps, rare terms large ones.

**Variable-byte (VB):** split the number into 7-bit groups; put the groups most-significant first; set the high bit (continuation bit) to 1 only on the **last** byte.
**Gamma code:** write the length of the binary offset in unary, then the offset, where offset = binary number without its leading 1. Length of γ(n) = 2⌊log₂n⌋ + 1 bits. Gamma codes are bit-aligned, so slightly smaller than VB but slower to decode.

steps.title: Solved example 2 · Savings
steps.body: Docs 824, 829, 215406 stored as 4-byte ints = 12 bytes. With gaps + VB: 2 + 1 + 3 = **6 bytes**, half the space. Decoding: read bytes until one with high bit 1, concatenate 7-bit groups.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Putting the continuation bit on the first byte (in this convention the *last* byte has the high bit set).
- Gamma length: 2⌊log₂n⌋+1, not 2log₂n.
- Encoding docIDs rather than gaps (loses almost all the compression).

lessons.title: Term weighting: tf, idf and tf-idf

scenes.text: A user searches 'the quantum computer'. Pages with 'the' hundreds of times should not beat pages about quantum computers.
The engine must weigh how often a term occurs in a document and how rare it is in the collection.

steps.title: Ingredients
steps.body:
- **Term frequency tf(t,d)**: occurrences of t in d. Raw tf overstates: 20 occurrences is not 20× as relevant as 1, so use **log-weighting**: w = 1 + log₁₀ tf if tf > 0 else 0.
- **Document frequency df(t)**: number of documents containing t. Rare terms are informative.
- **Inverse document frequency idf(t) = log₁₀(N/df)** with N documents. For N = 10⁶: df = 1 → 6; df = 10⁶ (a term in every doc) → 0.
- **tf-idf weight = (1 + log₁₀ tf) × log₁₀(N/df)**. It increases with the number of occurrences in a document and with the rarity of the term in the collection.

steps.title: Notes
steps.body: idf affects ranking only for queries with at least two terms: for a one-word query it scales every document equally. Logs use any base consistently; base 10 is used in these notes. Collection frequency is a poorer weight than df because a term concentrated in few documents (e.g. 'insurance') is more discriminating than one spread evenly (e.g. 'try') at equal cf.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body:
N = 1,000,000; term 'calpurnia' has df = 1, 'animal' 100, 'sunday' 1,000, 'fly' 10,000, 'under' 100,000, 'the' 1,000,000.
idf = 6, 4, 3, 2, 1, 0 respectively.

A document with tf(animal) = 100 has weight (1+2)×4 = **12**; with tf(the)=500 the weight is (1+2.699)×0 = **0**.

steps.title: Solved example 2 · Raw vs log tf
steps.body: tf = 1 → w = 1; tf = 10 → 2; tf = 100 → 3; tf = 1000 → 4. Raw counts would give 1, 10, 100, 1000: one long document would dominate. For tf=0 define w=0 (log 0 is undefined).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Computing idf = N/df without the log; the weight then explodes for rare terms.
- Using natural log in one place and base 10 in another.
- Forgetting the +1 in 1+log tf (a term occurring once would get weight 0).

lessons.title: The vector space model and cosine similarity

scenes.text: Think of each document as an arrow in a space with one axis per term.
A query is another arrow; the smaller the angle between them, the better the match.

steps.title: The model
steps.body:
Each document and query is a vector in ℝᴹ (M = vocabulary size) with tf-idf components. Ranking by **Euclidean distance** is bad: a document and its double (d concatenated with itself) are far apart yet say the same thing. Instead rank by the **angle**:

cos(q,d) = (q·d)/(|q||d|) = Σ qᵢdᵢ / (√Σqᵢ² √Σdᵢ²)

After **length normalisation** (dividing each vector by its L2 norm) cosine equals the dot product. Values lie in [0,1] for non-negative weights; 1 = same direction, 0 = no shared terms.

steps.title: SMART notation and efficiency
steps.body: Weighting schemes are written *ddd.qqq* (term-frequency, document-frequency, normalisation). A classic is **lnc.ltc**: documents use log tf, no idf, cosine normalisation; queries use log tf, idf, cosine normalisation. Retrieval accumulates scores term by term from postings lists (**term-at-a-time**); for top-K results use a heap and heuristics such as champion lists and index elimination. Weakness: assumes terms are independent and has no explicit notion of relevance.

steps.title: Solved example 2 · Length invariance
steps.body: d' = (4,2,2) is d doubled. q·d' = 6; |d'| = √24 = 4.899; cos = 6/(1.4142×4.899) = 6/6.928 = **0.866**: same score as d, unlike Euclidean distance (|d−d'| = 2.449).

steps.title: Common mistakes

steps.title: The BM25 formula
steps.body:
For query q and document d:

score(q,d) = Σ over t∈q of IDF(t) · [ tf·(k₁+1) ] / [ tf + k₁·(1 − b + b·dl/avgdl) ]

with the Robertson–Spärck Jones IDF = ln((N − n + 0.5)/(n + 0.5)) (n = df). Parameters: **k₁** (typically 1.2–2.0) controls tf saturation: as tf → ∞ the tf factor tends to k₁+1. **b** (typically 0.75) controls length normalisation: b = 0 ignores length, b = 1 fully normalises by dl/avgdl. BM25 descends from the probabilistic **binary independence model** with a 2-Poisson-inspired tf term and is a strong baseline in engines such as Lucene.

steps.body:

If dl = 2·avgdl and tf = 3: denominator = 3 + 1.2(0.25 + 0.75×2) = 3 + 1.2×1.75 = 5.1 → tf factor = 6.6/5.1 = 1.294.
Score = 2.193 × 1.294 = **2.838**; with dl = avgdl it would be 2.193 × 1.571 = 3.446. A longer document with the same tf scores lower.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using the idf of tf-idf (log10 N/df) inside BM25 without checking the variant; negative IDF values occur when n > N/2 in the original formula.
- Setting b > 1 or negative; b ∈ [0,1].
- Treating k₁ as the weight of a term; it only sets how quickly tf saturates.

lessons.title: Probabilistic ranking and query-likelihood language models

story.title: Which document would have produced this query?

scenes.text: Imagine each document as a tiny word-generating machine.
A user's query is most likely to come from the machine whose document is relevant.

steps.title: Probability ranking principle and BIM
steps.body: **PRP:** if documents are ranked by decreasing probability of relevance P(R=1|d,q), the ranking is optimal for effectiveness (under stated assumptions: independent relevance and known probabilities). The **binary independence model** assumes terms are binary and independent; with pᵢ = P(term in doc | relevant), uᵢ = P(term in doc | non-relevant) the retrieval status value is RSV = Σ log[ pᵢ(1−uᵢ) / (uᵢ(1−pᵢ)) ] over matching query terms. With no relevance information uᵢ ≈ dfᵢ/N and pᵢ = 0.5 gives an idf-like weight.

steps.title: Query likelihood and smoothing
steps.body: Rank documents by **P(q|M_d)**. With a unigram model, P(q|M_d) = Π P(t|M_d), and the MLE P(t|M_d) = tf(t,d)/|d|. A single unseen term gives probability 0, so **smooth**: Jelinek–Mercer mixes the document model with the collection model: **P(t|d) = λ·P_mle(t|d) + (1−λ)·P(t|C)** (here λ weights the document); Dirichlet smoothing uses (tf + μP(t|C))/(|d| + μ). Smoothing also plays an idf-like role. Use log-probabilities to avoid underflow.

steps.title: Solved example 1 · MLE
steps.body: Document 'to be or not to be' (6 tokens): P(to)=2/6, P(be)=2/6. Query 'to be': P = 1/3 × 1/3 = **0.111**. A query containing 'hamlet' would have P = 0 without smoothing.

steps.title: Solved example 2 · Jelinek–Mercer
steps.body:
Document 'the cat sat on the mat' (6 tokens), query 'cat mat', λ = 0.5, P(cat|C) = 0.01, P(mat|C) = 0.005.
- P(cat|d) = 0.5×(1/6) + 0.5×0.01 = 0.08333 + 0.005 = 0.08833
- P(mat|d) = 0.08333 + 0.0025 = 0.08583
- Product = **0.00758**.
A document lacking 'mat' now gets 0.5×0.005 = 0.0025 instead of 0.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting to smooth, so one missing term zeroes the whole product.
- Multiplying many small probabilities in floating point instead of summing logs.
- Confusing λ's role: in this notation λ is the weight on the document model.

lessons.title: Evaluating IR: precision, recall, F-measure and test collections

scenes.text: A search team changes its ranker and must decide, objectively, whether results improved.
They need a test collection, relevance judgments and measures.

steps.title: Test collections and measures
steps.body:
A **test collection** (Cranfield paradigm; TREC, CLEF, FIRE are evaluation forums) has (1) documents, (2) topics/information needs, (3) **relevance judgments**, usually pooled from top results of many systems. Judges disagree, so agreement is measured with **Cohen's kappa** κ = (P(A) − P(E)) / (1 − P(E)).

For an unranked result set: **Precision = relevant retrieved / retrieved**; **Recall = relevant retrieved / relevant in collection**; **F₁ = 2PR/(P+R)** (harmonic mean). **Accuracy** (fraction of correct decisions) is useless in IR because nearly all documents are non-relevant: returning nothing gets 99.99% accuracy.

steps.title: Why harmonic mean
steps.body: The arithmetic mean of P=1 and R=0.01 is 0.505, which flatters a system that returns everything or nothing useful. The harmonic mean is dominated by the smaller value (F₁ ≈ 0.0198). The weighted form is F_β = (1+β²)PR/(β²P+R); β>1 emphasises recall (e.g. legal discovery), β<1 emphasises precision.

steps.title: Solved example 1 · P, R, F
steps.body:
A system returns 10 documents; 4 are relevant; the collection has 8 relevant documents.
P = 4/10 = 0.4, R = 4/8 = 0.5, F₁ = 2(0.4)(0.5)/(0.9) = 0.4/0.9 = **0.444**.

steps.title: Solved example 2 · Cohen's kappa
steps.body:
Two judges label 100 documents: both relevant 60, both non-relevant 20, A-rel/B-non 10, A-non/B-rel 10.
P(A) = 80/100 = 0.8. Each judge calls 70 relevant → pooled P(rel) = 140/200 = 0.7, P(non) = 0.3; P(E) = 0.7² + 0.3² = 0.58.
κ = (0.8 − 0.58)/(1 − 0.58) = 0.22/0.42 = **0.524** (moderate agreement).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using accuracy for IR.
- Computing recall with the number retrieved in the denominator.
- Forgetting that recall needs knowledge of all relevant documents; test collections approximate it with pooling.

lessons.title: Evaluating rankings: P@k, AP, MAP, MRR and nDCG

scenes.text: A user rarely scrolls past the first page; a relevant result at rank 1 is worth far more than at rank 50.

steps.title: Binary-relevance measures
steps.body:
- **Precision@k (P@k)** = relevant in the top k / k. Ignores order within k.
- **Average precision (AP)** = (1/R)·Σ over ranks i with a relevant document of P@i, where R = total relevant documents (unretrieved relevant docs contribute 0). **MAP** = mean AP over queries.
- **MRR** = mean of 1/rank of the first relevant result, suited to known-item or question answering.

steps.title: Graded relevance: DCG and nDCG
steps.body: With gains relᵢ (e.g. 0–3): **DCG@k = Σ relᵢ / log₂(i+1)** (rank 1 divided by log₂2 = 1). **IDCG** is the DCG of the ideal ordering; **nDCG = DCG/IDCG** ∈ [0,1], averaged across queries. Variants use (2^rel − 1) as gain. Web search also uses click-based and online A/B evaluation, but offline judged measures remain the standard for controlled comparison.

For three queries whose first relevant rank is 1, 3 and 2: MRR = (1 + 1/3 + 1/2)/3 = **0.611**.

- Using log₂(i) at rank 1 (division by zero): the denominator is log₂(i+1).
- Averaging nDCG over queries without per-query normalisation.

steps.title: Rocchio algorithm
steps.body:
Relevance feedback: retrieve, let the user mark relevant (Dᵣ) and non-relevant (Dₙᵣ) documents, then move the query vector:

**q_m = α·q₀ + β·(1/|Dᵣ|)Σ_{d∈Dᵣ} d − γ·(1/|Dₙᵣ|)Σ_{d∈Dₙᵣ} d**

Typical weights α = 1, β = 0.75, γ = 0.15 (positive feedback is more valuable). Negative components are set to 0. It improves recall for synonym and vocabulary mismatch problems but fails if the query is ambiguous or the relevant documents are very different from one another.

steps.title: Variants
steps.body:
- **Pseudo (blind) relevance feedback:** assume the top k results are relevant; no user effort, but query drift can happen.
- **Implicit feedback:** clicks and dwell time.
- **Global query expansion:** add synonyms from a thesaurus or word-embedding neighbours, or terms co-occurring in logs; **local expansion** uses the top results (as above).

q_m = (1 + 0.75, 0 + 0.375, 0 + 0.375 − 0.15) = **(1.75, 0.375, 0.225)**. Terms 2 and 3 were absent from the original query and now contribute.

- Setting γ larger than β (distrusting positive evidence).
- Applying pseudo-relevance feedback to queries whose top results are mostly wrong; the query drifts.

lessons.title: Lab: Edit distance, k-grams and spelling correction

scenes.text: Someone types 'bord' when they meant 'board' or 'border'.

steps.title: Tolerant retrieval toolkit
steps.body:
- **Wildcards:** a **permuterm index** rotates each term with a $ end marker (hello$, ello$h, llo$he …) so any single-* query becomes a prefix search; a **k-gram index** maps character k-grams (with $ boundaries) to terms, so 'mon*' → $m, mo, on and the candidates are post-filtered.
- **Edit (Levenshtein) distance:** minimum insertions, deletions and substitutions turning s₁ into s₂, computed by dynamic programming in O(|s₁||s₂|): D[i][j] = min(D[i−1][j]+1, D[i][j−1]+1, D[i−1][j−1] + (s₁[i]≠s₂[j])).
- **Jaccard on k-grams:** |A∩B|/|A∪B| selects candidates quickly before the exact distance.
- **Soundex** hashes names by sound: keep the first letter, map consonants to digits (b,f,p,v→1; c,g,j,k,q,s,x,z→2; d,t→3; l→4; m,n→5; r→6), drop vowels and h,w,y, collapse repeats, pad to 4 characters. Robert → R163.

steps.title: Solved example 1 · Bigram Jaccard
steps.body:
'bord' → {$b, bo, or, rd, d$} (5). 'border' → {$b, bo, or, rd, de, er, r$} (7).
Intersection = {$b, bo, or, rd} = 4; union = 8; Jaccard = **0.5**. 'board' → {$b, bo, oa, ar, rd, d$}; shares {$b, bo, rd, d$} = 4 with 'bord'; union = 5+6−4 = 7; Jaccard = 0.571, so 'board' is the better candidate.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting the $ boundary markers in k-grams (then 'or' and 'ord' are not anchored).
- Mixing cost models: with substitution cost 2, intention→execution is 8; with cost 1 it is 5.
- Correcting rare but valid terms; engines also use query logs and context.

lessons.title: Web crawling: frontier, politeness and Bloom filters

story.title: Fetching a billion pages without annoying anyone

scenes.text: A crawler discovers pages by following links, starting from a few seed URLs.
It must be fast, but also polite: no website should be hammered with requests.

steps.title: Crawler architecture
steps.body:
Basic loop: take a URL from the **frontier** → resolve DNS → fetch → parse and extract links → normalise URLs → test **URL-seen** → add new URLs → send content to the indexer.

Requirements: **robustness** (spider traps, malformed HTML), **politeness** (respect **robots.txt**, crawl-delay, limit requests per host), **freshness**, **scalability** (distributed across machines, hash URLs by host), **quality** (prefer important pages). The frontier has *front queues* for priority and *back queues*, one per host, with a heap of next-allowed fetch times to enforce politeness. Duplicate URLs and near-duplicate content are detected to save work.

steps.title: URL-seen test with a Bloom filter
steps.body: A **Bloom filter** with m bits and k hash functions represents a set of n items. Insert: set k bits. Query: all k bits set → 'probably present', any 0 → 'definitely absent'. No false negatives; false-positive probability ≈ (1 − e^(−kn/m))^k, minimised at k = (m/n)·ln 2. It uses a few bits per URL instead of storing the URL string.

steps.title: Solved example 1 · Politeness
steps.body: A host allows one request per 2 seconds. To fetch 10,000 pages from it: 10,000 × 2 s = 20,000 s = **5.56 hours** for that host, so the crawler overlaps work on thousands of other hosts instead of going faster on one.

steps.title: Solved example 2 · Bloom filter
steps.body: m/n = 10 bits per element, k = 7 hashes. kn/m = 0.7; e^−0.7 = 0.4966; (1 − 0.4966)^7 = 0.5034^7 ≈ **0.0082** (0.82% false positives). Optimal k = 10 × 0.693 = 6.9 → 7. For 10⁹ URLs the filter needs 10¹⁰ bits ≈ 1.25 GB.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking robots.txt is access control: it is a convention for polite crawlers, not security.
- Believing a Bloom filter can have false negatives; it cannot (without deletions).
- Ignoring URL normalisation (lower-case host, remove fragments, resolve relative links, sort query parameters).

lessons.title: Lab: PageRank by equations and power iteration

scenes.text: A surfer clicks random links forever; sometimes, bored, she jumps to a random page.
The fraction of time she spends on each page is its PageRank.

steps.title: Definition
steps.body:
PageRank is the stationary distribution of a Markov chain. With N pages, damping (follow-link) probability d = 0.85 and teleport probability 1 − d:

**PR(p) = (1−d)/N + d · Σ_{q→p} PR(q)/out(q)**

In matrix form r = (1−d)/N·1 + d·M r, where M is the column-stochastic link matrix. **Dangling nodes** (no out-links) are treated as linking to every page. Teleportation makes the chain irreducible and aperiodic, guaranteeing a unique stationary vector; iterate from any start (**power iteration**) until the change is below a tolerance; about 50–100 iterations suffice for the web. PageRank is query-independent and is combined with text scores.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Dividing by the number of in-links instead of the out-degree of the linking page.
- Forgetting the (1−d)/N term (ranks then leak to 0 in cycles with sinks).
- Using d = 1 on graphs with sinks or disconnected parts: no unique solution.

lessons.title: HITS, topic-sensitive PageRank and web spam

scenes.text: A blog that links to the best tutorials is a hub; the tutorials everyone cites are authorities.
Spammers build link farms to fake authority; engines need defences.

steps.title: HITS
steps.body:
Kleinberg's **Hyperlink-Induced Topic Search** works on a query-specific base set (top results + their neighbours). Each page has a **hub score h** and an **authority score a**:

**a = Aᵀ h**, **h = A a** (A = adjacency matrix, A[i][j] = 1 if i links to j), each normalised after every step. Iteration converges to the principal eigenvectors of AᵀA (authorities) and AAᵀ (hubs). Compared with PageRank: HITS is query-dependent, has two scores and is vulnerable to topic drift and manipulation.

steps.title: Other ideas
steps.body:
- **Topic-sensitive PageRank:** teleport only to pages of a topic (e.g. sports), giving one vector per topic.
- **Spam:** keyword stuffing, cloaking, link farms, hijacked links; counters include TrustRank (propagate trust from hand-checked seeds), spam mass, and link-based features in classifiers.
- **Anchor text** is indexed with the *target* page because it describes it well.

steps.title: Solved example 1 · HITS iteration
steps.body:
Edges 1→2, 1→3, 2→3. Start h = (1,1,1).
- a = Aᵀh: a₁ = 0 (no in-links), a₂ = h₁ = 1, a₃ = h₁ + h₂ = 2 → (0,1,2); L2 norm √5 = 2.236 → **(0, 0.447, 0.894)**.
- h = A a: h₁ = a₂ + a₃ = 3 (using the unnormalised a), h₂ = a₃ = 2, h₃ = 0 → (3,2,0); norm √13 = 3.606 → **(0.832, 0.555, 0)**.
Page 3 is the best authority; page 1 the best hub.

steps.title: Solved example 2 · Link farm effect
steps.body: A spam page S receives links from 1,000 farm pages each with PR 0.0001 and out-degree 1: inflow = 0.85 × 1000 × 0.0001 = 0.085 — a large boost relative to an average page (1/N). TrustRank discounts it because the farm pages are far from trusted seeds.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Mixing the roles: authority a = Aᵀh uses incoming links, hub h = A a uses outgoing links.
- Forgetting normalisation (scores grow without bound).
- Calling HITS 'query-independent'; it is computed per query.

lessons.title: Lab: Near-duplicate detection — shingles, MinHash and LSH

scenes.text: A news story is copied across dozens of sites with tiny edits.
The engine fingerprints each page so near-copies cluster without comparing every pair.

steps.title: Shingling and Jaccard
steps.body:
A **k-shingle** is a contiguous sequence of k tokens (or characters). Represent a document as its set of shingles; similarity is **Jaccard J(A,B) = |A∩B| / |A∪B|**. Comparing all pairs is quadratic, so we compress sets.

**MinHash:** under a random permutation π of the shingle universe, P[min π(A) = min π(B)] = J(A,B). A signature of n independent minhashes estimates J as the fraction of matching positions.

**LSH banding:** split a signature of b·r values into b bands of r rows; two documents become candidates if they agree on *all rows of at least one band*. Candidate probability for similarity s: **P = 1 − (1 − sʳ)ᵇ**, an S-curve whose threshold is about (1/b)^(1/r).

steps.title: Solved example 1 · Jaccard of word bigrams
steps.body: A = 'a rose is a rose' → shingles {a rose, rose is, is a} (3). B = 'a rose is a flower' → {a rose, rose is, is a, a flower} (4). Intersection 3, union 4 → **J = 0.75**.

steps.title: Solved example 2 · Banding
steps.body: b = 20 bands, r = 5 rows (signature length 100). For s = 0.5: s⁵ = 0.03125; (1 − 0.03125)²⁰ = 0.5299; P = **0.470**. For s = 0.8: 0.8⁵ = 0.32768; (0.67232)²⁰ ≈ 0.00035; P ≈ **0.9996**. Similar pairs are almost always caught; dissimilar ones (s = 0.2: P = 1 − (1 − 0.00032)²⁰ ≈ 0.0064) rarely are.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using single-word shingles (k = 1) so that unrelated documents look similar; use k ≈ 3–5 words or 5–9 characters.
- Forgetting that LSH gives candidates; verify with the real Jaccard.
- Swapping b and r in the formula.

courses.title: Unit 6 · Web Mining: Classification, Clustering, Recommenders & Modern Ranking
courses.summary: Text classification with Naive Bayes, clustering with k-means, collaborative filtering and web usage mining (association rules), learning to rank and hybrid dense/sparse retrieval with reciprocal rank fusion.
outcomes: Learners can train and apply multinomial Naive Bayes with Laplace smoothing
Learners can run k-means by hand and compute SSE
Learners can compute neighbour-based predictions and support, confidence and lift
Learners can explain learning to rank and fuse rankings with RRF

scenes.text: A mail provider filters millions of messages per minute.
A Naive Bayes classifier counts words per class and multiplies probabilities — simple, fast and surprisingly strong.

steps.title: Multinomial Naive Bayes
steps.body:
Choose the class c maximising **P(c|d) ∝ P(c) Π P(tₖ|c)** (the 'naive' assumption: terms are conditionally independent given the class).
- Prior **P(c) = Nc/N** (documents in class / all documents).
- **P(t|c) = (T_ct + 1) / (Σ T_ct' + |V|)** with **add-one (Laplace) smoothing**, where T_ct = occurrences of t in training documents of c and |V| = vocabulary size.
Use **log probabilities** in code. Training is one pass over the data: O(|D|·L). Other classifiers for text: k-NN, Rocchio, logistic regression, linear SVM; evaluate with micro/macro-averaged F₁ and cross-validation. Feature selection (chi-square, mutual information) reduces noise.

steps.title: Solved example 1 · Training
steps.body:
Training set: c: 'Chinese Beijing Chinese', 'Chinese Chinese Shanghai', 'Chinese Macao'; not-c: 'Tokyo Japan Chinese'. Vocabulary: Chinese, Beijing, Shanghai, Macao, Tokyo, Japan → |V| = 6.
P(c) = 3/4, P(c̄) = 1/4. In c: 8 tokens, Chinese appears 5 times. **P(Chinese|c) = (5+1)/(8+6) = 3/7**, P(Tokyo|c) = P(Japan|c) = 1/14. In c̄: 3 tokens, Chinese once: P(Chinese|c̄) = 2/9, P(Tokyo|c̄) = P(Japan|c̄) = 2/9.

- Smoothing the numerator but forgetting |V| in the denominator.
- Multiplying many small probabilities directly (underflow): sum logs.
- Thinking independence is true; it is wrong but the classification often still works because only the ranking of classes matters.

scenes.text: A news aggregator wants to group thousands of articles by story without anyone labelling them.
Clustering finds groups of similar items automatically.

steps.title: k-means
steps.body:
1. Choose k initial centroids.
2. **Assign** every point to its nearest centroid.
3. **Update** each centroid as the mean of its points.
4. Repeat until assignments stop changing.

Objective: minimise the **SSE (RSS) = Σ‖x − μ_cluster‖²**; it decreases every iteration and converges to a *local* minimum, so results depend on initialisation (use k-means++ and restarts). Each iteration costs O(k·n·m). For text use cosine distance on normalised tf-idf vectors (spherical k-means). Choosing k: elbow, silhouette.

steps.title: Hierarchical agglomerative clustering (HAC)
steps.body: Start with n singleton clusters and repeatedly merge the closest pair. Linkage: **single** (min distance; chaining effect), **complete** (max distance; compact clusters), **average**, **centroid**. Output is a dendrogram; cut at a level to obtain clusters. Complexity at least O(n²). Evaluation: **purity**, NMI, Rand index and F-measure against labels (external), or silhouette (internal).

steps.title: Solved example 1 · k-means on 1-D data
steps.body:
Points 1, 2, 9, 10, 11 with initial centroids 1 and 2.
- Iteration 1: 1→c₁; 2→c₂ (distance 0); 9, 10, 11 are nearer to 2 than to 1 → c₂. c₁ = {1}, c₂ = {2, 9, 10, 11} → new centroids 1 and 8.
- Iteration 2: 2 is 1 from 1 and 6 from 8 → c₁; 9 is 8 from 1 and 1 from 8 → c₂. c₁ = {1, 2} (mean 1.5), c₂ = {9, 10, 11} (mean 10).
- Iteration 3: no changes → converged.
**SSE** = (0.5² + 0.5²) + (1² + 0 + 1²) = 0.5 + 2 = **2.5**.

steps.title: Solved example 2 · Purity
steps.body: Cluster 1 has 10 docs: 8 sports, 2 politics. Cluster 2 has 10 docs: 7 politics, 3 sports. Purity = (8 + 7)/20 = **0.75**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking k-means finds the global optimum.
- Not normalising text vectors before Euclidean k-means.
- Reading purity as quality when k = n (singletons give purity 1).

lessons.title: Lab: Recommenders and web usage mining (association rules)

story.title: People who viewed this also viewed…

scenes.text: An e-commerce site logs which products appear together in a session.
Association rules and collaborative filtering turn clicks into recommendations.

steps.title: Collaborative filtering
steps.body: **User-based CF** predicts a rating from similar users: r̂(u,i) = Σ sim(u,v)·r(v,i) / Σ|sim(u,v)| over neighbours v who rated i (with mean-centring for bias). **Item-based CF** uses item–item similarity (adjusted cosine) and scales better. **Cold start** (new users/items) is handled with content features. Matrix factorisation learns latent factors r ≈ pᵤ·qᵢ.

steps.title: Web usage mining
steps.body:
Pipeline: log data (timestamp, IP, URL, user agent) → cleaning (drop bots/images) → **sessionisation** (e.g. a 30-minute inactivity timeout) → pattern discovery (association rules, sequential patterns, clustering of sessions) → recommendations or site redesign.

For a rule A → B: **support = P(A∧B)**, **confidence = P(B|A)**, **lift = confidence / P(B)** (lift > 1: positive association).

steps.title: Solved example 1 · Neighbour prediction
steps.body: Two neighbours rated the item 4 and 2 with similarities 0.9 and 0.3. r̂ = (4·0.9 + 2·0.3)/(0.9 + 0.3) = 4.2/1.2 = **3.5**.

steps.title: Solved example 2 · Rule metrics
steps.body: 1000 sessions: A in 200, B in 250, both in 100. Support = 0.10; confidence(A→B) = 100/200 = 0.50; P(B) = 0.25; lift = 0.5/0.25 = **2.0**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Reading high confidence as a strong association when B is simply very common (check lift).
- Treating every IP as a person (proxies, NAT) and ignoring bot traffic when sessionising.
- Recommending using only popularity (no personalisation).

lessons.title: Lab: Learning to rank, dense retrieval and rank fusion

scenes.text: A query 'cheap flights to goa' also matches pages saying 'budget airfare Goa' that share no words.
Modern engines fuse keyword (BM25) and embedding (dense) results with rank fusion.

steps.title: Learning to rank (LTR)
steps.body:
Combine many features (BM25, PageRank, anchor match, freshness, click rate) into one score learned from judgments or clicks.
- **Pointwise:** regress/classify each document's relevance.
- **Pairwise:** learn to order pairs (RankNet, RankSVM); loss on score differences.
- **Listwise:** optimise a list-level measure (LambdaRank/LambdaMART, ListNet), often gradient-boosted trees.
Click data are biased by **position bias**: higher results get more clicks regardless of relevance, so models correct for it.

steps.title: Dense retrieval and RRF
steps.body:
**Dense retrieval:** encode query and document with a neural encoder into vectors; rank by cosine/dot product using an approximate nearest-neighbour index (HNSW, IVF). It captures synonyms but can miss exact identifiers, so it is combined with BM25 (**hybrid search**).

**Reciprocal Rank Fusion:** RRF(d) = Σ over rankers 1/(k + rank_r(d)), commonly k = 60. It needs no score calibration.

steps.title: Solved example 1 · RRF score
steps.body: A document is rank 1 in list A and rank 3 in list B, k = 60: 1/61 + 1/63 = 0.016393 + 0.015873 = **0.032266**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Adding raw BM25 and cosine scores directly (different scales).
- Believing dense retrieval replaces keyword search; exact terms (product codes, names) still need lexical matching.
- Training a ranker on raw clicks without correcting position bias.

steps.title: Specification

steps.title: Implementation notes
steps.body: Store token counts per class and the vocabulary set. P(t|c) = (count + 1)/(total_c + |V|). In real code take logs: score = log P(c) + Σ log P(t|c).

steps.title: Common mistakes

- Using the vocabulary of the test document instead of the training set.
- Computing priors from token counts instead of document counts.

courses.title: Unit 7 · Revision, Practicals & Exam
courses.summary: A formula and key-point sheet for the whole subject, the standard practical experiments (index and Boolean search, tf-idf ranking, PageRank/HITS, evaluation) with procedures, observation tables and viva questions, original exam-style questions and a 20-question exam.
outcomes: Learners can recall every key formula of the subject

scenes.text: Sana has one hour left; she needs the whole course on one page.
She builds a compact sheet of definitions and formulas, grouped by unit.

steps.title: Units 1–2: indexing
steps.body:
- Inverted index: dictionary + sorted postings; df = #docs, cf = #occurrences.
- AND merge O(x+y); order by increasing df; OR estimate = sum of dfs.
- Skips: √P; positional index answers phrase/proximity, 2–4× larger.
- Heaps: **M = k·Tᵇ** (k≈30–100, b≈0.5). Zipf: **cfᵢ ∝ 1/i**.
- BSBI: sort (termID,docID) blocks, merge; SPIMI: per-block dictionary, no global termID.
- Gaps; VB (high bit set on last byte); **γ length = 2⌊log₂n⌋+1**.

steps.title: Units 3–4: ranking and evaluation
steps.body:
- **idf = log₁₀(N/df)**; tf weight **1+log₁₀tf**; tf-idf = product.
- **cos(q,d) = q·d / (|q||d|)**.
- **BM25** = Σ IDF · tf(k₁+1)/(tf + k₁(1−b+b·dl/avgdl)); limit k₁+1.
- Query likelihood: P(q|d)=ΠP(t|d); JM: λP_mle+(1−λ)P(t|C).
- P = rel retrieved/retrieved; R = rel retrieved/all rel; **F₁ = 2PR/(P+R)**; AP = (1/R)ΣP@i at relevant ranks; **DCG = Σ relᵢ/log₂(i+1)**, nDCG = DCG/IDCG.
- **Rocchio:** q_m = αq₀ + β·mean(Dᵣ) − γ·mean(Dₙᵣ).
- Edit distance DP; k-gram Jaccard; Soundex.

steps.title: Units 5–6: web
steps.body:
- Crawler: frontier, politeness, robots.txt, Bloom filter FP ≈ (1−e^(−kn/m))ᵏ, optimal k=(m/n)ln2.
- **PR(p) = (1−d)/N + d·Σ PR(q)/out(q)**, d=0.85; HITS a=Aᵀh, h=Aa, normalise.
- Shingles, **Jaccard**, MinHash estimates J; LSH **P = 1−(1−sʳ)ᵇ**.
- Naive Bayes: **P(t|c) = (T_ct+1)/(ΣT_ct'+|V|)**; k-means minimises SSE; purity.
- Support = P(A∧B); confidence = P(B|A); lift = conf/P(B).
- RRF = Σ 1/(k+rank), k=60.

steps.title: Top ten examiner traps
steps.body: 1. df vs cf. 2. Sorting postings. 3. Skipping the +1 in 1+log tf. 4. log₂(i+1) in DCG. 5. AP divides by *all* relevant docs. 6. Out-degree (not in-degree) in PageRank. 7. LSH formula uses b and r in the right places. 8. Add |V| in NB smoothing. 9. VB continuation bit is on the last byte here. 10. Gamma length 2⌊log₂n⌋+1.

cards.back: M = k·T^b — vocabulary grows as a power of tokens, b≈0.5

courses.title: Unit 1 · React Fundamentals
courses.summary: Components and JSX, props and state, hooks (useState, useEffect), lists, keys and controlled forms — topics commonly taught in B.Tech full-stack electives.
outcomes: Learners can build function components with JSX and props
Learners can manage state immutably with useState
Learners can run side effects with useEffect and correct dependencies

scenes.text: Farhan's canteen menu page repeats the same card HTML 40 times.
With React he writes one MenuCard component and reuses it for every dish.

steps.title: What React does
