steps.body: React builds UIs from **components** — functions that return a description of UI. When data changes, React re-runs the component and updates only the parts of the real DOM that changed (reconciliation using a virtual DOM).

steps.title: JSX rules
steps.body:
JSX looks like HTML but compiles to `React.createElement` calls. - Return **one root** (use a fragment `<>...` if needed). - `className` instead of `class`, `htmlFor` instead of `for`. - Embed expressions in `{ }`: `

{title}

`. - Component names start with a **capital letter**; lowercase means an HTML tag. - Self-close empty tags: ``.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** `function Hello({ name }) { return

Hello, {name}

; }` used as `` renders 'Hello, Farhan'. **Example 2. Conditional rendering.** `{isVeg ? 🟢 Veg : 🔴 Non-veg}` or `{offer && 20% off}`. Beware `{count && ...}` when count is 0 — React renders '0'.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Returning two sibling elements without a wrapper.
- Writing `class=` instead of `className=`.
- Naming a component `menuCard` (lowercase) — React treats it as an unknown HTML tag.
- Putting statements like `if` directly inside JSX braces (use ternary or compute before return).

activity.prompt:
Write a component Greeting that takes a prop name and renders

Hello, {name}

.
activity.hint: Destructure name from props and place it inside braces.

quiz.q: In JSX the HTML class attribute is written as…
quiz.why: class is a reserved word in JavaScript, so JSX uses className for the HTML class attribute.

quiz.q: Why must component names start with a capital letter?
options: Lowercase names are treated as HTML tags
quiz.why: JSX treats lowercase names like div as built-in HTML tags. A capital letter tells React it is your own component.
The value 0 is falsy, so && stops and returns 0. React renders the number 0 as text, so you see 0 instead of nothing.

quiz.q: A component can return multiple siblings by wrapping them in…
quiz.why: A component must return a single root. A fragment (<>...</>) groups siblings without adding an extra DOM element.
JSX is syntax sugar. The compiler turns each tag into a React.createElement call (or the newer equivalent).

story.title: The cart that would not update

scenes.text: Jaya pushes an item into her cart array, but the screen never changes.
She learns React compares references: she must create a new array with setCart([...cart, item]).

steps.title: Props vs state
steps.body:
- **Props**: inputs passed from parent to child; read-only inside the child.
- **State**: data a component owns and can change with `const [value, setValue] = useState(initial)`.
- Data flows **down** via props; events flow **up** via callback props (`onAdd={handleAdd}`).
- When two siblings need the same data, **lift state up** to their common parent.

steps.title: Updating state correctly
steps.body:
- Never mutate: create new arrays/objects: `setCart([...cart, item])`, `setUser({...user, name: 'J'})`.
- Use the updater form when the next value depends on the previous: `setCount(c => c + 1)`.
- State updates are batched; the new value is visible on the **next render**, not on the next line.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** Clicking a button running `setCount(count + 1); setCount(count + 1);` with count = 0 gives **1** (both use stale 0). With `setCount(c => c + 1)` twice → **2**.

**Example 2. Remove item id 3.** `setCart(cart.filter(i => i.id !== 3))` — filter returns a new array, so React re-renders.

**Example 3. Toggle done.** `setTodos(todos.map(t => t.id === id ? {...t, done: !t.done} : t))`.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- `cart.push(item); setCart(cart)` — same reference, no re-render.
- Reading state immediately after setting it.
- Copying props into state and wondering why it doesn't update.
- Calling a setter during render (infinite loop).

activity.prompt: Simulate an immutable cart update: create newCart with the item added, without changing cart. Print both lengths.
activity.hint: Spread the old array into a new one.

quiz.q: Inside a child component, props are…
quiz.why: Props flow down from the parent and must be treated as read-only in the child. Changes should go through the parent's state.

quiz.q: count = 5; setCount(count+1) twice in one click → next count?
quiz.why: Both calls read the same stale count of 5 in that render, so each sets it to 6. The result is 6, not 7.

quiz.q: Correct way to add to array state?
quiz.why: State must be replaced, not mutated. setArr([...arr, x]) creates a new array, so React sees a change and re-renders.

quiz.q: Two sibling components need the same value. You should…
options: Lift it to the common parent
quiz.why: When siblings need the same data, lift the state up to their closest common parent and pass it down as props. This keeps one source of truth.

quiz.q: The updater form setX(prev => ...) is needed when…
options: The new value depends on the old one
quiz.why: Use the updater form when the new value depends on the previous one. It gets the latest state, avoiding stale values.

scenes.text: Nikhil fetches products inside his component body and the server logs explode with requests.
Moving the fetch into useEffect with an empty dependency array makes it run once after mounting.

steps.title: Side effects
steps.body:
Rendering should be pure. Work that touches the outside world — fetching, timers, subscriptions, document.title — goes in `useEffect(() => { ... }, [deps])`.

- No array: runs after **every** render.
- `[]`: runs once after the first render (mount).
- `[id]`: runs after mount and whenever id changes.
- Return a **cleanup** function to clear timers or cancel requests.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1. Fetch once.**
`useEffect(() => { fetch('/api/products').then(r => r.json()).then(setProducts); }, []);`

**Example 2. Timer with cleanup.**
`useEffect(() => { const t = setInterval(tick, 1000); return () => clearInterval(t); }, []);` Without cleanup, each remount adds another interval.

**Example 3. Stale request.** When `id` changes quickly, use an `ignore` flag or `AbortController` in cleanup so an old response cannot overwrite a newer one.

steps.title: Rules of hooks and other hooks
steps.body:
- Call hooks only at the top level of components or custom hooks — never in loops or conditions.
- `useRef` holds a mutable value or DOM node without re-rendering; `useMemo`/`useCallback` cache values/functions; `useContext` reads shared data without prop drilling.
- Custom hook: a function named `useSomething` that calls other hooks.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Missing dependencies → stale data; extra object dependencies created every render → infinite loop.
- Making the effect function itself `async` (it must return nothing or a cleanup). Define an async function inside and call it.
- Forgetting loading and error states.

activity.prompt: Match the dependency array to when the effect runs.

quiz.why: With an empty dependency array, the effect has nothing to react to. So it runs once, after the first render (mount).

options: The effect would return a promise instead of a cleanup
quiz.why: An async function always returns a promise, but an effect may only return nothing or a cleanup function. Define an async function inside and call it instead.

options: At the top level of components/custom hooks
quiz.why: Hooks must be called at the top level of components or custom hooks, never in loops, conditions or handlers. This keeps the call order the same on every render.

quiz.q: To keep a value between renders without re-rendering, use…
quiz.why: useRef holds a mutable value that persists across renders. Changing it does not trigger a re-render, unlike state.

quiz.q: An interval started in an effect should be…
quiz.why: An interval keeps running unless stopped. Clear it in the effect's cleanup function to avoid leaks and duplicate timers.

scenes.text: When Ritu deletes the first row of her editable table, the text in the inputs jumps to the wrong rows.
She was using the array index as key; switching to the item's id fixes it.

steps.title: Rendering lists
steps.body:
`{items.map(it =>
  • {it.name}
    • )}` Keys must be **stable and unique among siblings** so React can match old and new items. Index keys are acceptable only for static lists that never reorder.

steps.title: Controlled forms
steps.body:
A **controlled** input's value comes from state: `<input value={name} onChange={e => setName(e.target.value)} />`. On submit: `e.preventDefault()`, validate, then send.

For many fields, keep one object: `setForm({...form, [e.target.name]: e.target.value})`.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1. Search filter.** state `q`; `const shown = products.filter(p => p.name.toLowerCase().includes(q.toLowerCase()));` — derived data, no extra state needed.

**Example 2. Client-side routing.** With React Router, `<Route path='/products/:id' element={<Product />} />` and inside Product `const { id } = useParams();`. Navigation uses `<Link to='/products/7'>` so the page does not fully reload.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Missing keys (console warning) or using Math.random() as key (remounts every render).
- Storing derived values (like filtered lists) in separate state.
- Using `<a href>` for internal routes, causing full reloads.
- Mixing controlled and uncontrolled (value undefined at first).

activity.prompt: Derived data: print the names of products containing the search text (case-insensitive), joined by commas.
activity.hint: Lower-case both sides before includes().

quiz.q: Best key for a list of database rows?
quiz.why: A key must be stable and unique among siblings. The database row id fits; index changes with reordering, and a random key changes every render.

quiz.q: A controlled input gets its value from…
quiz.why: A controlled input's value comes from React state and its onChange updates that state. So state is the single source of truth.

quiz.q: Filtered results based on a query should be…
quiz.why: Filtered results can be derived from the list and the query during render. Storing them in separate state duplicates data and can get out of sync.

quiz.q: Why use <Link> instead of <a> in React Router?
quiz.why: <Link> changes the URL and updates the view on the client without a full page reload. A plain <a> reloads the whole page.

quiz.q: Using index as key breaks when…
options: Items are inserted, deleted or reordered
quiz.why: Index keys break when items are inserted, deleted or reordered, because an item's index (identity) changes. React then mixes up state between rows.

questions.q: React updates the real DOM by…
options: Diffing the new UI description with the old and applying changes
questions.why: React builds a new description of the UI, compares it with the old one (reconciliation), and applies only the differences to the real DOM.

questions.q: Which is valid JSX?
questions.why: JSX uses className, and lowercase names for HTML tags. <div className='a'> is valid; class, classname and capital Div are not.

questions.q: Props are passed…
questions.why: Props flow from a parent to its children in one direction. Children send information back using callback props.

questions.q: setCount(c=>c+1) called 3 times in one handler starting from 0 →
questions.why: Each updater receives the latest value: 0 → 1 → 2 → 3. So three calls give 3.

questions.q: useEffect with [a, b] re-runs when…
questions.why: An effect re-runs whenever any dependency in the array changes. With [a, b], that means a changing or b changing.

questions.q: Cleanup function in useEffect runs…
options: Before the next effect run and on unmount
questions.why: The cleanup function runs before the effect runs again and when the component unmounts. It undoes the previous effect.

questions.q: Assertion: arr.push then setArr(arr) re-renders. Reason: React compares state by reference.
questions.why: push mutates the same array, so setArr(arr) passes the same reference and React skips the re-render. The reason (comparison by reference) is true, but the assertion is false.

questions.q: Which hook shares data without prop drilling?
questions.why: useContext reads a value supplied by a Context provider, so deep children get data without passing props through every level.

questions.q: Calling a hook inside an if block…
questions.why: React tracks hooks by call order. A hook in a condition may be skipped on some renders, which shifts the order and breaks state matching.

questions.q: Case: an effect depends on an options object created in render; it runs endlessly. Best fix?
options: Memoise the object with useMemo or move it inside the effect
questions.why: An object created in render is new each time, so the effect sees a changed dependency and re-runs forever. Memoising it (useMemo) or moving it inside the effect keeps it stable.

questions.q: useParams() returns…
questions.why: useParams returns the dynamic route segments, e.g. { id: '5' } for /users/:id.

questions.q: Which renders nothing when list is empty and avoids printing 0?
questions.why: list.length > 0 is a boolean, so && renders the list or nothing. list.length && ... would print 0 for an empty list.

questions.q: A component re-renders when…
options: Its state or props change, or its parent re-renders
questions.why: A component renders again when its own state or props change, or when its parent re-renders. CSS changes alone do not trigger it.

questions.q: useMemo is used to…
options: Cache an expensive computed value between renders
questions.why: useMemo remembers the result of an expensive calculation and recomputes it only when its dependencies change.

questions.q: Case: switching quickly between users shows the wrong profile from a slow earlier request. Fix?
options: Ignore or abort stale requests in the effect cleanup
questions.why: A slow earlier request can finish after a newer one and overwrite it. In the effect cleanup, ignore or abort the stale request so only the latest response is used.

courses.title: Unit 2 · Node.js and Express APIs
courses.summary: The Node.js runtime and npm, modules, Express routing and middleware, REST API design, validation and error handling.
outcomes: Learners can explain the Node event-driven, non-blocking model
Learners can manage dependencies with npm and package.json
Learners can write Express routes with params, query and JSON bodies
Learners can write middleware and central error handling

scenes.text: Ankit is surprised that the same JavaScript he wrote for buttons can run a server.
npm init creates package.json, and one command installs Express with all its dependencies.

steps.title: What Node is
steps.body: Node.js runs JavaScript outside the browser using the V8 engine plus **libuv**, which handles file and network I/O asynchronously. One main thread serves many connections because it never waits idle on I/O — great for APIs, less suited to heavy CPU work (use worker threads or separate services).

steps.title: Modules and npm
steps.body:
- CommonJS: `const fs = require('fs'); module.exports = fn;`
- ES modules: `import express from 'express'; export default fn;` (set `"type": "module"` in package.json or use .mjs).
- `package.json` lists `dependencies`, `devDependencies` and `scripts` (`npm run dev`).
- Semantic versioning MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH; `^4.18.0` allows minor/patch updates.
- `package-lock.json` pins exact versions — commit it. Never commit `node_modules`.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** A version range `^1.4.2` accepts 1.4.3 and 1.9.0 but not 2.0.0. `~1.4.2` accepts 1.4.9 but not 1.5.0.

**Example 2. Environment config.** Read `process.env.PORT || 3000` so the hosting platform can choose the port; keep secrets in environment variables, not code.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using synchronous file functions (`readFileSync`) inside request handlers — blocks all users.
- Mixing require and import without configuring module type.
- Committing `.env` files with secrets.
- Installing unknown packages without checking maintenance and audit warnings (`npm audit`).

activity.prompt: Create a tiny module-style function: export-free version. Write function slugify(s) that lower-cases and replaces spaces with '-'. Print slugify('Hello MERN World').
activity.hint: toLowerCase, then split on spaces and join with '-'.

quiz.q: Node handles many connections on one thread because…
quiz.why: Node uses an event-driven, non-blocking I/O model (libuv). One thread can handle many connections because it does not wait for each I/O to finish.
^2.3.1 allows changes that keep the major version at 2 and are at least 2.3.1. So 2.9.0 is fine, but 3.0.0 or 1.9.9 is not.

quiz.q: Which file pins exact installed versions?
quiz.why: package-lock.json records the exact versions of every installed package. package.json only holds version ranges.
Secrets such as database passwords belong in environment variables or a secret store. Putting them in code, a public repo or the front end exposes them.

options: Blocks the event loop for all users
quiz.why: readFileSync blocks the single Node thread until the read finishes. Every other request has to wait, so use the async version.

scenes.text: The college library wants an API so a mobile app can list and search books.
Sneha maps each action to a route: GET /books, GET /books/:id, POST /books.

steps.title: Basic server and routes
steps.body:
`const app = express(); app.use(express.json());`
`app.get('/books', (req, res) => res.json(books));`
`app.listen(3000);`

- `req.params` — path parts (`/books/:id`).
- `req.query` — query string (`/books?author=Tagore`).
- `req.body` — parsed JSON body (needs `express.json()`).
- `res.status(201).json(obj)`, `res.sendStatus(204)`.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1. Get by id.**
`app.get('/books/:id', (req, res) => { const b = books.find(x => x.id === Number(req.params.id)); if (!b) return res.status(404).json({error: 'Not found'}); res.json(b); });`
Note: params are strings, so convert.

**Example 2. Create.** `app.post('/books', (req, res) => { const b = {id: nextId++, ...req.body}; books.push(b); res.status(201).json(b); });`

**Example 3. Routers.** `const r = express.Router(); r.get('/', ...); app.use('/books', r);` keeps files small.

steps.title: Testing APIs
steps.body: Use an HTTP client (curl, a REST client extension, or automated tests with a library such as supertest) to call endpoints and check status codes and JSON.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting `express.json()` → `req.body` is undefined.
- Comparing string param '3' with number 3 using ===.
- Sending two responses (missing `return` after an error response) → 'headers already sent'.
- Declaring `/books/:id` before `/books/search`, so 'search' is captured as an id.

activity.prompt: Simulate a route handler: write getBook(id) that returns {status, body}. It should return status 404 when missing. Print the status for id '2' and '9'.
activity.hint: Convert idParam with Number() before comparing.

quiz.why: In ?author=Tagore, the part after ? is the query string. Express exposes it as req.query.author.

quiz.q: req.body is undefined in a POST. Likely cause?
quiz.why: Express does not parse JSON bodies by default. Without express.json() middleware, req.body stays undefined.

quiz.q: Status to send after creating a resource?
quiz.why: 201 Created tells the client a new resource was made. 200 is a generic success and 204 means no content.

quiz.q: 'Cannot set headers after they are sent' usually means…
quiz.why: This error means the code tried to send a second response for the same request. Add return after the first res.send/res.json.
URL segments are text, so req.params.id is a string, even if it looks like a number. Convert it when you need a number.

scenes.text: Every request passes a series of checkpoints: logging, JSON parsing, authentication, then the route.
If any checkpoint finds a problem it stops the request and sends a clear error.

steps.title: What middleware is
steps.body:
Middleware is a function `(req, res, next)` that runs in order. It can read/modify req and res, end the response, or call `next()` to pass control.

- App-level: `app.use(logger)`. Route-level: `app.post('/books', requireLogin, handler)`.
- Built-in: `express.json()`, `express.static('public')`.
- Common packages: CORS configuration, security headers (e.g. helmet), rate limiting.

steps.title: Validation and central error handler
steps.body:
- Validate every input on the server (type, length, range, allowed values) and reply **400** with a helpful message.
- An error handler has **four** parameters: `app.use((err, req, res, next) => { res.status(err.status || 500).json({error: 'Something went wrong'}); });` — log details on the server, but don't leak stack traces to users.
- Errors in async handlers must be passed to `next(err)` (or use a wrapper).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1. Logger.** `app.use((req, res, next) => { console.log(req.method, req.url); next(); });` Forgetting `next()` makes every request hang.

**Example 2. Order matters.** If `app.use(express.json())` is placed after the routes, those routes see no body. Middleware runs top to bottom.

**Example 3. Validation.** For POST /books require `title` as a non-empty string ≤ 200 chars; otherwise `400 {error: 'title is required'}`.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting `next()`.
- Error handler with three params (Express won't treat it as an error handler).
- Returning raw error messages or stack traces to clients.
- Validating only on the front end.

activity.prompt: Simulate a middleware chain: run each function in order; each calls next() to continue. Print the order of execution.
activity.hint: next for step i is a function that calls run(i + 1).

quiz.why: Express middleware gets (req, res, next). Calling next() hands control to the next handler.

quiz.q: An Express error handler has how many parameters?
quiz.why: Express recognises an error handler by its four parameters (err, req, res, next). With fewer, it is treated as normal middleware.
Invalid input is a client error, so respond with 400 Bad Request. 500 would wrongly blame the server.

quiz.q: If a middleware neither responds nor calls next()…
quiz.why: If middleware neither sends a response nor calls next(), nothing continues the chain. The client waits and the request hangs.

quiz.q: Why hide stack traces from API users?
options: They reveal internal details useful to attackers
quiz.why: Stack traces expose file paths, libraries and logic. Attackers can use these details, so log them on the server and return a safe message.

scenes.text: A startup renamed a JSON field and every mobile app in users' pockets crashed.
They introduce /api/v1, consistent errors and pagination — and changes stop breaking clients.

steps.title: Design principles
steps.body:
- Nouns and plural collections: `/api/v1/students`, `/api/v1/students/42/marks`.
- Methods carry the action; status codes carry the outcome.
- **Stateless**: each request carries what is needed (e.g. a token).
- Consistent error shape: `{ "error": { "code": "NOT_FOUND", "message": "..." } }`.
- Versioning (`/v1`) so old clients keep working.

steps.title: Pagination, filtering, sorting
steps.body:
`GET /students?branch=CSE&sort=-cgpa&page=2&limit=20`

- Offset pagination: skip = (page − 1) × limit.
- Cursor pagination (`?after=<id>`) is stable for fast-changing data.
- Return metadata: total, page, limit or next cursor.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** page = 3, limit = 25 → skip = **50**; items 51–75 are returned.

**Example 2. Redesign** `POST /deleteStudent?id=4` → `DELETE /api/v1/students/4` returning 204.

**Example 3. Idempotency.** A payment POST retried after a timeout could charge twice; APIs accept an `Idempotency-Key` header so the server recognises a repeat.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Returning 200 with `{error: ...}` for failures.
- Unbounded list endpoints (returning 1 million rows).
- Breaking field names without a new version.
- Inconsistent naming (camelCase in one endpoint, snake_case in another).

activity.prompt: Offset pagination: page = 5, limit = 12. How many records are skipped?

quiz.q: Best endpoint to fetch marks of student 9?
quiz.why: A good REST URL uses nouns and nesting for relations, and the verb comes from the HTTP method. /students/9/marks with GET fits.

options: Each request contains all info needed; no server session dependence
quiz.why: Stateless means each request carries everything needed, e.g. a token, and the server does not rely on stored session state between requests. This makes scaling easier.
Skip = (page − 1) × limit = (2 − 1) × 10 = 10. The first page (page 1) skips 0.

options: So changes don't break existing clients
quiz.why: Versioning (e.g. /v1/) lets you change the API in /v2/ while old clients keep working on the old version.

quiz.q: Retrying a POST safely is helped by…
quiz.why: A client sends a unique idempotency key with each request. If a retry carries the same key, the server recognises it and does not create a duplicate.

questions.q: Node.js is built on which JS engine?
questions.why: Node.js runs JavaScript on Google's V8 engine. SpiderMonkey is Firefox's and Chakra was Edge's old engine.

questions.q: Which command adds a dependency to package.json?
questions.why: npm install express downloads the package and records it as a dependency in package.json.

questions.q: ~3.2.1 accepts…
questions.why: ~3.2.1 allows only patch updates, i.e. 3.2.x with x ≥ 1. So 3.2.9 fits, but 3.3.0 does not.

questions.q: /users/:id with request /users/abc → req.params.id =
questions.why: Route params are strings taken from the URL. For /users/abc the value of id is the string 'abc'.

questions.q: Which line enables JSON bodies?
questions.why: app.use(express.json()) registers middleware that parses JSON request bodies into req.body.

questions.q: Middleware order is…
questions.why: Express runs middleware and routes in the order they were registered, top to bottom, until one responds.

questions.q: Assertion: Node is ideal for CPU-heavy image processing on the main thread. Reason: Node's main thread is single-threaded.
questions.why: Node's main thread is single-threaded, so the reason is true. CPU-heavy work blocks it for all requests, so the assertion is false.

questions.q: Routes /items/:id and /items/search: which order is correct?
questions.why: Express matches routes in order. If /items/:id comes first, it would capture 'search' as an id, so the specific /items/search route must come first.

questions.q: Correct status for invalid JSON fields?
questions.why: Invalid fields in the request are a client mistake, so respond with 400 Bad Request.

questions.q: Errors thrown in an async Express 4 route are…
options: Must be passed to next(err) or wrapped
questions.why: In Express 4, a rejected promise in an async handler is not caught automatically. Use try/catch with next(err) or a wrapper.

questions.q: page=4, limit=30: first record number returned (1-based)?
questions.why: Skip = (4 − 1) × 30 = 90 records, so the first record returned is number 91.

questions.q: Which should never be committed to Git?
questions.why: A .env file holds secrets such as keys and passwords. It must not be committed, or anyone with the repository can read them.

questions.q: express.static('public') is used to…
options: Serve files like images and CSS
questions.why: express.static serves files from a folder, like images, CSS and client-side JS, directly to the browser.

questions.q: Case: a POST /orders times out and the app retries; two orders appear. Best server-side fix?
questions.why: A retry resends the same POST, creating a duplicate. An idempotency key lets the server detect the repeat and return the original result.

questions.q: A rate limiter responds to excess requests with…
questions.why: 429 Too Many Requests is the standard status for requests blocked by a rate limit.

questions.q: Which is a good uniform error response?
questions.why: A good error response uses the right status code (404 for missing) and a consistent body with a code and message. It does not leak a stack trace.

courses.title: Unit 3 · MongoDB and Mongoose
courses.summary: Document databases, CRUD operations, query operators, indexes, the aggregation pipeline and data modelling with Mongoose schemas.
outcomes: Learners can compare documents with relational rows
Learners can write find, insert, update and delete queries with operators
Learners can build aggregation pipelines with $match, $group and $sort
Learners can design schemas choosing embedding vs referencing and add indexes

scenes.text: Pooja's student data has varying fields: some students have hostel info, some have scholarships.
In MongoDB each student is one flexible JSON-like document.

steps.title: The document model
steps.body:
MongoDB stores **documents** (BSON — binary JSON) in **collections** inside a **database**.

- Each document has a unique `_id` (ObjectId by default).
- Fields can hold arrays and nested documents.
- Relational analogy: table ≈ collection, row ≈ document, column ≈ field, JOIN ≈ embedding or `$lookup`.

steps.title: CRUD in the shell
steps.body:
- Create: `db.students.insertOne({name: 'Pooja', branch: 'CSE', cgpa: 8.4})`, `insertMany([...])`.
- Read: `db.students.find({branch: 'CSE'})`, `findOne`, projection `find({}, {name: 1, _id: 0})`.
- Update: `updateOne({name: 'Pooja'}, {$set: {cgpa: 8.6}})`, `$inc`, `$push`, `$unset`; `upsert: true` inserts if missing.
- Delete: `deleteOne`, `deleteMany`.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** Increase every ECE student's fee by 500: `db.students.updateMany({branch: 'ECE'}, {$inc: {fee: 500}})`.

**Example 2.** Add a skill to an array: `updateOne({name: 'Pooja'}, {$push: {skills: 'React'}})`; use `$addToSet` to avoid duplicates.

**Example 3.** Without `$set`, `updateOne(filter, {cgpa: 9})` is rejected in modern drivers (or would replace the document in old replace semantics) — always use update operators.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting `$set` and wiping other fields with a replace.
- `deleteMany({})` deletes **everything** in the collection.
- Storing numbers as strings, making range queries wrong.
- Assuming find returns an array in drivers — it returns a cursor.

activity.prompt: Find the names of all CSE students (hide _id).
activity.starter: db.students.find({ /* filter */ }, { /* projection */ })
activity.solution: db.students.find({ branch: 'CSE' }, { name: 1, _id: 0 })
activity.hint: Filter by branch; projection {name: 1, _id: 0}.

quiz.why: MongoDB stores records as documents in BSON, a binary form of JSON that supports extra types like dates and ObjectIds.

quiz.q: Operator to add 1 to a numeric field?
quiz.why: $inc adds a number to a numeric field (use a negative to subtract). $set would overwrite the value.
$push always appends, even if the value is already there. $addToSet adds it only if it is not already present, avoiding duplicates.
An empty filter {} matches every document, so deleteMany({}) removes all documents. The collection and its indexes remain.

quiz.q: Every document has a unique field called…
quiz.why: Every MongoDB document has a unique _id field, added automatically as an ObjectId if you do not supply one.

scenes.text: Searching 2 million orders by email takes 8 seconds.
An index on email turns a collection scan into an index lookup of a few milliseconds.

steps.title: Operators
steps.body:
- Comparison: `$eq $ne $gt $gte $lt $lte $in $nin` — `{cgpa: {$gte: 8}}`.
- Logical: `$and $or $not $nor` — `{$or: [{branch: 'CSE'}, {cgpa: {$gt: 9}}]}`.
- Element/array: `$exists`, `$type`, `$all`, `$elemMatch`, `$size`.
- Cursor methods: `.sort({cgpa: -1}).skip(20).limit(10)`, `.countDocuments()`.

steps.title: Indexes
steps.body:
Without an index, MongoDB scans every document (COLLSCAN). An index (B-tree) lets it jump to matches (IXSCAN).

- `db.orders.createIndex({email: 1})`; unique: `{unique: true}`.
- **Compound** index `{branch: 1, cgpa: -1}` supports queries on branch, or branch + cgpa (prefix rule).
- Check with `.explain('executionStats')`.
- Trade-off: indexes speed reads but slow writes and use memory.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** CSE students with cgpa 8–9 inclusive: `find({branch: 'CSE', cgpa: {$gte: 8, $lte: 9}})`.

**Example 2.** Index `{branch:1, year:1, cgpa:-1}` can serve `{branch}`, `{branch, year}`, `{branch, year, cgpa}` but **not** `{year}` alone (not a prefix).

**Example 3.** Top 3 by cgpa: `find().sort({cgpa: -1}).limit(3)`.

steps.title: Common mistakes (including injection)
steps.body:
- Passing raw request objects into filters: if a client sends an object where a string was expected, it can change the meaning of the query (NoSQL injection). Validate types and allow only expected fields.
- Creating indexes on every field.
- Using skip for very deep pagination (slow); prefer range/cursor pagination.

activity.prompt: Find students with cgpa greater than 8, sorted by cgpa descending, names only.
activity.starter: db.students.find({ }, { name: 1, _id: 0 }).sort({ })
activity.solution: db.students.find({ cgpa: { $gt: 8 } }, { name: 1, _id: 0 }).sort({ cgpa: -1 })
activity.hint: Use $gt in the filter and -1 in sort.

quiz.why: $in matches when the field equals any value in the list. So age 18 or age 19 matches, not values between them.
COLLSCAN means MongoDB read every document in the collection, because no suitable index was available. IXSCAN would mean an index was used.

quiz.q: Compound index {a:1,b:1} supports a query on b alone?
options: No, b is not a prefix
quiz.why: A compound index {a, b} is sorted by a first. A query on b alone is not a prefix of the index, so it cannot use it efficiently.
Every insert, update or delete must also update each index. So many indexes slow writes and use more storage.

options: Validate input types and whitelist fields
quiz.why: NoSQL injection often passes objects like {$ne: null} where a string is expected. Check types and allow only expected fields, never pass raw input into queries.

scenes.text: The dean wants average CGPA by branch, highest first.
Documents flow through a pipeline: filter, group, sort — like an assembly line.

steps.title: Stages
steps.body:
`db.students.aggregate([ stage1, stage2, ... ])`

- `$match` filter (place early to use indexes).
- `$group` by key with accumulators `$sum $avg $min $max $push $count`.
- `$sort`, `$limit`, `$skip`, `$project` (reshape), `$unwind` (one doc per array element), `$lookup` (left outer join with another collection).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1. Average per branch.**
`[{$group: {_id: '$branch', avg: {$avg: '$cgpa'}}}, {$sort: {avg: -1}}]`
With CSE: 8.4, 9.1 and ECE: 7.9 → CSE 8.75, ECE 7.9.

**Example 2. Count skills.** `[{$unwind: '$skills'}, {$group: {_id: '$skills', n: {$sum: 1}}}]` counts how many students list each skill.

**Example 3. Join.** `{$lookup: {from: 'courses', localField: 'courseIds', foreignField: '_id', as: 'courses'}}`.

steps.title: SQL equivalents
steps.body: $match ≈ WHERE, $group ≈ GROUP BY, $match after $group ≈ HAVING, $project ≈ SELECT list, $sort ≈ ORDER BY, $lookup ≈ LEFT JOIN.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting the `$` in field paths (`'$cgpa'`).
- `$match` at the end instead of the beginning (slower).
- Expecting `$unwind` to keep documents whose array is empty (it drops them unless `preserveNullAndEmptyArrays`).

activity.prompt: Order the pipeline to get the top 2 branches by average CGPA among final-year students.

quiz.why: In $group, $avg computes the mean of a field. $sum adds values and there is no $mean or $average accumulator.

quiz.q: Which stage is like SQL WHERE?
quiz.why: $match filters documents by a condition, like SQL WHERE. $project selects fields and $group groups documents.

quiz.q: $unwind on a doc with skills ['a','b','c'] produces…
quiz.why: $unwind outputs one document per array element. With 3 skills, it produces 3 documents.

quiz.q: Filtering groups after $group is like SQL…
quiz.why: A $match after $group filters the grouped results, like SQL HAVING. WHERE filters rows before grouping.

options: A left outer join with another collection
quiz.why: $lookup joins another collection into the document as an array. It behaves like a left outer join, keeping documents with no match.

scenes.text: Varun embeds every comment inside each blog post. A viral post hits MongoDB's 16 MB document limit.
He moves comments to their own collection with a postId reference.

steps.title: Embed or reference?
steps.body:
- **Embed** when data is read together and bounded (address inside user, a few line items in an order).
- **Reference** when data is large/unbounded, shared, or updated independently (comments, products in many orders).
- Max document size is **16 MB**.
- Design around your app's most frequent queries.

steps.title: Mongoose schemas and models
steps.body:
`const Student = mongoose.model('Student', new mongoose.Schema({ name: {type: String, required: true, trim: true}, cgpa: {type: Number, min: 0, max: 10}, email: {type: String, unique: true} }, {timestamps: true}));`

- Validation runs on save/create.
- `ref` + `.populate('courses')` resolves references.
- Middleware hooks (`pre('save')`), virtuals, and `lean()` for faster read-only queries.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1. E-commerce.** Order embeds a **snapshot** of item name and price (so later price changes don't alter old orders) and references productId.

**Example 2. Validation.** `Student.create({name: 'A', cgpa: 11})` fails with a ValidationError because max is 10 → respond 400.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Unbounded arrays inside documents.
- Treating `unique: true` as a validator — it creates a unique **index**; duplicate inserts fail with an index error.
- Over-normalising like SQL, causing many lookups.
- Not handling connection errors at startup.

activity.prompt: Embed or reference?

items.text: Thousands of comments on a post
Price snapshot inside an order line
Author profile used by many posts

quiz.why: A single BSON document is limited to 16 MB. Larger data needs a different design, such as GridFS or separate documents.

quiz.q: Comments that can grow without limit should be…
quiz.why: Embedding an array that can grow without limit risks hitting the 16 MB limit and slows updates. Store such comments in their own collection and reference them.
populate() follows a reference stored as an id and replaces it with the actual referenced document in the query result.
In Mongoose, unique: true builds a unique index in MongoDB. It is not a validator, so duplicates are rejected by the database.

quiz.q: Why store a price snapshot in orders?
options: Old orders keep the price paid
quiz.why: A product's price may change later. Saving the price in the order keeps a record of what the customer actually paid.

questions.q: In MongoDB, a table is roughly a…
questions.why: A MongoDB collection is similar to a table in SQL. Each document in it is like a row.

questions.q: Operator to set a field value?
questions.why: $set assigns a value to a field. $inc adds to a number and $push appends to an array.

questions.q: find({cgpa: {$gt: 8, $lt: 9}}) returns cgpa…
questions.why: $gt and $lt are strict, so values must be above 8 and below 9. Exactly 8 or 9 are excluded.

questions.q: Which needs upsert: true?
questions.why: With upsert: true, an update modifies a matching document if one exists and inserts a new one otherwise.

questions.q: Aggregation stage to reshape fields?
questions.why: $project chooses, renames or reshapes the fields in each document. $group aggregates and $limit restricts the count.

questions.q: Index {a:1, b:-1, c:1} can serve a query on…
questions.why: A compound index can support queries on its leading fields (prefix): a, or a and b. A query on c alone, or b alone, does not start at the prefix.

questions.q: Assertion: Placing $match early in a pipeline is better. Reason: It reduces documents for later stages and can use indexes.
questions.why: An early $match shrinks the data passed to later stages and can use an index. Both statements are true and the reason explains the assertion.

questions.q: Data: CSE [8,9,10], ECE [6,8]. $group avg by branch then $sort avg -1. First result?
questions.why: CSE average (8 + 9 + 10)/3 = 9 and ECE average (6 + 8)/2 = 7. Sorting averages in descending order puts CSE with 9 first.

questions.q: Case: an endpoint passes req.body.email directly into findOne. A client sends an object instead of a string. Best defence?
options: Validate that email is a string before querying
questions.why: If a client sends {$ne: null} instead of a string, findOne may match any user. Validate that email is a string before querying.

questions.q: Which is best for very deep pagination on a large collection?
questions.why: skip() makes the database walk past all skipped documents, which is slow for huge offsets. Querying for _id greater than the last seen one uses the index and stays fast.

questions.q: $unwind on a document whose array is empty (default options)…
questions.why: By default, $unwind drops documents whose array is empty or missing. The preserveNullAndEmptyArrays option keeps them.

questions.q: Mongoose validation error should map to HTTP…
questions.why: A Mongoose validation error means the client sent invalid data, so respond with 400 Bad Request, not 500.

questions.q: To speed read-only Mongoose queries returning plain objects use…
questions.why: lean() returns plain JavaScript objects instead of full Mongoose documents. That skips hydration, making read-only queries faster and lighter.

questions.q: Which is an anti-pattern?
options: An ever-growing array of log entries in one document
questions.why: An ever-growing array in a single document can hit the 16 MB limit and slow updates. Embedding an address, indexing email, and $match first are fine.

questions.q: Count students per skill requires which stage before $group?
questions.why: To count students per skill, first $unwind the skills array so each skill becomes its own document. Then $group by skill and count.

courses.title: Unit 4 · Full-Stack Integration, Authentication and Deployment
courses.summary: Connecting React to an Express API, CORS, password hashing and token/session authentication concepts, protected routes, environment configuration, testing and deployment.
outcomes: Learners can connect a React client to an Express + MongoDB API
Learners can explain password hashing and session vs token authentication
Learners can protect routes with middleware and role checks
Learners can configure environments, tests and a deployment pipeline

lessons.title: Connecting the client and the API

scenes.text: Ishaan runs React on port 5173 and Express on 5000; the browser blocks his fetch with a CORS error.
He configures the dev proxy and the API's allowed origin — data flows.

steps.title: Architecture
steps.body: Browser (React) → HTTP/JSON → Express API → Mongoose → MongoDB. The API is the only part that talks to the database; the client never holds database credentials.

steps.title: CORS and proxies
steps.body:
Different ports = different **origins**. Options:

- In development, a front-end dev-server proxy forwards `/api` to the backend.
- In production, serve both from one origin, or have the API allow only your site's origin (not `*` when using credentials).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1. A data hook.**
`function useBooks(){ const [data,setData]=useState([]); const [err,setErr]=useState(null); useEffect(()=>{ fetch('/api/books').then(r=>{ if(!r.ok) throw new Error(r.status); return r.json(); }).then(setData).catch(setErr); },[]); return {data, err}; }`

**Example 2. Optimistic update.** Remove a book from the UI immediately, call DELETE, and restore it if the server returns an error.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Database connection strings in front-end code.
- Allowing every origin with credentials.
- No loading/error states.
- Hard-coding `http://localhost:5000` in production builds — use environment config.

activity.prompt: Order what happens when a user clicks 'Add book'.
items: React handler calls fetch POST /api/books with JSON
Express middleware parses and validates the body
Route calls Mongoose to insert the document
MongoDB stores it and returns the new document
React updates state and re-renders the list

quiz.q: Which layer should talk to MongoDB?
quiz.why: Only the Express API should talk to MongoDB. The browser must never hold database credentials, so React calls the API instead.
An origin is protocol + host + port. Ports 5173 and 5000 differ, so they are different origins and CORS applies.

options: Forwarding /api to the backend so requests look same-origin
quiz.why: A dev proxy forwards /api calls from the front-end server to the backend. The browser sees the same origin, so it avoids CORS problems in development.

options: Update UI before server confirms, roll back on error
quiz.why: Optimistic UI updates the screen straight away, assuming the server will succeed, then rolls back if the request fails. This makes the app feel fast.

quiz.q: API base URLs in production should come from…
quiz.why: The API URL differs between development and production, so it should come from environment configuration, not be hard-coded.

scenes.text: A news story describes a small company whose plain-text passwords leaked.
Maya makes sure her app stores only slow, salted hashes — even she cannot read users' passwords.

steps.title: Storing passwords safely
steps.body:
- Never store plain text or reversible encryption.
- Use a slow, salted password-hashing function such as **bcrypt**, **scrypt** or **Argon2**. A **salt** (random per user) makes identical passwords hash differently.
- On login: hash the attempt with the stored salt and compare.
- Fast hashes like plain SHA-256 are unsuitable for passwords.

steps.title: Sessions vs tokens
steps.body:
- **Session**: server stores session data; browser holds a random session id in an HttpOnly cookie. Easy to revoke.
- **JWT**: a signed token (header.payload.signature) the client sends, often as `Authorization: Bearer <token>`. The server verifies the signature — the payload is **readable by anyone** (base64url), so never put secrets in it.
- Keep access tokens short-lived; use refresh tokens with rotation; always HTTPS.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1. Login flow.** Step 1: find user by email. Step 2: compare password with stored hash. Step 3: on success issue a session cookie or token; on failure reply 401 with a **generic** message ('Invalid email or password') so attackers cannot learn which emails exist.

**Example 2. Brute-force protection.** Rate-limit login attempts per account and IP, add delays or CAPTCHA after failures, and offer multi-factor authentication.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Putting the password or role trust only in the client.
- Long-lived JWTs with no way to revoke.
- Different error messages for 'no such user' vs 'wrong password'.
- Weak or committed signing secrets.

statements.s: A JWT payload is encrypted by default.
statements.why: It is only encoded and signed; anyone can read it.

statements.s: Salts make identical passwords produce different hashes.
statements.why: Each user gets a unique salt.

statements.s: SHA-256 alone is a good password hash.
Session ids should be stored in HttpOnly cookies.
Login errors should reveal whether the email exists.

quiz.q: Which is designed for password hashing?
quiz.why: bcrypt is a slow, salted hash made for passwords. MD5 and CRC32 are fast and weak, and Base64 is just encoding.

quiz.q: The three parts of a JWT are…
quiz.why: A JWT has three dot-separated parts: header, payload and signature.

quiz.q: Easiest auth type to revoke instantly?
quiz.why: With a server-side session, you can revoke access instantly by deleting the session. A long-lived JWT stays valid until it expires unless extra tracking is added.

options: Make each hash unique and defeat precomputed tables
quiz.why: A random salt makes the same password produce different hashes, and defeats precomputed (rainbow) tables.
Return 401 with a generic message. Saying 'user not found' reveals which emails exist, helping attackers.

scenes.text: Kiran hides the 'Delete user' button for non-admins and thinks the app is secure.
His reviewer explains the API itself must check the role on every request.

steps.title: Authentication vs authorisation
steps.body:
- **Authentication**: who are you? (login)
- **Authorisation**: what may you do? (roles/permissions)

Server middleware: `requireAuth` verifies the session/token and sets `req.user`; `requireRole('admin')` checks permission → 403 if not allowed.

steps.title: Object-level checks
steps.body: Checking the role is not enough: a student may edit **their own** profile but not someone else's. Always confirm ownership: `if (doc.owner.toString() !== req.user.id) return res.sendStatus(403);` Missing this is a very common real-world flaw (broken access control).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1. Route chain.** `app.delete('/api/users/:id', requireAuth, requireRole('admin'), deleteUser)`.

**Example 2. Client route guard.** In React, redirect to /login when there is no user — improves UX, but the **API** checks are what protect data.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Relying on hidden buttons or client checks.
- Trusting a role sent in the request body.
- Returning other users' data because the query filters only by id.
- Using 401 when the user is logged in but not allowed (use 403).

a.text: A logged-in student calls PATCH /api/profiles/77, which belongs to another student. What should the API do?

choices.label: Allow it — the user is logged in
choices.feedback: Being logged in is authentication, not permission.

choices.label: Check profile.owner equals req.user.id; reply 403 if not

bad.text: Any student could edit anyone's profile. This is broken access control.

good.text: The request is refused with 403 and logged. Data stays safe.

options: What are you allowed to do?
quiz.why: Authentication asks who you are. Authorisation asks what you are allowed to do.

quiz.q: Hiding an admin button in React is…
options: UX only; the API must enforce
quiz.why: Hiding a button only improves the UI. Users can still call the API directly, so the server must enforce permissions.

quiz.q: Logged in but lacking permission → status
quiz.why: 401 means not authenticated, while 403 Forbidden means you are logged in but lack permission.

quiz.q: Where should the user's role come from?
quiz.why: The role must come from data the server verified, such as a signed token or session. Anything the client sends (query, body, localStorage) can be forged.
Object-level authorisation checks that the user owns or may access that specific record, not just that they are logged in.

scenes.text: A team deploys by copying files at 7 pm on Friday; the site breaks and nobody knows why.
They add automated tests and a CI pipeline; every change is checked and deployed the same way.

steps.title: Testing levels
steps.body:
- **Unit tests**: one function (e.g. Jest/Vitest).
- **Integration tests**: API route + test database (e.g. supertest).
- **Component tests**: React components (e.g. Testing Library).
- **End-to-end**: real browser flows (e.g. Playwright/Cypress).
The testing pyramid: many unit tests, fewer integration, few E2E.

steps.title: Config and deployment
steps.body:
- Twelve-factor ideas: config in environment variables, stateless processes, logs to stdout.
- Build React to static files (`npm run build`) and host on a static host/CDN; run the API on a platform or container; use a managed MongoDB service with network restrictions.
- **CI/CD**: on every push run lint + tests; deploy on merge to main.
- Production: HTTPS, security headers, rate limiting, backups, monitoring and health-check endpoint.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1. Unit test.** `test('slugify', () => expect(slugify('A B')).toBe('a-b'));`

**Example 2. Pipeline order.** install → lint → unit tests → build → integration tests → deploy to staging → smoke test → deploy to production.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Testing against the production database.
- No `.env.example` documenting required variables.
- Opening the database to the whole internet.
- Deploying without a rollback plan.

activity.prompt: Write a tiny test helper expectEqual(actual, expected) that prints PASS or FAIL. Test sum(2,3) === 5.
activity.hint: Use a ternary on actual === expected.

quiz.q: The testing pyramid recommends most tests be…
quiz.why: The testing pyramid recommends many fast, cheap unit tests, fewer integration tests, and few slow end-to-end tests.
CI is Continuous Integration: every change is automatically built and tested.
Production settings and secrets belong in environment variables or a secret manager, not in source code or a front-end bundle.
Integration tests need a database, but not production. A separate test database keeps real data safe and tests repeatable.
Building a React app produces static HTML, JS and CSS files that any web server or CDN can serve.

questions.q: In MERN, the 'E' is…
questions.why: MERN stands for MongoDB, Express, React and Node. The E is Express.

questions.q: Which part should never ship to the browser?
questions.why: Anything sent to the browser can be read by users. Database credentials must stay on the server.

questions.q: A CORS error appears when…
options: The browser blocks reading a cross-origin response not permitted by the server
questions.why: A CORS error is the browser blocking a page from reading a response from another origin, because the server did not allow it. The server may still have processed the request.

questions.q: Which is true of JWTs?
options: Signature lets the server detect tampering
questions.why: A JWT's signature lets the server detect tampering. The payload is only encoded, not secret, and tokens can carry an expiry.

questions.q: Best password storage?
questions.why: Store passwords with a slow, salted one-way hash such as bcrypt or Argon2. Plain text, Base64 and reversible encryption are unsafe.

questions.q: Assertion: Hiding UI controls enforces permissions. Reason: Users can call the API directly.
questions.why: Users can call the API directly, so the reason is true. Hiding UI controls therefore does not enforce permissions, so the assertion is false and the API must check.

questions.q: Middleware order for an admin route?
questions.why: First verify who the user is (requireAuth), then check the role (requireRole), then run the handler. The order identifies, authorises, then acts.

questions.q: Case: GET /api/orders/123 returns any user's order if they know the id. The flaw is…
questions.why: If anyone who knows an id can read the order, the server is missing a check that it belongs to the user. That is broken object-level access control.

questions.q: Why rate-limit the login endpoint?
questions.why: Rate limiting slows repeated attempts, making password-guessing (brute force) much harder.

questions.q: Which test level runs a real browser?
questions.why: End-to-end tests drive a real browser through the whole app. Unit and integration tests do not need a browser.

questions.q: Short-lived access tokens are combined with…
questions.why: Access tokens live briefly to limit damage if stolen. A refresh token, rotated on use, gets new access tokens without asking for a password again.

questions.q: A health-check endpoint is used by…
options: Load balancers/monitors to know the service is alive
questions.why: A health-check endpoint tells load balancers and monitors that the service is running, so traffic can be routed or alerts raised.

questions.q: Which is a good CI step order?
questions.why: Run cheap checks first so failures stop early: lint, then tests, then build, then deploy.

questions.q: Case: users report stale data after an optimistic delete fails silently. Missing piece?
options: Rollback and error message on failure
questions.why: If a deletion fails on the server but the UI already removed the item, the UI is wrong. Roll back the change and show an error message.

questions.q: With credentials, Access-Control-Allow-Origin must be…
questions.why: For requests with credentials, the browser rejects a wildcard *. The server must send the exact allowed origin in Access-Control-Allow-Origin.

courses.title: Revision & Practice · MERN Stack
courses.summary: Quick-recall sheets for React, Express and MongoDB plus a mixed mock paper and a mini-project checklist.
outcomes: Learners can recall core hooks, route patterns and MongoDB operators
Learners can solve mixed full-stack questions
Learners can plan a small MERN project end to end

scenes.text: Your campus placement interview for a full-stack role is tomorrow.
These two pages cover what interviewers ask most.

steps.title: React
steps.body:
- Components return JSX; capitalised names; className.
- Props down, events up; lift state up.
- Never mutate state; use updater form for previous-value updates.
- useEffect deps: none = every render, [] = mount, [x] = when x changes; return cleanup.
- Stable keys (ids), controlled inputs, derived data computed in render.

steps.title: Express
steps.body:
- `app.use(express.json())` before routes.
- req.params (path), req.query (?a=b), req.body (JSON).
- Middleware (req,res,next); error handler (err,req,res,next).
- 200, 201, 204, 400, 401, 403, 404, 409, 429, 500.
- Validate on server; consistent error JSON; versioned routes.

steps.title: Explain-it-simply answers
steps.body: Virtual DOM: 'React compares the new UI description with the old and changes only what differs.' Middleware: 'checkpoints every request passes through in order.'

cards.back: To match list items between renders

quiz.why: State must be replaced, not mutated. Creating a new object with the spread and the change makes React notice the update.
In ?page=2, the page is in the query string, available as req.query.page. req.params holds route parameters.

quiz.q: Status for duplicate email on signup?
quiz.why: A duplicate email conflicts with an existing resource, so 409 Conflict fits best.

scenes.text: A senior reviews your pull request and asks three questions about queries and auth.
You answer each confidently using this sheet.

steps.title: MongoDB
steps.body:
- CRUD: insertOne/Many, find/findOne, updateOne/Many with $set/$inc/$push/$addToSet, deleteOne/Many.
- Operators: $gt $gte $lt $lte $in $or $exists $elemMatch.
- Indexes: prefix rule for compound; explain() COLLSCAN vs IXSCAN.
- Aggregation: $match → $group → $sort → $limit; $unwind; $lookup.
- Embed bounded data read together; reference unbounded/shared data; 16 MB limit.

steps.title: Security essentials
steps.body:
- Hash passwords with bcrypt/scrypt/Argon2.
- HttpOnly + Secure + SameSite cookies; short-lived tokens.
- Authorise on the server, including ownership checks.
- Validate types to avoid query injection; rate-limit logins; HTTPS everywhere; secrets in env vars.

steps.title: Practice
steps.body: Write the pipeline: top 3 cities by number of users. Answer: `[{$group:{_id:'$city', n:{$sum:1}}}, {$sort:{n:-1}}, {$limit:3}]`.

activity.prompt: Match the MongoDB concept to its SQL equivalent.

quiz.why: A compound index {x, y} supports queries on its prefix: x alone, or x and y together. A query on y alone cannot use it efficiently.

quiz.q: Which keeps duplicates out of an array?
quiz.why: $addToSet adds a value to an array only if it is not already there. $push would add duplicates.
Password hashing should be slow and salted, so guessing is expensive. A fast hash lets attackers try billions of guesses.

scenes.text: Recruiters ask for one complete project. You choose a 'College Lost & Found' app.
Plan it end to end, then take the mock paper below.

steps.title: Project plan
steps.body:
- Data: users, items (title, description, location, status lost/found, owner ref, createdAt).
- API: auth routes; CRUD /api/v1/items with filters (?status=lost&q=bottle) and pagination.
- Front end: list + search, item detail route, create form, 'my items' page.
- Security: hashed passwords, owner-only edits, input validation, rate limiting.
- Tests + CI + deploy.

steps.title: Talk about trade-offs
steps.body: In interviews, explain one decision: e.g. 'I referenced owners rather than embedding them because a user's profile changes independently.'

steps.title: Frequent exam traps
steps.body:
- Stale state with repeated setX(x+1).
- Missing express.json().
- $set forgotten in updates.
- 401 vs 403.
- Index prefix rule.

activity.prompt: My MERN project is ready when…
items: Users can sign up and log in
Only owners can edit their items

quiz.q: Owner reference in items should store…
quiz.why: Store the owner's _id as a reference. It keeps one source of truth and avoids copying sensitive data such as the password.
Search and filter options go in the query string of a GET request, e.g. ?q=pen&city=Pune.

quiz.q: Which proves only owners can edit?
options: An API ownership check plus a test
quiz.why: A hidden button is only cosmetic. The API must check ownership, and a test shows that it really blocks non-owners.

questions.q: Which hook stores component state?
questions.why: useState is the hook that stores component state. useRef keeps values without re-rendering and useEffect runs side effects.

questions.q: MongoDB query for age ≥ 18?
questions.why: $gte means greater than or equal to. So {age: {$gte: 18}} matches ages 18 and above.

questions.q: Express route param syntax?
questions.why: Express marks route parameters with a colon, as in /users/:id. The value is then in req.params.id.

questions.q: useEffect(() => {...}) with no deps runs…
questions.why: Without a dependency array, the effect has no restriction, so it runs after every render.

questions.q: Which status for 'email already registered'?
questions.why: A duplicate registration conflicts with existing data, so respond with 409 Conflict.

questions.q: Aggregation to count users per city?
questions.why: Group by the city field and add 1 per document with $sum: 1. This counts users per city.

questions.q: Which is NOT a reason to reference instead of embed?
questions.why: Data that is always read together and small is better embedded. Referencing fits unbounded growth, shared data or independent updates.

questions.q: count=2; handler runs setCount(count+1) three times. Next count?
questions.why: All three calls use the same stale count of 2 in that render, so each sets 3. The result is 3, not 5.

questions.q: Assertion: JWT payloads must not contain secrets. Reason: They are base64url-encoded, not encrypted.
questions.why: A JWT payload is only base64url-encoded, so anyone can decode it. So never put secrets in it, and the reason explains the assertion.

questions.q: Which line causes 'req.body undefined'?
questions.why: Express applies middleware in order. If routes come before app.use(express.json()), their requests are not parsed, so req.body is undefined.

questions.q: Case: list rows lose input text after deleting the first row. Cause?
questions.why: With index keys, deleting the first row shifts all the indexes. React then matches the old input states to the wrong rows. Use a stable id as the key.

questions.q: page=6, limit=15 → skip?
questions.why: Skip = (page − 1) × limit = 5 × 15 = 75.

questions.q: Which prevents login brute force best?
questions.why: Rate limiting slows repeated guesses and multi-factor authentication stops a stolen or guessed password alone from working. Together they give layered defence.

questions.q: explain() shows IXSCAN means…
questions.why: IXSCAN means MongoDB used an index scan to answer the query. COLLSCAN would be a full scan.

questions.q: Which React pattern avoids duplicate state for search results?
options: Store results in a second state
questions.why: Filtered results can be computed from the list and the query each render. Storing them separately duplicates state and risks inconsistency.

questions.q: Case: an effect fetches /users/{id}; id changes 1→2 quickly; response for 1 arrives last and shows. Best fix?
options: Cleanup that ignores/aborts the stale request
questions.why: The slow response for id 1 can arrive after id 2's and overwrite it. A cleanup that ignores or aborts the stale request prevents that race.

questions.q: Which statement about middleware is correct?
options: It can end the response or call next()
It runs after the route only
It must always send a response
questions.why: Middleware can modify req and res, then either end the response or call next() to pass control on. It does not have to respond.

questions.q: Index {email:1}, {unique:true}: inserting an existing email…
questions.why: A unique index rejects duplicates. Inserting an existing email fails with a duplicate key error.

uni-cse-ml.title: Machine Learning
uni-cse-ml.description: A complete B.Tech-level machine learning course: data preparation, regression and gradient descent, classification algorithms, evaluation and model selection, and unsupervised learning — with Python code activities.

courses.title: Unit 1 · Foundations and Data Preprocessing
courses.summary: What learning from data means, types of ML, the ML workflow, and preparing data: cleaning, encoding, scaling and train/test splits. Covers topics commonly taught in B.Tech ML courses and the GATE Data Science & AI syllabus.
outcomes: Learners can distinguish supervised, unsupervised and reinforcement learning
Learners can describe the end-to-end ML workflow
Learners can handle missing values, encode categories and scale features
Learners can split data correctly and avoid data leakage

scenes.text: Writing rules for every spam email is impossible — spammers change words daily.
Instead, Aditi trains a model on thousands of labelled emails, and it learns the patterns itself.

steps.title: Definition
steps.body:
A program **learns** from experience E with respect to task T and performance measure P if its performance on T, measured by P, improves with E (Mitchell's definition).

Example: T = classify email, P = accuracy, E = labelled emails.

steps.title: Types of learning
steps.body:
- **Supervised**: labelled examples (x, y). Regression (y is a number) and classification (y is a class).
- **Unsupervised**: no labels; find structure — clustering, dimensionality reduction.
- **Semi-supervised**: few labels, many unlabelled.
- **Reinforcement learning**: an agent takes actions and learns from rewards.
- **Self-supervised**: labels created from the data itself (e.g. predict the next word).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1. Classify the task.** Predict house price → supervised regression. Group customers by behaviour → unsupervised clustering. Detect fraud yes/no → supervised classification. A robot learning to walk → reinforcement learning.

**Example 2. Features and label.** For loan default: features = income, existing EMIs, credit history length; label = defaulted (yes/no).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling any if-else program 'AI/ML'.
- Confusing regression (numeric output) with logistic regression (a classifier).
- Using ML when a simple rule works reliably.
- Forgetting that models learn **bias present in the data** too.

activity.prompt: Which kind of learning fits each task?

items.text: Predict tomorrow's temperature from past data
Group news articles by topic without labels

quiz.why: Regression predicts a continuous number such as a price. Classification predicts a category.
Clustering finds groups without labels, so it is unsupervised learning.

quiz.q: In Mitchell's definition, P stands for…
quiz.why: In Mitchell's definition, a program learns from experience E on task T with performance measure P, which shows how success is judged.
Despite its name, logistic regression outputs probabilities for classes, so it is used for classification.

quiz.q: An agent learning from rewards is…
quiz.why: An agent that learns by acting and receiving rewards or penalties is doing reinforcement learning.

scenes.text: A hospital asks: can we predict which patients will miss appointments?
The team defines the goal, collects data, builds a baseline, iterates, deploys and keeps monitoring.

steps.title: Steps
steps.body:
- Define the problem and success metric (and the cost of errors).
- Collect and understand data (EDA).
- Clean and prepare features.
- Split into train / validation / test.
- Train a **baseline**, then better models.
- Tune hyperparameters on validation data.
- Evaluate once on the test set.
- Deploy, monitor for **drift**, retrain.

steps.title: Parameters vs hyperparameters
steps.body:
- **Parameters** are learned from data (weights of a linear model, split thresholds of a tree).
- **Hyperparameters** are set before training (learning rate, k in kNN, tree depth, regularisation strength) and tuned using validation data.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1. Baseline.** 90% of patients attend. A model that always predicts 'attends' has 90% accuracy — any real model must beat this and must be judged with recall on the 'miss' class.

**Example 2. Classify.** Learning rate 0.01 → hyperparameter. Coefficient of age = 0.37 → parameter. Number of trees = 200 → hyperparameter.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Tuning on the test set (it stops being an honest estimate).
- Skipping a baseline.
- Optimising accuracy when the real cost is in missed positives.
- Deploying and never monitoring.

activity.prompt: Put the ML workflow in order.

quiz.why: Hyperparameters are set before training, like k in kNN. Weights, biases and learned thresholds are learned from the data.

quiz.q: The test set should be used…
quiz.why: The test set gives an honest estimate of final performance, so use it once at the end. Using it for tuning leaks information.

options: Input data distribution changes over time
quiz.why: Data drift is when the distribution of incoming data changes from what the model was trained on, which can make performance fall.
A baseline is a simple reference model, such as predicting the mean. A real model should beat it to be worthwhile.

quiz.q: 95% of emails are not spam. Always predicting 'not spam' gives accuracy…
quiz.why: If 95% of emails are not spam, always predicting not spam is right 95% of the time. High accuracy can hide a useless model on imbalanced data.

story.title: The salary column in lakhs and rupees

scenes.text: Half the salary values are in rupees and half in lakhs; city is text; some ages are blank.
Rahul standardises units, encodes cities, fills gaps and scales features before training.

steps.title: Missing values and outliers
steps.body:
- Drop rows/columns only if few are missing and data is plentiful.
- **Impute**: mean/median (numeric; median is robust to outliers), mode (categorical), or model-based.
- Add a 'was_missing' indicator when missingness itself carries information.
- Outliers: check if errors (fix/remove) or genuine (keep; use robust methods). IQR rule: outlier if < Q1 − 1.5·IQR or > Q3 + 1.5·IQR.

steps.title: Encoding categories
steps.body:
- **One-hot** for nominal categories (city): one 0/1 column per value.
- **Ordinal** encoding for ordered categories (low < medium < high).
- Label-encoding nominal data as 0,1,2 implies a false order for linear models.

steps.title: Scaling
steps.body:
- **Standardisation** z = (x − μ)/σ → mean 0, std 1.
- **Min–max** x' = (x − min)/(max − min) → [0, 1].
- Needed for distance-based (kNN, k-means, SVM) and gradient-based models; trees don't need it.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Computing scaling statistics on the whole dataset before splitting (leakage).
- Mean-imputing heavily skewed data.
- Label-encoding nominal features for linear models.
- One-hot encoding a feature with 10,000 categories without thinking (use hashing/target encoding carefully or grouping).

activity.prompt: Min–max scale the list to [0, 1] and print values rounded to 2 decimals.
activity.starter:
xs = [10, 20, 35, 60]
# scaled = ...
print(scaled)
activity.solution:
xs = [10, 20, 35, 60]
lo, hi = min(xs), max(xs)
scaled = [round((x - lo) / (hi - lo), 2) for x in xs]
print(scaled)
activity.hint: (x - min) / (max - min) for each x.

quiz.q: Best imputation for a skewed income column?
quiz.why: Income is skewed with outliers that pull the mean. The median is robust, so it is a better fill value.

quiz.q: Nominal 'city' for a linear model should be…
quiz.why: City has no order. One-hot encoding gives each city its own column, whereas 0, 1, 2 would imply a false ordering to a linear model.

quiz.q: Which model does NOT need feature scaling?
quiz.why: Decision trees split on thresholds of single features, so scaling does not change the splits. kNN, SVM and k-means depend on distances.
IQR = 30 − 10 = 20. The upper fence is Q3 + 1.5·IQR = 30 + 30 = 60.

scenes.text: A student's churn model scores 99% in the lab.
In production it fails: a feature 'cancellation_date' only exists after the customer has churned.

steps.title: Splitting
steps.body:
- Typical: 70–80% train, 10–15% validation, 10–15% test.
- **Stratified** split keeps class proportions (important for imbalanced data).
- **Time-series**: split by time (train on past, test on future), never shuffle.
- Group splits: keep all records of a patient/user in the same split.

steps.title: Data leakage
steps.body:
Leakage = information unavailable at prediction time sneaks into training.

- **Target leakage**: features derived from the label (cancellation_date).
- **Train–test contamination**: fitting scalers/imputers/feature selection on all data.
- Duplicate rows across splits.
Fix: build a **pipeline** that fits preprocessing on training folds only.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** 1,000 samples, 10% positive, stratified 80/20 split → test has 200 samples with **20** positives.

**Example 2. Spot the leak.** Predicting hospital readmission using 'number of days readmitted' → target leakage, remove it.

**Example 3. Time series.** Sales Jan 2020–Dec 2024: train 2020–2023, test 2024.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Shuffling time-series data.
- Normalising before splitting.
- Same user's images in both train and test (model memorises the person).
- Peeking at test results repeatedly.

activity.prompt: Split the list into train (first 80%) and test (last 20%) without shuffling (time order). Print the lengths.
activity.starter:
data = list(range(50))
# train, test = ...
print(len(train), len(test))
activity.solution:
data = list(range(50))
cut = int(0.8 * len(data))
train, test = data[:cut], data[cut:]
print(len(train), len(test))
activity.hint: cut = int(0.8 * len(data)); slice before and after.

quiz.why: Stratified splitting keeps the class proportions the same in each split. This matters for imbalanced data.

options: Train on past, test on future
quiz.why: For forecasting, train on the past and test on the future, like real use. Random shuffling would let the model see future data.

quiz.q: Fitting a scaler on all data before splitting causes…
quiz.why: Fitting a scaler on all data lets statistics from the test set influence training. That is data leakage.

quiz.q: A feature only known after the outcome is…
quiz.why: A feature only known after the outcome would not be available at prediction time. That is target leakage and makes results look unrealistically good.

quiz.q: 2,000 samples, 5% positive, stratified 75/25. Positives in test?
quiz.why: Test set = 25% of 2,000 = 500 samples. Stratification keeps 5%: 500 × 0.05 = 25 positives.

questions.q: Predicting whether a tumour is malignant is…
questions.why: Malignant versus benign is a discrete label, so this is classification.

questions.q: Which is learned during training?
questions.why: Model weights are learned from data during training. Learning rate, tree depth and number of folds are set beforehand.

questions.q: Unlabelled grouping of customers is…
questions.why: Grouping customers without labels is clustering, an unsupervised task.

questions.q: Min–max of 40 in range [20, 100]?
z-score of 35 with μ = 50, σ = 5?
Q1=40, Q3=60. Lower fence?
questions.why: IQR = 60 − 40 = 20. The lower fence is Q1 − 1.5·IQR = 40 − 30 = 10.

questions.q: Assertion: Decision trees need standardised features. Reason: Trees split on thresholds of single features.
questions.why: Trees split on a threshold for one feature, so scaling does not matter. So the reason is true, but the assertion that trees need standardised features is false.

questions.q: Which encoding suits 'size: S < M < L'?
questions.why: Sizes S < M < L have a natural order, so ordinal encoding (1, 2, 3) keeps it. One-hot would discard the order.

questions.q: Case: a credit model uses 'number of collection calls after default'. Problem?
questions.why: Collection calls after default happen only because the loan has defaulted. The feature uses information from after the outcome, which is target leakage.

questions.q: Which split is correct for monthly sales forecasting?
questions.why: For sales over time, split chronologically, training on earlier months and testing on later ones. Random splits would leak future information.

questions.q: Why must preprocessing be fitted only on training data?
options: To prevent test information leaking into training
questions.why: Fitting on test data lets its information influence training, making evaluation too optimistic. So fit preprocessing on training data only, then apply it to the test set.

questions.q: 1,000 rows, 2% fraud. Accuracy of always predicting 'not fraud'?
questions.why: If 98% of rows are not fraud, always predicting not fraud is right 98% of the time, yet it catches no fraud at all.

questions.q: Photos of the same 50 people are randomly split. Risk?
questions.why: If photos of the same person are in both train and test, the model can recognise the person rather than generalise. Split by person (group split).

questions.q: Std of [2, 4, 4, 4, 5, 5, 7, 9] (population)?
questions.why: The mean is (2+4+4+4+5+5+7+9)/8 = 5. Squared deviations sum to 32, so variance 4 and standard deviation √4 = 2.

questions.q: Which is NOT a valid reason to add a missing-indicator column?
options: It preserves information lost by imputation
Values are missing not at random
questions.why: A missing-indicator can preserve useful information about missingness, but it cannot guarantee higher accuracy. No technique guarantees that.

questions.q: Case: a model scores 0.99 AUC on validation but 0.62 live. Most likely first check?
questions.why: A big gap between validation (0.99) and real-world (0.62) performance usually points to leakage or a validation set that is not like the real data. Check this first.

courses.title: Unit 2 · Regression and Gradient Descent
courses.summary: Simple and multiple linear regression, least squares and the normal equation, gradient descent, polynomial features, bias–variance and regularisation (ridge, lasso).
outcomes: Learners can fit simple linear regression by least squares
Learners can perform gradient descent updates by hand and in code
Learners can explain bias–variance and over/underfitting
Learners can apply ridge and lasso regularisation and interpret R²

lessons.title: Simple linear regression and least squares

scenes.text: A teacher collects study hours and marks for five students.
