C++ runtime dispatch needs a virtual function called through a base pointer or reference. The call looks up the function in the vtable.

quiz.q: In Java, instance methods are virtual unless
quiz.why: Java instance methods are dynamically dispatched unless they are final, private or static. Those cannot be overridden, so they are bound at compile time.
Assigning a Derived object to a Base variable by value copies only the Base part, dropping the rest. This is object slicing.

quiz.q: Overloading by return type alone is
quiz.why: Overloads must differ in their parameter lists. The compiler cannot choose by return type alone, because a call does not say what type is expected.

lessons.title: Abstract classes, interfaces and virtual destructors

scenes.text: A geometry library wants every shape to have area(), but 'Shape' itself has no sensible area.
Making Shape abstract forces each concrete shape to provide its own area().

steps.title: Abstract classes
steps.body:
- C++: a class with at least one **pure virtual** function `virtual double area() const = 0;` cannot be instantiated.
- Java: `abstract class Shape { abstract double area(); }` — may also have fields, constructors and concrete methods.
- A derived class stays abstract until it overrides all pure/abstract methods.

steps.title: Java interfaces
steps.body:
- `interface Drawable { void draw(); }` — a contract; a class can implement many.
- Since Java 8: `default` and `static` methods; Java 9: private methods. Fields are implicitly `public static final`.
- Abstract class: shared state + partial implementation (is-a). Interface: capability (can-do), multiple allowed.

steps.title: Solved example: virtual destructor
Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Trying `new Shape()` for an abstract class.
- Forgetting `const` in an override signature in C++ (creates a new function, the base stays pure; `override` catches it).
- Declaring interface methods with weaker access in the implementing class (must be public).

activity.prompt: Define abstract class Shape with pure virtual double area() const and a virtual destructor. Implement Circle(r) (use 3.14159) and Rect(w,h). Read n shapes (`C r` or `R w h`), store as unique_ptr<Shape> in a vector, and print the total area with 2 decimals.
activity.hint: virtual ~Shape() = default; ensures correct cleanup through base pointers.

quiz.q: A C++ class with a pure virtual function is
quiz.why: A class with at least one pure virtual function (= 0) is abstract. It cannot be instantiated and derived classes must implement it.
A Java class can extend one class but implement any number of interfaces.

quiz.q: Fields in a Java interface are
quiz.why: Fields in a Java interface are implicitly public, static and final, i.e. constants.

quiz.q: Deleting a Derived through Base* without a virtual destructor
quiz.why: Deleting a derived object through a base pointer when the destructor is not virtual is undefined behaviour. Typically only the base part is destroyed, leaking the derived part.
Since Java 8, interfaces can include default methods (with bodies) and static methods. They still cannot have constructors or instance fields.

lessons.title: Multiple inheritance and the diamond problem

scenes.text: A SmartTV class inherits from both Display and NetworkDevice, and both inherit from Device.
Suddenly SmartTV has two copies of Device's serial number — the diamond problem.

steps.title: The diamond
steps.body:
B and C both derive from A; D derives from B and C. Without care, D contains **two A subobjects**, and `d.aField` is ambiguous.

C++ fix: **virtual inheritance** — `class B : virtual public A`, `class C : virtual public A`. Now D holds one shared A, and D's constructor initialises A directly.

steps.title: Solved example
Java's approach
steps.body: Java avoids state diamonds by allowing only one superclass. With interfaces, if two default methods clash, the class **must override** and may call a specific one: `Iface1.super.greet()`.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using virtual inheritance on only one side of the diamond.
- Ambiguous member access without qualification (`d.B::x`).
- Assuming Java has no diamond issues at all — default-method conflicts are a compile error until resolved.

activity.prompt: Build the diamond A ← B, C ← D with VIRTUAL inheritance; constructors print their letter. The given main creates one D and prints a newline — output must be ABCD.
activity.hint: Both B and C must inherit A virtually.

quiz.q: Without virtual inheritance, D in the diamond contains how many A subobjects?
quiz.why: In a non-virtual diamond, D inherits A once through B and once through C. So D contains 2 separate A subobjects.

quiz.q: Who constructs the virtual base A in the diamond?
quiz.why: With virtual inheritance, the most-derived class (D) constructs the single shared A. The intermediate classes B and C do not.

quiz.q: Java resolves conflicting default methods by
quiz.why: If a class inherits two default methods with the same signature, it must override the method to resolve the conflict. Otherwise there is a compile error.

quiz.q: Syntax to call a specific interface's default method
quiz.why: Java 8 lets a class call a specific interface's default method with Iface.super.m().

quiz.q: Output order with non-virtual diamond D d;
quiz.why: Without virtual inheritance, D builds B (which builds A first) and then C (which builds A again), then D. The output is A B A C D.

questions.q: Run-time polymorphism in C++ is achieved through
questions.why: Run-time polymorphism in C++ uses virtual functions, where the function chosen depends on the actual object at run time. Templates and overloading are resolved at compile time.

questions.q: Output: struct B{virtual void f(){cout<<1;}}; struct D:B{void f(){cout<<2;}}; B* p=new D; p->f();
questions.why: f is virtual and p points to a D object, so D::f runs. It prints 2.

questions.q: Output: same but f not virtual
questions.why: Without virtual, the call is bound at compile time to the pointer's static type B. So B::f runs and it prints 1.

questions.q: Output: D d; B b = d; b.f(); (f virtual)
questions.why: B b = d copies only the B part (slicing), so b is a real B object. The virtual call then runs B::f and prints 1.

questions.q: Which can't be overridden in Java?
questions.why: Static methods belong to the class and are bound at compile time. A subclass method with the same signature hides the base one rather than overriding it.

questions.q: Assertion: a base class intended for polymorphic deletion needs a virtual destructor. Reason: delete via a base pointer otherwise skips the derived destructor (undefined behaviour).
questions.why: If you delete a derived object through a base pointer and the destructor is not virtual, the derived destructor is skipped (undefined behaviour). So a virtual destructor is needed, and the reason explains the rule.

questions.q: Size impact of adding the first virtual function to a C++ class (typical)
options: a copy of the vtable per object
questions.why: The first virtual function typically adds one hidden vptr to each object. The vtable itself exists once per class, not per object.

questions.q: Case: Bird has fly(); Penguin extends Bird and throws in fly(). Which principle is broken?
questions.why: If Penguin cannot do fly(), it cannot replace Bird wherever a Bird is expected. This breaks the Liskov substitution principle.

questions.q: Java: class X implements I1, I2 where both declare default void m(). Then
questions.why: When two interfaces supply default m(), the class must override m() to resolve the ambiguity. Otherwise it does not compile.

questions.q: Which is true about abstract classes in Java?
options: they must have only abstract methods
questions.why: Abstract classes in Java can have constructors, which subclasses call via super(). They can also have fields and concrete methods, but cannot be instantiated.

questions.q: In C++, a derived class's override must match the base signature including
questions.why: The const qualifier is part of a C++ member function's signature. If it differs, the derived function does not override the base one.

questions.q: Order of constructor calls for class D : public B1, public B2 {M m;}
questions.why: Bases are constructed first in declaration order (B1, B2), then members (m), and then the body of D's constructor.

questions.q: Calling a virtual function inside a base class constructor (C++) calls
questions.why: During base construction the derived part is not built yet. So a virtual call in the base constructor runs the base version.

questions.q: Overloading example
questions.why: Overloading means the same function name with different parameter lists, like add(int,int) and add(double,double).

questions.q: Java's @Override annotation
options: makes the compiler check the method really overrides
questions.why: @Override asks the compiler to check that the method really overrides a superclass method. It catches typos in names or signatures.

questions.q: The diamond problem in C++ is solved by
questions.why: Virtual inheritance makes B and C share one A subobject in D, which solves the diamond problem.

questions.q: `final` on a Java class means
questions.why: A final class cannot be extended, as with String.

courses.title: Unit 3 · C++ Power Features: Operator Overloading, Templates, STL and Smart Pointers
courses.summary: Operator overloading and friend functions, function and class templates, the Standard Template Library (containers, iterators, algorithms), move semantics, and modern memory management with RAII and smart pointers.
outcomes: Learners can overload arithmetic, comparison and stream operators correctly
Learners can write function and class templates
Learners can choose the right STL container and use algorithms with lambdas
Learners can manage ownership with unique_ptr and shared_ptr

scenes.text: A finance module writes total = add(add(a, b), c) for money values. It is hard to read.
Overloading + lets the team write total = a + b + c, with paise handled correctly inside.

steps.title: Rules
steps.body:
- Overload as a member (`T operator+(const T&) const`) or a non-member (often a **friend** for access).
- Cannot overload `::`, `.`, `.*`, `?:`, `sizeof`. Cannot change precedence, arity or create new operators.
- `<<` and `>>` for streams must be non-members (left operand is the stream).
- Return by value for +, by reference for += and assignment.

steps.title: Solved example: Complex
Solved example: prefix vs postfix ++
steps.body:
- Prefix: `T& operator++()` — increment, return *this.
- Postfix: `T operator++(int)` — copy old value, increment, return the copy.
Prefix is cheaper for heavy objects (no copy).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Returning a reference to a local from operator+ (dangling).
- Making << a member (then usage would be `obj << cout`).
- Overloading operators with surprising meaning (e.g. + that subtracts).

activity.prompt: Implement struct Complex (integer parts) with operator+, operator* and a friend operator<< printing `a+bi` or `a-bi` (e.g. -5+10i, 3-2i). Read two complex numbers (re im re im) and print their sum and product on two lines.
activity.hint: (a+bi)(c+di) = (ac−bd) + (ad+bc)i.

quiz.why: The scope resolution operator :: is one of the few C++ operators that cannot be overloaded. The others listed are overloadable.
For cout << obj, the left operand is the stream, not your class. So operator<< is written as a non-member (often a friend).
Prefix and postfix ++ share a name. Postfix gets an unused int parameter, operator++(int), to tell them apart.
operator+= modifies the left object and returns *this by reference. This allows chaining and avoids a copy.

scenes.text: A team has maxInt, maxDouble and maxString — identical code three times.
One template function replaces all three, and the compiler generates each version on demand.

steps.title: Function templates
Class templates
Solved example
steps.body:
`maxOf(3, 7.5)` → **compile error**: T deduced as int and double. Fix: `maxOf<double>(3, 7.5)` → 7.5.

Java generics differ: they use **type erasure** (one compiled class, casts inserted), cannot use primitives directly (`List<int>` invalid; use `List<Integer>`).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Putting template definitions in a .cpp file and getting linker errors.
- Expecting templates to work for types lacking the required operators — errors appear at instantiation.
- Comparing C-strings with a template max (compares pointers, not text).

activity.prompt: Write a class template Stack<T> (push, pop, empty, size). Read n integers and push them; then read m words and push them on a Stack<string>. Print the integers popped (space separated) on line 1 and the words popped on line 2.
activity.hint: One template, two instantiations.

quiz.why: C++ templates are instantiated by the compiler for each type used. This gives compile-time polymorphism, unlike virtual functions.

quiz.q: maxOf(3, 7.5) with template<typename T> T maxOf(T,T)
quiz.why: The call maxOf(3, 7.5) gives T = int from one argument and double from the other. Deduction conflicts, so the call does not compile.
Java generics use type erasure: type parameters are checked at compile time and removed, leaving one class at run time.

quiz.q: Why do templates usually live in headers?
options: the definition is needed where it is instantiated
quiz.why: The compiler needs the full template definition wherever it instantiates the template. So definitions usually go in headers.
Java generics cannot use primitive types. Use the wrapper class, so List<Integer>.

scenes.text: A coding club needs a live leaderboard: count each user's solved problems and show the top scorers alphabetically on ties.
An unordered_map for counts, a vector for sorting and std::sort with a lambda do it in 15 lines.

steps.title: Containers at a glance
steps.body:
- **vector**: dynamic array; push_back amortised O(1); random access O(1).
- **deque**, **list** (doubly linked).
- **set/map**: balanced BST (red-black); sorted; O(log n).
- **unordered_set/unordered_map**: hash tables; average O(1).
- Adaptors: **stack**, **queue**, **priority_queue** (max-heap by default).

steps.title: Iterators and algorithms
steps.body:
Algorithms work on iterator ranges [begin, end):
- `sort(v.begin(), v.end(), cmp)` O(n log n); `stable_sort`
- `find`, `count`, `accumulate`, `reverse`, `unique`, `lower_bound` (sorted ranges)
- Lambdas: `[](const P& a, const P& b){ return a.second > b.second; }`
- Range-for: `for (auto& x : v)`

steps.title: Solved example: word frequencies
steps.body:
Input words: to be or not to be
- map<string,int>: be 2, not 1, or 1, to 2 (sorted keys).
- Sort pairs by count desc, then word asc → **be 2, to 2, not 1, or 1**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- `m[key]` on a map inserts a default value when the key is missing — use `find` or `count` to test.
- Invalidating iterators: erasing from a vector while iterating with the same iterator.
- A comparator that is not a strict weak ordering (using <=) → undefined behaviour in sort.

activity.prompt: Read n words. Print each distinct word with its count, sorted by count descending and then alphabetically, one `word count` per line.

tests.stdin:
6
to be or not to be

activity.hint: Compare counts first, then words.

quiz.why: std::map keeps keys ordered and is typically implemented with a balanced tree, a red-black tree. unordered_map is the hash-based one.
unordered_map uses hashing, so average lookup is O(1). Worst case is O(n) with many collisions.

quiz.q: m["x"] on a map without key x
options: inserts x with a default value
quiz.why: In C++, operator[] on a map inserts the key with a default-constructed value if it is missing. Use find or at to avoid inserting.
std::priority_queue uses less<int> by default, which puts the largest element on top. So it is a max-heap.
lower_bound does a binary search, so the range must be sorted (or partitioned) with respect to the search value.

scenes.text: A C++ service crashes at night: two objects deleted the same buffer.
Replacing raw new/delete with unique_ptr and shared_ptr makes ownership explicit — and the crash disappears.

steps.title: Smart pointers
steps.body:
- **unique_ptr<T>**: sole owner; cannot be copied, only moved (`std::move`). Deletes automatically. Create with `make_unique<T>(…)`.
- **shared_ptr<T>**: shared ownership with a reference count; the object is deleted when the count hits 0. Create with `make_shared`.
- **weak_ptr<T>**: non-owning observer; breaks shared_ptr cycles.

steps.title: Move semantics
steps.body:
An rvalue reference `T&&` binds to temporaries. A **move constructor** `T(T&& o) noexcept` steals o's resources instead of copying, leaving o valid but empty.
- Rule of five: destructor, copy ctor, copy assign, move ctor, move assign — or follow the **rule of zero** (use smart pointers and containers, write none).

steps.title: Solved example: reference counts
steps.body:
```
auto a = make_shared<int>(5);   // count 1
{ auto b = a;                    // count 2
  auto c = b; }                  // count 3, then 1 after the block
weak_ptr<int> w = a;             // still 1
a.reset();                       // count 0 → deleted; w.expired() == true
```

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Creating two shared_ptrs from the same raw pointer (two control blocks → double delete).
- Cycles of shared_ptr (parent ↔ child) leak — use weak_ptr for back-links.
- Using an object after `std::move` as if it still held its value.

activity.prompt: Demonstrate shared_ptr counts: create `auto a = make_shared<int>(42)`, print use_count; copy into b, print; create c from b inside a block, print inside; after the block print again; then reset a and b and print whether a weak_ptr w (made from a at the start) is expired (YES/NO). Expected 5 lines: 1, 2, 3, 2, YES.
activity.hint: weak_ptr does not increase use_count.

quiz.why: unique_ptr has sole ownership, so copying would give two owners and is disallowed. Ownership can be moved with std::move.

options: observe without owning and break cycles
quiz.why: A weak_ptr observes an object managed by shared_ptr without adding to its reference count. This breaks ownership cycles that would leak memory.

quiz.q: When does a shared_ptr's object get deleted?
options: at scope end of the first pointer
when the last shared_ptr owning it is destroyed or reset
quiz.why: A shared_ptr keeps a reference count. The object is deleted when the count drops to 0, i.e. the last owning shared_ptr is destroyed or reset.

options: use RAII members so you write no special member functions
quiz.why: The rule of zero says: let members like vectors and smart pointers manage resources. Then you need not write a destructor, copy or move operations yourself.

quiz.q: T&& in a parameter usually means
quiz.why: In a function parameter, T&& usually denotes an rvalue reference, which binds to temporaries and enables move semantics. In a deduced template it can be a forwarding reference.

questions.q: Which operator must be overloaded as a non-member to support `cout << obj`?
questions.why: For cout << obj, the left operand is an ostream, which you cannot modify. So operator<< must be a non-member function.

questions.q: Which cannot be overloaded in C++?
questions.why: The ternary conditional operator ?: cannot be overloaded in C++, whereas ==, -> and () can.

questions.q: template<class T> T sq(T x){return x*x;} sq(3) + sq(1.5) =
questions.why: sq(3) with T = int gives 9, and sq(1.5) with T = double gives 2.25. The sum is 11.25.

questions.q: Container giving sorted unique keys with O(log n) insert
questions.why: std::set stores unique keys in sorted order, typically using a balanced BST, so insertion is O(log n). unordered_set is not sorted.

questions.q: vector<int> v{1,2,3}; v.push_back(4); auto it = v.begin(); v.push_back(5); *it is
questions.why: push_back can reallocate the vector's storage when capacity is exceeded. Then old iterators (like it) are invalidated, and using *it is undefined behaviour.

questions.q: Assertion: std::sort needs a strict weak ordering. Reason: using <= can make sort read out of bounds or misbehave.
questions.why: std::sort requires a strict weak ordering, so comparisons like < work but <= can return true for equal elements. That breaks the algorithm's assumptions and may crash or misorder, so the reason explains the assertion.

questions.q: use_count after: auto a=make_shared<int>(1); auto b=a; auto c=a; b.reset();
questions.why: The pointers a, b and c share ownership, so the count is 3. b.reset() releases one, so a and c remain, giving 2.

questions.q: Case: a tree node holds shared_ptr to children and to its parent. Memory is never freed. Fix
options: make the parent link a weak_ptr
questions.why: A parent and child holding shared_ptr to each other form a cycle, so counts never reach 0. Making the parent link a weak_ptr breaks the cycle without owning.

questions.q: Return type of a well-written operator=
questions.why: operator= returns T& (a reference to *this), so assignments can chain like a = b = c without copying.

questions.q: `std::move(x)` itself
options: only casts x to an rvalue
questions.why: std::move does not move anything. It only casts its argument to an rvalue, so that a move constructor or assignment can be chosen to do the move.

questions.q: Best STL container for FIFO processing
questions.why: std::queue (usually built on deque) gives first-in, first-out processing. A stack is last-in, first-out, and map and set are ordered containers.

questions.q: Which runs in O(n) on a vector?
questions.why: std::find scans elements one by one, so it is O(n). binary_search and lower_bound are O(log n) on sorted data, and sort is O(n log n).

questions.q: Template specialisation lets you
options: provide a custom implementation for a specific type
questions.why: Template specialisation gives a different implementation for a specific type, as std::vector<bool> does to pack bits.

questions.q: A friend function of class X is
options: a non-member with access to X's private members
questions.why: A friend function is not a member of the class, but it is granted access to its private members. Friendship is not inherited.

questions.q: Prefix ++ is generally preferred for iterators because
options: it avoids creating a temporary copy
questions.why: Postfix ++ must return a copy of the old value, creating a temporary. Prefix ++ just increments and returns a reference, so it is cheaper for iterators.

questions.q: make_unique<T>() was introduced in
questions.why: make_shared came with C++11, but make_unique was added in C++14.

questions.q: Average insertion into std::unordered_map
questions.why: unordered_map uses hashing, so average insertion is O(1). Many collisions can make it O(n) in the worst case.

courses.title: Unit 4 · Java Essentials: Strings, Packages and Exception Handling
courses.summary: The Java platform (JDK, JRE, JVM, bytecode), primitive vs reference types and wrapper classes, String immutability, StringBuilder, equals vs ==, packages and access, and exception handling with checked vs unchecked exceptions, finally, try-with-resources and custom exceptions.
outcomes: Learners can explain how Java source becomes bytecode and runs on the JVM
Learners can use String, StringBuilder and equals correctly
Learners can organise classes into packages with correct access
Learners can design exception handling with checked, unchecked and custom exceptions

scenes.text: Asha writes a Java program on Windows; her teammate runs the same .class file on a Linux server.
Both machines have a JVM that understands the same bytecode.

steps.title: JDK, JRE, JVM
steps.body:
- `javac Main.java` → **bytecode** `Main.class`.
- The **JVM** loads, verifies and runs bytecode (interpreter + **JIT** compiler for hot code).
- JRE = JVM + standard libraries; JDK = JRE + tools (javac, jar, javadoc, jdb).

steps.title: Primitive vs reference
steps.body:
- 8 primitives: byte (1), short (2), int (4), long (8), float (4), double (8), char (2, UTF-16), boolean.
- Everything else is a reference to a heap object.
- Java is **pass-by-value** always: for objects, the reference is copied (so the method can mutate the object but not rebind the caller's variable).
- Wrappers: Integer, Double…; autoboxing converts automatically.

steps.title: Solved example: Integer cache trap
steps.body:
```
Integer a = 127, b = 127;  a == b  → true (cached −128..127)
Integer c = 128, d = 128;  c == d  → false (different objects)
c.equals(d) → true
```
Always compare wrapper values with **equals** (or unbox).

steps.title: Solved example: pass-by-value
steps.body:
```
static void f(int[] a){ a[0] = 9; a = new int[]{7}; }
int[] x = {1}; f(x); // x[0] is 9
```
The method changed the shared array, but reassigning `a` did not affect `x`.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying Java passes objects by reference.
- Integer division: 5/2 = 2; use 5/2.0.
- char arithmetic: 'a' + 1 is the int 98, not 'b' (cast back with (char)).

activity.prompt: Read two integers a and b (in the range −1000..1000). Box them into Integer objects with Integer.valueOf, and print two lines: the result of (x == y) and of x.equals(y).
activity.hint: valueOf caches −128..127 by default.

quiz.why: javac compiles Java source into platform-independent bytecode (.class files). The JVM then runs it.
Java fixes the size of primitives. An int is always 4 bytes (32 bits), whatever the platform.
Java always passes by value. For objects, the value copied is the reference, so the method can change the object but cannot change which object the caller's variable refers to.
A Java char is a 16-bit UTF-16 code unit, which is 2 bytes. C's char is 1 byte.

options: compiles hot bytecode to native code at run time
quiz.why: The just-in-time compiler translates frequently executed bytecode into native machine code at run time. That makes it much faster.

scenes.text: A report generator builds a 50,000-line string with += in a loop and takes a minute.
Switching to StringBuilder makes it finish in milliseconds.

steps.title: Immutability
steps.body:
`String` objects never change; methods like `toUpperCase()` return new strings.
- Literals are interned in the **string pool**: `"hi" == "hi"` is true, but `new String("hi") == "hi"` is false.
- Compare content with `equals` / `equalsIgnoreCase`; order with `compareTo`.

steps.title: StringBuilder
steps.body:
Mutable, not synchronised (StringBuffer is the synchronised legacy version). `append`, `insert`, `reverse`, `deleteCharAt`, `toString`.
- s += x in a loop of n iterations copies O(n²) characters in total; StringBuilder is amortised O(n).

steps.title: equals and hashCode contract
steps.body:
If you override `equals`, override `hashCode` too: equal objects **must** have equal hash codes, or HashMap/HashSet will misbehave.
- `Objects.equals(a, b)` and `Objects.hash(f1, f2)` help.
- Java 16+ **records** generate both automatically.

steps.title: Solved example: palindrome check
steps.body:
"Madam" → lower case "madam" → `new StringBuilder(s).reverse().toString()` = "madam" → equals → **palindrome**.

"Java" reversed = "avaJ" → not a palindrome.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using == to compare strings read from input (they are not pooled).
- Forgetting that `s.toUpperCase();` alone does nothing (result discarded).
- Overriding `equals(Student s)` instead of `equals(Object o)` — that is overloading, not overriding.

activity.prompt: Read n words. For each, print YES if it is a palindrome ignoring case, else NO. Use StringBuilder.reverse and equalsIgnoreCase.
activity.hint: equalsIgnoreCase compares content without case.

quiz.why: A Java String cannot be changed after creation. Methods like toUpperCase return a new String.

quiz.q: Best way to build a long string in a loop
quiz.why: Since Strings are immutable, += in a loop creates a new string every time, which costs O(n²). StringBuilder appends in place.
new String("a") creates a new object on the heap, whereas the literal "a" refers to the pooled one. == compares references, so the result is false.
The equals/hashCode contract says equal objects must have equal hash codes. Otherwise hash-based collections would fail to find them.
Object.equals takes an Object parameter. A method equals(Student) has a different signature, so it overloads rather than overrides.

scenes.text: A fee-payment form crashes when a student types 'abc' in the amount box, showing a stack trace.
Catching NumberFormatException and showing a friendly message keeps the app running.

steps.title: Hierarchy
steps.body:
Throwable → **Error** (serious, e.g. OutOfMemoryError — don't catch) and **Exception**.
- **Checked** exceptions (IOException, SQLException…): must be caught or declared with `throws`.
- **Unchecked** (RuntimeException subclasses: NullPointerException, ArithmeticException, ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException, NumberFormatException, IllegalArgumentException): not enforced by the compiler.

steps.title: try / catch / finally
steps.body:
```
try { risky(); }
catch (NumberFormatException e) { … }
catch (IOException | SQLException e) { … }   // multi-catch
finally { cleanup(); }                         // always runs
```
- Catch more specific types first.
- `throw new IllegalArgumentException("…")` to signal; `throws X` in the signature to propagate.
- **try-with-resources** closes AutoCloseable resources automatically.

steps.title: Solved example: control flow
Custom exceptions and C++ comparison
steps.body:
`class InsufficientFundsException extends Exception { InsufficientFundsException(String m){ super(m); } }` (checked) or extend RuntimeException (unchecked).

C++: `try { throw std::runtime_error("x"); } catch (const std::exception& e) { … }` — no checked exceptions; destructors run during stack unwinding (RAII).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Empty catch blocks that swallow errors.
- Catching Exception before a more specific type (compile error: unreachable).
- Returning from finally (it overrides the try's return or exception).

activity.prompt: Read q lines, each with two tokens a and b. Try to parse both as int and print a/b. On NumberFormatException print `BAD INPUT`; on ArithmeticException print `DIVIDE BY ZERO`. After all lines, print `DONE` (from a finally block of an outer try).

tests.expect:
5
DIVIDE BY ZERO
BAD INPUT
DONE

activity.hint: Each pair gets its own inner try.

quiz.why: IOException is a checked exception. The compiler requires it to be caught or declared with throws.
NullPointerException extends RuntimeException, so it is unchecked. The compiler does not force you to handle it.

options: whether or not an exception occurs (normally)
quiz.why: A finally block runs whether or not an exception occurs, for cleanup. (It would not run if the JVM exits or the thread is killed.)
Java floating-point division follows IEEE 754. So 5.0 / 0 gives Infinity, not an exception. Integer division by zero throws ArithmeticException.

quiz.q: try-with-resources requires the resource to implement
quiz.why: try-with-resources requires the resource to implement AutoCloseable, so close() is called automatically at the end of the block.

scenes.text: A hackathon team merges code and finds two classes named User — one for auth, one for analytics.
Packages com.team.auth and com.team.analytics give each its own namespace.

steps.title: Packages
steps.body:
- `package com.college.fees;` must be the first statement; the folder path must match (com/college/fees/).
- `import java.util.List;` or `import java.util.*;` (no sub-packages).
- java.lang is imported automatically.
- Fully qualified names resolve clashes: `java.util.Date` vs `java.sql.Date`.

steps.title: Access table
steps.body:
| Modifier | Class | Package | Subclass (other pkg) | World |
- private: ✔ ✗ ✗ ✗
- default: ✔ ✔ ✗ ✗
- protected: ✔ ✔ ✔ ✗
- public: ✔ ✔ ✔ ✔

A file can hold one public top-level class, named after the file.

steps.title: Solved example
steps.body: Class `Fee` in package a has a default-access method `calc()`. Class `Report` in package b imports a.Fee and calls `calc()` → **compile error** (not visible outside package a). Making it `public` or moving Report to package a fixes it.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Folder structure not matching the package name.
- Expecting `import java.awt.*` to import java.awt.event classes.
- Two public classes in one file.

activity.prompt: Where is a member visible? Sort each case into the right bucket.

items.text: private field, accessed from the same class
private field, accessed from another class in the same package
default method, accessed from the same package
default method, accessed from a subclass in another package
protected method, accessed from a subclass in another package
protected method, accessed from an unrelated class in another package

quiz.why: java.lang is imported automatically. It holds basic classes like String, Math and System.
import java.util.* imports classes directly in java.util, but not those in sub-packages like java.util.function. They need their own import.
In Java, protected members are visible within the same package and to subclasses, even in other packages.

quiz.q: How many public top-level classes per .java file?
quiz.why: A Java source file can have at most one public top-level class, and the file must be named after it.

options: the first statement in the file
quiz.why: If present, the package statement must come first in the file, before imports. Only comments may appear before it.

questions.q: The JVM executes
questions.why: The JVM executes bytecode, not source. This lets the same compiled class run on any platform with a JVM.

questions.q: Output: String a="hi"; String b="hi"; System.out.println(a==b);
questions.why: Both literals "hi" refer to the same pooled String object, so == compares equal references and gives true.

questions.q: Output: String s="abc"; s.toUpperCase(); System.out.println(s);
questions.why: Strings are immutable. s.toUpperCase() returns a new string, which is discarded, so s is still abc.

questions.q: Output: System.out.println(1 + 2 + "3" + 4 + 5);
questions.why: Evaluate left to right: 1 + 2 = 3 as ints, then 3 + "3" = "33", then "334", then "3345".

questions.q: Which is unchecked?
questions.why: ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException extends RuntimeException, so it is unchecked. The others are checked exceptions.

questions.q: Assertion: catch(Exception e) before catch(IOException e) fails to compile. Reason: the second catch becomes unreachable.
questions.why: catch(Exception) already catches IOException. A later catch(IOException) could never run, so Java reports an error. Put the specific one first.

questions.q: Output: try{ throw new RuntimeException(); } catch(Exception e){ System.out.print("C"); } finally { System.out.print("F"); }
questions.why: The RuntimeException is caught by catch(Exception), printing C. The finally block then always runs, printing F. So CF.

questions.q: Value returned by: int f(){ try{ return 1; } finally { return 2; } }
questions.why: A return in finally overrides the earlier return, so the method returns 2. This is bad practice.

questions.q: Case: a method reads a config file and the caller should decide what to do if it is missing. Best design
questions.why: If the caller should decide what to do when the file is missing, declare throws IOException. The checked exception forces the caller to deal with it.

questions.q: Output: Integer a=1000, b=1000; System.out.println(a.equals(b) + " " + (a==b));
questions.why: Integer caches only small values (−128 to 127). 1000 creates two objects, so equals gives true but == compares references and gives false.

questions.q: char c='A'; System.out.println(c + 1);
questions.why: c + 1 promotes the char to an int, 65 + 1 = 66. So it prints 66, not B.

questions.q: Which statement about StringBuilder is true?
options: it is mutable and not synchronised
questions.why: StringBuilder is mutable and not synchronised, so it is fast but not thread-safe. StringBuffer is the synchronised one.

questions.q: Overriding equals without hashCode breaks
questions.why: HashMap and HashSet use hashCode to find a bucket. If equals is overridden without hashCode, equal objects can have different hashes and lookups fail.

questions.q: A default-access class member is visible to a subclass in another package?
questions.why: Default (package-private) access allows only classes in the same package. A subclass in another package cannot see it.

questions.q: OutOfMemoryError is
questions.why: OutOfMemoryError is an Error, a serious JVM problem. It is usually not caught because there is little the program can do.

questions.q: Output: int[] a={1,2}; change(a); where change does a=new int[]{9,9}; then print a[0]
questions.why: Java passes the reference by value. Inside change, reassigning the parameter a only changes the local copy, so the caller's array is unchanged and a[0] is 1.

questions.q: In C++, during stack unwinding after a throw
questions.why: When an exception is thrown in C++, the stack unwinds and destructors of local objects run. This is why RAII is safe. C++ has no finally block.

courses.title: Unit 5 · Java Collections, Generics, Lambdas and Multithreading
courses.summary: The Collections Framework (List, Set, Map, Queue and their implementations), generics and wildcards, Comparable and Comparator, lambdas and streams, and multithreading basics: threads, Runnable, synchronisation, race conditions and executors.
outcomes: Learners can pick the right collection implementation and state its complexities
Learners can write generic methods and sort with Comparator chains
Learners can transform data with lambdas and streams
Learners can create threads, detect race conditions and fix them with synchronisation

scenes.text: An attendance system stores roll numbers in an ArrayList and checks presence with contains() — slow for 10,000 students.
Switching to a HashSet makes each check almost instant.

steps.title: Interfaces and implementations
steps.body:
- **List** (ordered, duplicates): ArrayList (array, O(1) get), LinkedList (O(1) at ends).
- **Set** (no duplicates): HashSet (O(1) avg, no order), LinkedHashSet (insertion order), TreeSet (sorted, O(log n)).
- **Map** (key→value): HashMap, LinkedHashMap, TreeMap.
- **Queue/Deque**: ArrayDeque (stack or queue), PriorityQueue (min-heap).

steps.title: Solved example: pick the collection
steps.body:
- Unique visitors, fast lookup → **HashSet**.
- Leaderboard sorted by name → **TreeMap<String,Integer>**.
- Undo stack → **ArrayDeque** (push/pop).
- Keep insertion order, no duplicates → **LinkedHashSet**.
- Task scheduler by priority → **PriorityQueue**.

steps.title: Iteration
steps.body:
- for-each loop, Iterator (`it.remove()` is the safe way to delete during iteration).
- Modifying a collection inside a for-each → **ConcurrentModificationException**.
- `removeIf(x -> x < 0)` is the modern alternative.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- `list.remove(1)` on a List<Integer> removes index 1, not the value 1 (use `remove(Integer.valueOf(1))`).
- Using a mutable object as a HashMap key and then changing it.
- Choosing LinkedList for random access (get(i) is O(n)).

activity.prompt: Read n words. Print the distinct words in order of first appearance (space separated) on line 1, and in sorted order on line 2. Use LinkedHashSet and TreeSet.

tests.stdin:
6
pear apple pear kiwi apple fig
tests.expect:
pear apple kiwi fig
apple fig kiwi pear

activity.hint: String.join works on any Iterable<String>.

quiz.why: HashSet uses hashing, so membership tests are O(1) on average. It does not keep order. Lists need O(n) scans and TreeSet is O(log n).
A TreeMap keeps its keys sorted, using a red-black tree.

quiz.q: Deleting during a for-each loop causes
quiz.why: Removing from a list while iterating it with for-each makes the fail-fast iterator throw ConcurrentModificationException. Use Iterator.remove() instead.
On a List<Integer>, remove(1) chooses remove(int index), so it removes the element at index 1. Use remove(Integer.valueOf(1)) to remove the value.

quiz.q: Recommended stack class in modern Java
quiz.why: ArrayDeque is the recommended stack in modern Java. It is faster than Stack, which is a synchronised legacy class built on Vector.

scenes.text: The admissions office sorts applicants by marks (high first), then by age (younger first), then by name.
A Comparator chain expresses all three rules in one line.

steps.title: Generics
steps.body:
- Type-safe containers: `List<String>`; the compiler inserts casts.
- Generic method: `static <T extends Comparable<T>> T max(List<T> xs)`.
- Wildcards: `List<? extends Number>` (read, producer), `List<? super Integer>` (write, consumer) — **PECS**.
- Erasure: at run time `List<String>` and `List<Integer>` are the same class.

steps.title: Comparable vs Comparator
steps.body:
- **Comparable<T>**: natural order inside the class — `int compareTo(T o)`.
- **Comparator<T>**: external order — `Comparator.comparing(Student::marks).reversed().thenComparing(Student::name)`.
- Return negative / zero / positive. Use `Integer.compare(a, b)` instead of `a − b` (overflow).

steps.title: Solved example
steps.body:
Applicants (name, marks): (Ravi, 90), (Asha, 95), (Kiran, 90).
- Sort by marks desc, then name asc → **Asha 95, Kiran 90, Ravi 90**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- `return a.marks - b.marks;` overflows for large values.
- Raw types (`List list = new ArrayList();`) lose type safety.
- compareTo inconsistent with equals in TreeSet (elements considered equal are dropped).

activity.prompt: Read n lines `name marks`. Sort by marks descending, then name ascending, using a Comparator chain, and print `name marks` per line.
activity.hint: comparingInt(...).reversed().thenComparing(...)

quiz.why: Comparable defines a class's natural ordering through compareTo, inside the class itself. Comparator is the external alternative.
PECS means Producer Extends, Consumer Super. Use ? extends T when you only read from a collection and ? super T when you only write into it.

quiz.q: Why prefer Integer.compare(a, b) over a − b?
quiz.why: a − b can overflow for large values and give the wrong sign. Integer.compare handles all values correctly.

quiz.q: At run time, List<String>.class and List<Integer>.class are
quiz.why: Type erasure removes the generic type arguments at compile time. So at run time, List<String> and List<Integer> are the same class.
reversed() flips the comparator's order. So sorting by f ends up in descending order.

scenes.text: A report filters paid orders, extracts amounts, and sums them in a 20-line loop with flags.
A three-line stream pipeline says the same thing and is easier to verify.

steps.title: Lambdas
steps.body:
A lambda implements a **functional interface** (one abstract method): `Predicate<T>`, `Function<T,R>`, `Consumer<T>`, `Supplier<T>`, `Comparator<T>`, `Runnable`.
- `x -> x * x`, `(a, b) -> a + b`, method references `String::length`, `System.out::println`.
- Captured local variables must be effectively final.

steps.title: Streams
steps.body:
source → intermediate ops (lazy) → terminal op.
- Intermediate: `filter`, `map`, `sorted`, `distinct`, `limit`.
- Terminal: `forEach`, `collect(Collectors.toList())`, `count`, `sum` (on IntStream), `reduce`, `Collectors.groupingBy`.
- A stream can be consumed only once.

steps.title: Solved example
steps.body:
Numbers 1..10: sum of squares of even numbers.
```
IntStream.rangeClosed(1, 10).filter(x -> x % 2 == 0).map(x -> x * x).sum()
```
4 + 16 + 36 + 64 + 100 = **220**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Expecting intermediate operations to run without a terminal operation (they are lazy).
- Modifying the source collection inside a stream.
- Using parallel streams for tiny or order-dependent tasks.

activity.prompt: Read n integers. Using a stream, print the sum of squares of the even numbers on line 1, and on line 2 the distinct odd numbers sorted ascending, space separated (empty line if none).
activity.hint: Collectors.joining(" ") builds the second line.

quiz.why: A functional interface has exactly one abstract method. This lets a lambda or method reference implement it.
Intermediate stream operations such as map and filter are lazy. Nothing runs until a terminal operation like collect or forEach.
Function<T,R> has apply(T), taking a T and returning an R, so it is T → R.

quiz.q: Sum of squares of even numbers 1..6
quiz.why: The even numbers are 2, 4, 6. Their squares are 4 + 16 + 36 = 56.

quiz.q: A stream can be reused after a terminal operation?
quiz.why: A stream can be consumed only once. Reusing it after a terminal operation throws IllegalStateException.

scenes.text: Two booking threads update the same seat counter; sometimes the count ends lower than the number of tickets sold.
Making the update atomic — synchronized or AtomicInteger — fixes the race condition.

steps.title: Creating threads
steps.body:
- Extend `Thread` and override `run()`, or pass a `Runnable` (lambda) to `new Thread(r)`.
- `start()` creates a new thread (calling `run()` directly does not!). `join()` waits for it to finish.
- States: NEW, RUNNABLE, BLOCKED, WAITING, TIMED_WAITING, TERMINATED.

steps.title: Race conditions
steps.body:
`count++` is read–modify–write: two threads can read the same value and both write value+1, losing an update.
- Fix: `synchronized` method/block (monitor lock), `ReentrantLock`, or `AtomicInteger.incrementAndGet()`.
- `volatile` gives visibility, **not** atomicity of ++.

steps.title: Solved example: deadlock
steps.body:
Thread 1 locks A then waits for B; thread 2 locks B then waits for A → **deadlock**.
Prevention: always acquire locks in a global order (A before B), use timeouts (tryLock), or avoid nested locks.

Coffman conditions: mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no preemption, circular wait.

steps.title: Executors
steps.body: `ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(4); pool.submit(task); pool.shutdown();` — reuse threads instead of creating thousands. `Future<T>` gets results; `CompletableFuture` chains async steps.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling run() instead of start().
- Forgetting join() and printing results before threads finish.
- Synchronising on different lock objects in different threads (no mutual exclusion).

activity.prompt: Read t (threads) and k (increments per thread). Start t threads that each increment a shared AtomicInteger k times, join them all, and print the final value (must be exactly t*k).
activity.hint: join() every thread before printing.

quiz.why: start() creates a new thread that then calls run(). Calling run() directly just runs it on the caller's thread.

quiz.q: count++ on a shared int from many threads is
quiz.why: count++ is read, add, write as separate steps. Two threads can interleave and lose updates, so it is not atomic.

options: visibility, not atomicity of compound actions
quiz.why: volatile makes writes visible to other threads. But it does not make compound actions like count++ atomic, nor does it provide mutual exclusion.

options: acquire locks in a fixed global order
quiz.why: If every thread acquires locks in the same fixed global order, a circular wait cannot form, preventing this kind of deadlock.

options: wait for the thread to finish
quiz.why: t.join() makes the calling thread wait until thread t has finished.

questions.q: Which allows duplicates and keeps order?
questions.why: ArrayList is a List, so it keeps insertion order and allows duplicates. Sets and map keys do not allow duplicates.

questions.q: Time of get(i) on LinkedList
questions.why: A linked list has no index. get(i) must walk i nodes from the head or tail, so it takes O(n).

questions.q: HashMap allows
questions.why: Java's HashMap allows one null key (and many null values). Hashtable and ConcurrentHashMap do not allow null keys.

questions.q: TreeMap get/put complexity
questions.why: TreeMap is a balanced red-black tree, so get and put take O(log n).

questions.q: Output: List<Integer> l=new ArrayList<>(List.of(5,6,7)); l.remove(1); System.out.println(l);
questions.why: l.remove(1) uses remove(int index), removing the element at index 1 (6). The list becomes [5, 7].

questions.q: Assertion: List<Object> is not a supertype of List<String>. Reason: generics are invariant in Java.
questions.why: Java generics are invariant, so List<String> is not a List<Object> even though String is an Object. That is why List<Object> is not a supertype of List<String>.

questions.q: Stream output: Stream.of("a","bb","ccc").map(String::length).reduce(0, Integer::sum)
questions.why: The lengths are 1, 2, 3. Reducing with sum starting at 0 gives 1 + 2 + 3 = 6.

questions.q: Case: two threads increment a shared counter 1000 times each without synchronisation. The final value is
questions.why: count++ is not atomic, so two threads can overwrite each other's updates. The final total is at most 2000 and often less.

questions.q: Which interface does a lambda `() -> System.out.println("hi")` fit?
questions.why: The lambda takes no arguments and returns nothing, which matches Runnable's run().

questions.q: Coffman condition NOT required for deadlock
questions.why: The four Coffman conditions are mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no preemption and circular wait. Starvation is a separate problem, not a required condition.

questions.q: PriorityQueue<Integer> default poll() returns
questions.why: Java's PriorityQueue is a min-heap by natural ordering, so poll() removes the smallest element.

questions.q: What does `synchronized` on an instance method lock?
questions.why: A synchronized instance method locks the monitor of the object (this). Only one thread at a time can run synchronized methods of that object.

questions.q: A static synchronized method locks
questions.why: A static synchronized method locks the Class object, since there is no instance.

questions.q: Calling t.run() instead of t.start()
options: runs the code on the current thread
questions.why: run() is an ordinary method. Calling it directly runs the code on the current thread, with no new thread created.

questions.q: Which collection keeps insertion order and rejects duplicates?
questions.why: LinkedHashSet keeps insertion order and, as a set, rejects duplicates. HashSet loses the order and TreeSet sorts instead.

questions.q: Captured local variables in a lambda must be
questions.why: A lambda can use local variables only if they are final or effectively final (never reassigned). Otherwise there is a compile error.

questions.q: ConcurrentHashMap is preferred over Collections.synchronizedMap because
options: it allows concurrent reads and fine-grained updates
questions.why: ConcurrentHashMap supports concurrent reads and fine-grained locking for updates. synchronizedMap locks the whole map for each operation, which scales worse.

courses.title: Unit 6 · Object-Oriented Design: UML, SOLID and Design Patterns
courses.summary: Modelling with UML class and sequence diagrams, association, aggregation and composition, the SOLID principles, and the most-used design patterns (Singleton, Factory, Strategy, Observer, Decorator, Adapter) in Java and C++.
outcomes: Learners can read and draw UML class diagrams with correct relationships
Learners can spot SOLID violations and refactor them
Learners can implement Strategy, Observer and Factory patterns
Learners can justify when not to use a pattern

scenes.text: Before coding a library system, the team lead asks everyone to sketch the classes on the whiteboard.
Ten minutes of UML reveals that Book and Copy are different classes — saving days of rework.

steps.title: Class diagram notation
steps.body:
Box: name / attributes / methods. Visibility: + public, − private, # protected, ~ package.
- **Association** (line): uses / knows.
- **Aggregation** (hollow diamond): whole–part, parts can live alone (Department ◇— Professor).
- **Composition** (filled diamond): strong ownership, parts die with the whole (House ◆— Room).
- **Generalisation** (hollow triangle): inheritance. **Realisation** (dashed + triangle): implements an interface.
- **Dependency** (dashed arrow): temporary use. Multiplicity: 1, 0..1, *, 1..*.

steps.title: Solved example: library
steps.body:
- Library ◆— 1..* Book (composition if books belong to this catalogue).
- Book ◆— 1..* Copy (copies cannot exist without the title record).
- Member — 0..5 Loan — 1 Copy (association with multiplicity: a member borrows at most 5).
- Librarian ▷ Person, Member ▷ Person (generalisation).

steps.title: Sequence diagrams
steps.body: Show objects as lifelines and messages in time order (top to bottom): Member → Library: borrow(copyId) → Copy: isAvailable() → Loan: create(). Useful to design and explain a use case.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using inheritance where composition fits (Stack extends ArrayList exposes unwanted methods).
- Mixing up aggregation and composition diamonds.
- Drawing every getter/setter — diagrams are for communication, not code dumps.

activity.prompt: Match each relationship to its best example.

quiz.why: A filled diamond in UML shows composition, a strong ownership where the part cannot exist without the whole. A hollow diamond is aggregation.
In UML, − means private, + public, # protected and ~ package.
A solid line with a hollow triangle arrowhead is generalisation, i.e. inheritance (is-a).
0..* means zero or more instances may be related.
A sequence diagram shows the messages that objects send each other, ordered over time.

scenes.text: An Invoice class calculates tax, prints PDFs, emails customers and saves to the database. Every change breaks something.
Splitting it by responsibility — Invoice, TaxCalculator, InvoicePrinter, InvoiceRepository — makes each piece testable.

steps.title: The five principles
steps.body:
- **S**ingle responsibility: one reason to change per class.
- **O**pen/closed: open for extension, closed for modification (add new classes, don't edit old switch statements).
- **L**iskov substitution: subtypes must work wherever the base type is expected.
- **I**nterface segregation: many small interfaces beat one fat one.
- **D**ependency inversion: depend on abstractions; inject dependencies.

steps.title: Solved example: open/closed
steps.body:
Before: `double area(Shape s){ if(s.type==CIRCLE) … else if(s.type==SQUARE) … }` — every new shape edits this method.
After: `interface Shape { double area(); }` with Circle and Square implementing it; new shapes add a class, no edits.

steps.title: Solved example: Liskov
steps.body: Square extends Rectangle with setWidth also setting height. Code that does `r.setWidth(5); r.setHeight(4); assert r.area() == 20;` fails for Square (16) → **LSP violated**. Fix: no inheritance between them; both implement Shape.

steps.title: Dependency inversion in practice
steps.body: `class OrderService { private final PaymentGateway gw; OrderService(PaymentGateway gw){ this.gw = gw; } }` — pass a real gateway in production and a fake one in tests (constructor injection).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Splitting classes so finely that the design becomes hard to follow.
- Using interfaces everywhere 'just in case' (YAGNI).
- Confusing dependency inversion with dependency injection (injection is one technique to achieve inversion).

activity.prompt: Refactor to open/closed: create interface Shape { double area(); } with Circle(r) (use Math.PI), Square(s) and Triangle(b,h). Read n shapes (`C r`, `S s`, `T b h`) and print each area with 2 decimals, one per line.
activity.hint: Interface methods must be implemented as public.

quiz.q: 'A class should have one reason to change' is
quiz.why: The Single Responsibility Principle (S in SOLID) says a class should have only one reason to change.

quiz.q: Square extends Rectangle with coupled setters most directly violates
quiz.why: A Square that extends Rectangle with coupled width/height setters behaves differently from a Rectangle. Code using a Rectangle breaks, so it violates Liskov substitution.

quiz.q: Depending on an interface and injecting the implementation follows
quiz.why: Depending on an interface and injecting the concrete implementation follows the Dependency Inversion Principle: high-level code depends on abstractions.

quiz.q: A fat interface forcing classes to implement unused methods violates
quiz.why: The Interface Segregation Principle says classes should not be forced to implement methods they do not use. Split fat interfaces.

quiz.q: Adding a new shape without editing existing code shows
quiz.why: The Open/Closed Principle says software should be open for extension but closed for modification. A new shape added without editing existing code shows this.

scenes.text: An app reads its configuration once; every module should share the same object.
A legacy SMS library has a different method name from the new Notifier interface — an adapter bridges them.

steps.title: Creational
steps.body:
- **Singleton**: one instance with global access. Java: `enum Config { INSTANCE; }` or a static holder class; C++: function-local static (`static Config& get(){ static Config c; return c; }`, thread-safe since C++11). Use sparingly — it is hidden global state.
- **Factory method / simple factory**: create objects without exposing the concrete class (`Shape s = ShapeFactory.create("circle")`).
- **Builder**: step-by-step construction of complex objects (`new Pizza.Builder().size(12).cheese().build()`).

steps.title: Structural
steps.body:
- **Adapter**: converts one interface into another expected by clients.
- **Decorator**: wraps an object to add behaviour dynamically (Java I/O: `new BufferedReader(new InputStreamReader(in))`).
- **Facade**: a simple front for a complex subsystem.
- **Composite**: treat individual objects and groups uniformly (files and folders).

steps.title: Solved example: decorator
steps.body:
Coffee cost 50. Decorators: Milk +10, Sugar +5.
`new Sugar(new Milk(new Coffee())).cost()` = 50 + 10 + 5 = **65**, description "Coffee, Milk, Sugar". New add-ons need new classes only (open/closed).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Double-checked locking singletons without `volatile` in Java (broken).
- Using a pattern where a plain function would do.
- Confusing Adapter (changes interface) with Decorator (same interface, added behaviour).

activity.prompt: Implement the decorator pattern: abstract Beverage {cost(), desc()}, Coffee (50, "Coffee"), and decorators Milk (+10, ", Milk") and Sugar (+5, ", Sugar") that wrap a unique_ptr<Beverage>. Read a sequence of add-ons (M or S) terminated by X, wrap in order, and print `<desc> = <cost>`.
activity.hint: Each decorator holds the wrapped beverage and adds to its cost.

quiz.q: Java I/O stream wrapping (BufferedReader around a Reader) is an example of
quiz.why: BufferedReader wraps a Reader and adds buffering while keeping the same interface. That is the Decorator pattern.

quiz.q: Converting an old API to a new interface uses
quiz.why: The Adapter pattern wraps an existing API and translates it to the interface that clients expect.
In C++11, a function-local static is initialised once and thread-safely. That makes a simple lazy singleton.

quiz.q: Files and folders treated uniformly is
quiz.why: The Composite pattern treats single objects (files) and groups (folders) through one common interface, forming a tree.
The Builder pattern builds complex objects step by step. It is best when a class has many optional parameters, avoiding huge constructors.

scenes.text: An e-commerce checkout needs festive, student and no-discount rules that marketing changes every month.
When an order ships, the SMS, email and analytics modules must all be told — without the order class knowing about them.

steps.title: Strategy
steps.body:
Define a family of algorithms behind one interface and swap them at run time.
`interface Discount { int apply(int amt); }` → `Festive` (20% off), `Student` (10% off), `NoDiscount`. The checkout holds a Discount and calls apply(). In Java 8+ a lambda can be the strategy.

steps.title: Observer
steps.body:
A **subject** keeps a list of **observers** and notifies them on state change (publish–subscribe). Loose coupling: the subject knows only the Observer interface.
Used in GUI event listeners, MVC, reactive streams.

steps.title: Solved example
steps.body:
Amount 1000:
- Festive → 800, Student → 900, None → 1000.
Order shipped with observers [Sms, Email]: notify() calls Sms.update("shipped") then Email.update("shipped") in registration order.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Long if-else chains on a type code instead of a strategy.
- Observers that are never unregistered (memory leaks in long-running apps).
- Notifying observers while iterating and allowing them to modify the list (ConcurrentModificationException).

activity.prompt: Implement Strategy: interface Discount { int apply(int amt); } with FESTIVE (20% off, integer), STUDENT (10% off) and NONE. Read q lines `<TYPE> <amount>` and print the final amount for each, choosing the strategy from a Map<String, Discount> built with lambdas.

quiz.q: Swapping algorithms at run time behind one interface is
quiz.why: The Strategy pattern puts interchangeable algorithms behind one interface so one can be swapped at run time.

quiz.q: GUI button listeners are an example of
quiz.why: Button listeners register interest in an event and are notified when it happens. That is the Observer pattern.

quiz.q: In Observer, the subject depends on
quiz.why: The subject only knows the Observer interface, not concrete observer classes. That gives loose coupling.

quiz.q: A lambda can implement a strategy when the interface is
quiz.why: A lambda implements an interface with exactly one abstract method (a functional interface). So a strategy given as such an interface can be a lambda.
If observers are never unregistered, the subject keeps references to them, preventing garbage collection (a leak) and causing unwanted notifications.

questions.q: Composition differs from aggregation because
questions.why: In composition, the parts' lifetime is tied to the whole and they cannot outlive it. In aggregation, parts can exist independently and be shared.

questions.q: UML '#' visibility
questions.why: In UML, # marks protected visibility.

questions.q: Which SOLID principle says 'depend on abstractions, not concretions'?
questions.why: The Dependency Inversion Principle says to depend on abstractions rather than concrete classes.

questions.q: Case: a ReportService has methods for SQL queries, PDF rendering and SMTP sending. Main violation
questions.why: The class has three jobs: database access, PDF creation and email. It has several reasons to change, which violates the Single Responsibility Principle.

questions.q: Case: Bird interface has fly(); Ostrich implements it by throwing. Best refactor
options: split into Bird and FlyingBird interfaces
questions.why: Forcing Ostrich to implement fly() by throwing breaks substitution and forces unused methods. Splitting into Bird and FlyingBird lets only flying birds have fly().

questions.q: Assertion: Decorator follows open/closed. Reason: new behaviours are added by new wrapper classes without modifying existing ones.
questions.why: Decorators add new behaviour through new wrapper classes, without editing existing classes. That follows the open/closed principle, so the reason explains the assertion.

questions.q: Pattern that provides a simplified interface to a complex subsystem
questions.why: A Facade offers a simple interface that hides the complexity of a subsystem.

questions.q: Java enum singleton advantage
questions.why: An enum singleton is created once by the JVM. It is safe against multiple instances from serialisation and reflection.

questions.q: Decorators Milk(+10) and Sugar(+5) on Coffee(50), applied as Milk(Milk(Sugar(Coffee)))
questions.why: Each Milk adds 10 and Sugar adds 5 on the base 50. Milk(Milk(Sugar(Coffee))) costs 50 + 5 + 10 + 10 = 75.

questions.q: MVC's view updating when the model changes typically uses
questions.why: In MVC, views register with the model. When the model changes, it notifies them, which is the Observer pattern.

questions.q: Which is a creational pattern?
questions.why: The Factory Method pattern is creational because it deals with creating objects. Adapter is structural and Observer and Strategy are behavioural.

questions.q: Prefer composition over inheritance mainly because
options: it reduces coupling and allows behaviour change at run time
questions.why: Composition builds behaviour from parts and can be changed at run time. Inheritance couples subclass to base class tightly, so composition is favoured for flexibility.

questions.q: A Proxy pattern object
options: controls access to another object with the same interface
questions.why: A Proxy has the same interface as the real object and controls access to it, for example for lazy loading or permission checks.

questions.q: Double-checked locking singleton in Java needs the instance field to be
questions.why: In double-checked locking, without volatile another thread could see a partly constructed object because of instruction reordering. volatile prevents that.

questions.q: Strategy vs State pattern: State differs because
options: the object changes its own strategy as its internal state changes
questions.why: In State, the object itself changes its behaviour object as its internal state changes. In Strategy, the client chooses the algorithm from outside.

questions.q: UML dashed line with hollow triangle
questions.why: In UML, a dashed line with a hollow triangle shows realisation, i.e. a class implementing an interface. A solid line would be generalisation.

questions.q: Festive discount 20% on 1000 using strategy gives
questions.why: A 20% discount on 1000 is 200. The price is 1000 − 200 = 800.

courses.title: OOP in Java and C++ · Revision & Practice
courses.summary: A side-by-side C++ vs Java cheat sheet, an output-prediction drill, a design drill, and two mixed mock papers in the course exam.
outcomes: Learners can compare C++ and Java OOP features precisely
Learners can predict outputs involving constructors, virtual calls and exceptions
Learners can apply SOLID and patterns in short design questions

scenes.text: In her OOP lab viva, Shreya is asked ten 'C++ vs Java' questions in five minutes.
She had made a comparison table the night before and answers every one.

steps.title: Language model
steps.body:
- C++: compiled to native code; objects on stack or heap; manual/RAII memory; multiple inheritance; operator overloading; templates (code generation).
- Java: bytecode on JVM; objects on heap; garbage collection; single class inheritance + interfaces; no operator overloading (except + on String); generics (erasure).

steps.title: Polymorphism
steps.body:
- C++: `virtual` needed; `override`, `final`; pure virtual `= 0`; virtual destructor for polymorphic bases.
- Java: methods virtual by default (not static/private/final); `abstract`; `@Override`; interfaces with default methods.

steps.title: Errors and resources
steps.body:
- C++: exceptions unchecked; RAII destructors during unwinding; smart pointers.
- Java: checked vs unchecked exceptions; finally; try-with-resources (AutoCloseable).

steps.title: Access
steps.body:
- C++: private / protected / public; `friend`; class default private, struct default public.
- Java: private / default (package) / protected / public.

steps.title: Top viva traps
steps.body: - 'Java is pass-by-reference' ✗ · 'Overloading = overriding' ✗ · 'Abstract classes can't have constructors' ✗ · 'Static methods can be overridden' ✗ · 'struct can't have methods in C++' ✗

statements.s: Java supports operator overloading for user classes.
In C++, a function must be declared virtual to be dispatched dynamically.
Java abstract classes can have constructors.
A C++ struct can have member functions and constructors.
statements.why: Only default access differs from class.

statements.s: Java static methods can be overridden.
C++ templates use type erasure like Java generics.

quiz.why: Java has checked exceptions, enforced by the compiler. C++ has no checked exceptions.

quiz.q: Multiple class inheritance is allowed in
quiz.why: C++ allows a class to inherit from several classes. Java allows only one superclass and uses interfaces for multiple inheritance of type.

quiz.q: Deterministic destruction at scope end is a feature of
quiz.why: C++ destroys local objects at the end of scope, running the destructor immediately (RAII). Java uses garbage collection at an unspecified time.

quiz.q: Default member access in a C++ struct
quiz.why: In C++, struct members are public by default. This is the only difference from class, where they are private.
Java generics cannot take primitive types, so List<int> is invalid. Use the wrapper List<Integer>.

scenes.text: A senior trains juniors by asking them to predict output before running any snippet.
Within a month, they spot construction-order and virtual-call bugs on sight.

steps.title: Snippet 1 (C++)
Snippet 2 (Java)
Snippet 3 (Java)
Patterns to remember
steps.body:
- Constructors: base → derived; destructors reverse.
- Virtual calls inside constructors use the class being constructed (C++); Java calls the overridden version (danger: fields not initialised yet).
- Static = declared type; instance = runtime type.

activity.prompt: Reproduce Snippet 2: classes P and C with static s() and instance i() printing as shown. In main, do `P p = new C(); p.s(); p.i();` and then print a newline. Expected output: `Ps Ci `.
activity.starter:
// classes P and C
public class Main{ public static void main(String[] a){ P p = new C(); p.s(); p.i(); System.out.println(); } }
activity.hint: Calling a static method through an instance uses the declared type.

quiz.q: C++: virtual call inside base constructor dispatches to
quiz.why: While the base constructor runs, the object is still only a base object. So a virtual call there goes to the base version.

quiz.q: Java: p.s() where s is static and p is declared P
quiz.why: Static methods are bound at compile time using the declared type of the reference. So p.s() calls P.s(), not C.s().

quiz.q: Java: p.i() where i is overridden in C and p refers to a C
quiz.why: Instance methods are dispatched on the actual object at run time. Since p refers to a C, the overridden C.i() runs.

quiz.q: Output of try{print T; throw}catch{print C}finally{print F}
quiz.why: Print T, then throw is caught, so C prints, and finally always runs and prints F. Output T C F.

scenes.text: The end-sem paper asks: 'Design classes for a parking lot.' Many students write only code.
Top scorers draw a quick UML diagram, name the patterns used and justify each relationship.

steps.title: Design answer template
steps.body:
1. List nouns → candidate classes; verbs → methods.
2. Draw a class diagram with relationships and multiplicities.
3. Identify variation points → interfaces/strategies.
4. Mention SOLID checks and any pattern (Factory for vehicle creation, Strategy for fee calculation, Singleton for the lot — if justified).
5. Give a short code skeleton.

steps.title: Solved sketch: parking lot
steps.body:
- ParkingLot ◆— 1..* Level ◆— 1..* Spot
- Vehicle (abstract) ▷ Car, Bike, Truck; Spot has a size and fits(Vehicle)
- Ticket — 1 Vehicle, 1 Spot, entry time
- FeeStrategy (interface) ▷ HourlyFee, FlatFee — injected into the exit gate (DIP).

steps.title: Avoid
steps.body:
- One giant class doing everything.
- Inheritance for roles that change (a Person who is both Student and TA → use roles/composition).
- Naming patterns without explaining why they help.

activity.prompt: I can…
items: Write a class with constructors, destructor/RAII and static members
Explain virtual dispatch, vtables and slicing
Use abstract classes and interfaces correctly
Use STL and Java collections with the right complexity
Handle exceptions in Java and C++
Apply SOLID and three design patterns

quiz.q: A good first step in a design question
quiz.why: Start a design question by picking out the nouns (candidate classes) and verbs (their behaviour). This finds classes and responsibilities.

quiz.q: Fee rules that change often are best modelled as
quiz.why: Rules that change often should be separate, interchangeable objects behind a Strategy interface. Then you add new rules without editing old code, as open/closed requires.

quiz.q: A person who is both a student and a TA is best modelled with
options: multiple inheritance from Student and TA
quiz.why: A person can take on roles that change over time. Model roles with composition, not inheritance from both Student and TA.

questions.q: Mock A1. Output (C++): struct A{A(){cout<<'a';}~A(){cout<<'b';}}; int main(){A x[2];}
questions.why: Both array elements are constructed first, printing a a. At the end of main they are destroyed in reverse order, printing b b. So aabb.

questions.q: Mock A2. Which enables `Complex c = a + b;` in C++?
questions.why: Overloading operator+ lets you write a + b for your own class, so Complex c = a + b works.

questions.q: Mock A3. Java: String s1 = new String("x"); String s2 = "x"; s1.equals(s2) and s1 == s2
questions.why: equals compares contents, which are both x, so true. == compares references. new String creates a different object, so false.

questions.q: Mock A4. Which is resolved at compile time?
questions.why: Overloading is resolved by the compiler from argument types (compile time). Virtual, interface and abstract method calls are resolved at run time.

questions.q: Mock A5. Assertion: a C++ class with a pure virtual function cannot be instantiated. Reason: it has an incomplete vtable entry that must be provided by a derived class.
questions.why: A class with a pure virtual function is abstract and cannot be instantiated, because that function has no implementation to call. So the reason explains the assertion.

questions.q: Mock A6. Best Java collection for an LRU cache with O(1) operations
questions.why: A LinkedHashMap in access-order mode moves each accessed entry to the end. Overriding removeEldestEntry evicts the least recently used one, all in O(1).

questions.q: Mock A7. Case: two threads update a bank balance; the total sometimes drifts. First fix
options: make the update synchronized or atomic
questions.why: Two threads updating a shared balance without coordination cause a race condition. Making the update synchronized or atomic fixes it.

questions.q: Mock A8. Output (Java): class A{int f(){return 1;}} class B extends A{int f(){return 2;}} A a=new B(); System.out.println(a.f());
questions.why: a is declared as A but refers to a B. The overridden B.f() is chosen at run time, returning 2.

questions.q: Mock B1. In C++, `delete p;` where p is Base* to Derived and ~Base is not virtual
questions.why: Deleting a Derived object through a Base pointer without a virtual destructor is undefined behaviour. Make ~Base virtual.

questions.q: Mock B2. Which pattern adds responsibilities to objects dynamically?
questions.why: The Decorator pattern wraps an object to add responsibilities dynamically while keeping the same interface.

questions.q: Mock B3. Java: which is NOT allowed in an interface (Java 17)?
questions.why: Interfaces cannot hold instance fields with state. Their fields are implicitly public static final constants, though default, static and private methods are allowed.

questions.q: Mock B4. shared_ptr use_count after: auto a=make_shared<int>(1); { auto b=a; auto c=b; }
questions.why: Inside the block, b and c add to the count, but they are destroyed at the closing brace. Only a remains, so use_count is 1.

questions.q: Mock B5. Which violates Liskov substitution?
options: a subclass adding a new method
a subclass with a faster implementation
a subclass method that throws for valid base inputs
questions.why: Subclasses must be usable wherever the base is expected. A method that throws for inputs the base accepts breaks the base contract, violating Liskov substitution.

questions.q: Mock B6. Default ordering of TreeSet<String>
questions.why: TreeSet orders elements by their natural ordering. For Strings that is lexicographic (dictionary) order, via Comparable.

questions.q: Mock B7. Output (C++): Base* p = new Der; p->f(); where f is non-virtual in Base and redefined in Der
questions.why: f is non-virtual, so the call is bound at compile time to the pointer's type Base. So Base::f runs.

questions.q: Mock B8. In Java, finalize() is
options: deprecated and not guaranteed to run
questions.why: finalize() is deprecated and not guaranteed to run at all. Use try-with-resources to release resources reliably.

questions.q: Mock B9. Which statement about C++ templates is true?
options: each used type gets its own instantiation at compile time
they are resolved at run time
they cannot be used with classes
questions.why: C++ templates are instantiated by the compiler for each type used, generating separate code at compile time. They are not resolved at run time.

questions.q: Mock B10. Which is the correct way to give a Java class natural ordering?
questions.why: Implement Comparable<T> and compareTo to define a class's natural order. Comparator is a separate object for other orderings.
